[Explanation]
When a wicked person becomes an official, far from loving the state and its people, he even dares to act capriciously in despising and bullying the people of the world.
[Analysis]

Emperor Taizong of the Tang said: ‘The people are the foundation of the state, and virtue is the foundation of being human; if a person’s virtue is deeply accumulated, then he will be remembered and admired forever, and if the people can live in peace and contentment, then the state will naturally be secure and firm.’ Therefore, if a ruler has deep and generous virtue, then the people will turn to him just as they turn to their own parents! When we observe the sage-kings of ancient and modern times, at home and abroad, they all loved the people and cherished all things, regarding the people as if they were wounded, and caring for the common people as they would care for their own children. How much more should the officials who govern provinces and counties on behalf of the ruler embody this principle!
Story One:

Zheng Qingchen of the Song dynasty was by nature exceedingly cruel and ungrateful. When he served as magistrate of Huaili County, he mistreated the people of the county; and when his term of office ended and he was leaving, the people of Huaili County crowded and blocked the road, and spat and cursed at him. Zheng Qingchen then reported to the court that the people under his jurisdiction had insulted a superior official. Emperor Zhenzong of the Song said: ‘The most important thing in governing is to win the hearts of the people. Since the people have so utterly rejected and rebelled against your administration, then what you did and what you failed to do in Huaili County can be known without even asking! You even dare to complain, reporting to the court that the people insulted you in public — this is indeed brazen and outrageous!’ Zheng Qingchen was therefore convicted by the court and demoted.
Story Two:

In the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, because of the frost damage in autumn, the crops were severely harmed. The emperor, concerned about the disaster, ordered the provinces and counties to investigate the extent of the crop damage within their jurisdictions and report it to the court. But Liu Zao, the magistrate of Weinan County in Shaanxi, reported to the court: ‘The crops in my county have not suffered any damage at all!’ Because reports of damage were coming in from all over while Weinan County alone reported no damage, the emperor became very suspicious and sent someone to investigate. It turned out that the damaged crop area in Weinan County exceeded three thousand qing. When the emperor heard the investigation report, he sighed and said: ‘A magistrate is the parent-official of the people. Even if the county under his jurisdiction had suffered no disaster, he should still have said that it had suffered damage. Magistrate Liu Zao is indeed so inhumane!’ Therefore the emperor convicted Liu Zao and banished him to a far-off place.
When a wicked person becomes an official, not only can he not love the state and its people, he actually disturbs the governance of the state and disrupts the order of society!

A state must nurture the blessings of peace and must not arbitrarily alter its laws and institutions; even when there are projects to be undertaken or reforms to be made, they must be considered with great care and deliberation. If it is merely the private intent of one person to make changes, and he rashly proposes reforms, then with every measure implemented there will be corresponding disturbance and harm. Moreover, the laws and regulations established by the ancestors, which officials at all levels have administered for a very long time, and to which the people have grown accustomed and found convenient — why must they be repeatedly altered, merely to disturb the governance of the state?

When Li Hang of the Song dynasty was chief minister, Ma Liang said to Li Hang: ‘Among the outside world’s criticisms of your administration, many consider that you accomplish nothing.’ Li Hang replied: ‘I have no particular talent for handling the affairs of the state; but among the proposals on the benefits and harms of affairs at home and abroad, whenever the recommendations for change overflow with impatience and agitation, I do not adopt them. The reason I do this is that I wish to replenish the vital energy of the state! Today the laws and regulations of the state may be said to be as many as the hairs on an ox; if I follow their recommendations and implement them one by one, then it will cause much harm to the state and the people!’ Those officials who harbor unkind intentions, wanting to seize the opportunity to distinguish themselves and claim credit — how would they be willing to consider that doing so might disturb the people!

The Tang chief minister Li Linfu promoted the method of the fengqi conscripted cavalry; and the great ministers of the court debated this proposal of Li Linfu, with many taking an opposing stance. But Li Linfu stubbornly insisted on his own opinion, and the defensive strength of the Tang dynasty was never restored after the implementation of the fengqi method. Wang Anshi, the chief minister of the Song dynasty, instituted the new laws, and even stubbornly and hastily enforced them; as a result, he brought great distress to the people, so that the vitality of the Song state was greatly harmed by the implementation of the new laws, and the national strength declined with extreme rapidity. These are all the harmful consequences of disturbing the governance of the state!
To be unable to reward the good and punish the evil, so as to manifest the function of encouraging good and warning against evil, and instead go so far as to reward the unrighteous and wicked.

The principle of rewarding is precisely to honor virtue and repay merit, so ‘reward’ is an important institution of the state and court for encouraging and exhorting the people. To reward what should not be rewarded is called unrighteous. Thus, to go against right and wrong, to abandon the law and discipline, to encourage evil conduct, to be partial and selfish, to employ the wicked and replace the good — these measures most provoke the wrath of Heaven! So those responsible for rank and reward — can they fail to be careful?
Story:

In the Zhou dynasty, Duke Wen of Jin had a close attendant who had followed him in exile and shared his hardships, who said to him: ‘Among the three kinds of rewards you, the king, have conferred, none has been given to me, your humble servant! It must be that I, your humble servant, bear some fault, and so it is that I come to you to beg to be punished.’ Duke Wen of Jin said: ‘He who guides me with benevolence and righteousness, and exhorts me with virtue and kindness, receives my highest reward; he who assists me and helps me succeed in carrying out benevolent governance, receives my middle reward; he who shares my hardships, shedding blood and sweat and being wounded to protect my safety, receives my third reward. As for one who merely serves me with his physical labor and does nothing to help me correct my shortcomings, his reward comes only after the three kinds of reward have been bestowed; so today you will receive this kind of reward.’ When the people of Jin heard Duke Wen of Jin speak and act in this way regarding rewards, they were all overjoyed.
[Further Analysis]

Duke Wen of Jin’s rewards may be said to have been in accord with righteousness, and this was also an important reason why Duke Wen of Jin was able to dominate the feudal lords. If one achieves rewarding in accord with righteousness, then how could there be even the slightest negligence in bestowing a single rank or office, a single thread of silk or a single grain of rice upon the state? In this way, naturally, those who scheme, toady, flatter and send gifts can no longer prevail; while those who uphold the law, fulfill their duties and work seriously will all exhort and encourage one another, and render meritorious service to the state and society.
To inflict punishment upon innocent good people, causing them to bear injustice and suffer wrongs.

The purpose of punishment is to punish and warn the wicked; the sage could not help but establish punishment. Therefore punishment is by nature not auspicious, nor is it a good thing; and when the measure of the punishment and the crime committed by the offender are commensurate, one should still pity and commiserate with them, for they fell into the net of the law because they did not understand the principles. One must not rejoice because a case was solved and a merit was gained, for this may lead to an error in the case! Therefore the ancients were very careful in weighing punishment, and investigated and examined in meticulous detail. If the punishment is inappropriate, causing the innocent to suffer harm, then not only is it an unfair and flawed review of the case, it also violates the gracious intention of Heaven’s love of life! Moreover, the law is explicit that one who kills must die. If today, through one’s own negligence and error, one punishes the innocent, more than one person is killed, and the retribution to be borne by only one person — then how can the principle of a life for a life be made fair? Alas! For this kind of offense, even a normally upright and incorruptible official may, at a time when the case is beset with doubt and suspicion or the evidence is ambiguous, stubbornly insist on his own opinion in deciding the crime, without the humility to investigate carefully; and so end up with lifelong regret and remorse. Moreover, the innocent who were killed will certainly repay wrong with wrong and pursue relentlessly! How much more severe is the retribution for those officials who are careless in reviewing cases! Thinking of this, can one not be afraid?

When Ma Bing served as magistrate of Jiayu County, a river bandit leader with his followers dared to storm into the government office, set a fire, looted the official silver and then made off. The ringleader of these bandits had a very long beard. After the Jiayu County office was plundered, news happened to arrive saying that a boat at Tuanfeng Town was carrying over a dozen people who behaved quite suspiciously, one of whom had a long beard and was likely the bandit leader — but in fact he was not. Ma Bing nevertheless ordered the arrest of this person, and even publicized the breaking of the case. This unfortunate man, wrongly mistaken for the river bandit, was thrown into prison after his arrest and died an unjust death in jail. Later, when Ma Bing was promoted and became a censor, the real bandits were captured by another county office; and the head of that office happened to be a former colleague of Ma Bing, so he did not pursue this wrongful case. Later Ma Bing was promoted again and became chief censor. One time the boat he took happened to pass Tuanfeng Town, and that night they moored there to pass the night. Unexpectedly, that night they were robbed by bandits, and the whole family of Ma Bing was killed by the bandits.

In the past there was an official surnamed Yan who, when serving as governor of Nanjing, was told by someone that a resident of Zhenjiang named Zhou Zhilian was the leader of the bandits. Zhou Zhilian was thus summoned to the Nanjing office and subjected to interrogation and investigation. Zhou Zhilian’s family was wealthy and his life comfortable, and in his heart he greatly feared that the office would subject him to torture to extort a confession, so he found a way to bribe the powerful and influential to speak on his behalf. Therefore Governor Yan became even more suspicious of Zhou Zhilian, and actually had him beaten to death with a staff. Governor Yan later died, having his life taken by the vengeful spirit of Zhou Zhilian.

Governor Yan, suspecting that Zhou Zhilian had bribed [someone] and killing him, seems on the surface to be quite just. However, killing a person who had not committed a capital offense could still turn him into a fierce ghost to take revenge and demand his life. From this case one may know that whoever is an official must not presume that he is impartial and selfless, and can then arbitrarily and recklessly decide to condemn people to death!
Story Three:

Li Guizheng served as a judge and had been deciding cases for a very long time. One day, when he had business to attend to and was going out, passing over Sanjing Bridge, he personally saw more than a dozen people with disheveled hair, shouting loudly: ‘We have been wronged — we were wrongfully killed!’ They gradually approached and pressed upon him. Li Guizheng became extremely frightened, and immediately turned back home. After returning home, he admonished his son, saying: ‘When you study to become an official, never take up the task of hearing cases and judging the guilt of people! I served as a judge, and because I was incorruptible, cautious and fearful, I often followed precedent to pass judgment, and so wrongfully killed so many people. Even though I repent today, it is already too late!’ Not long after, Li Guizheng died.

Even a judge as incorruptible, cautious and fearful as Li Guizheng could make a wrong judgment and kill the wrong person. Then as for those judges who are neither incorruptible, nor cautious, nor fearful — when they see Li Guizheng’s fate, one wonders whether they will be stirred to vigilance!
To intentionally kill persons and take their wealth.

Killing a person to seize the wealth of the dead — such wicked conduct is not necessarily done only by bandits. For example, greedy and corrupt officials, in order to covet wealth that is not rightfully theirs, use the means of punishment to kill suspects in prison. The wealthy and powerful, insatiably greedy, may push those who owe them money — even when these people are reduced to penury and wander in distress — these wealthy families nevertheless, against their conscience, press them to repay within a deadline and even add heavy interest. Cruel and ruthless people, in order to covet wealth, actually take advantage of others’ peril to seize their wealth, without the least concern for others’ lives. Unscrupulous doctors covet wealth, disregard the lives of their patients, and exploit the critical condition of the sick to squeeze money out of them. All these people, because of coveting wealth, conceive the intention to kill and carry out the act of killing! Yet none of those who kill for wealth fails to be killed by a vengeful ghost demanding his life; and the wealth they plundered all turns into nothing in the end!

Along the Yangtze River there was a boatman named Gong Zhuan. Taking advantage of a great wind rising on the river, he pushed a wealthy merchant into the water and drowned him; then he seized the money left on the boat by the merchant. Because of this Gong Zhuan turned into a rich man and settled in Weiyang. Before long, his wife bore him a son; and when this son grew up, for some unknown reason he regarded his father as an enemy. Gong Zhuan was greatly enraged, and went to a temple to inquire of the planchette spirit. The spirit said: ‘In the eighth month of the gengzi year, the west wind was fierce; waves rose in the Yangtze River. Twenty years ago a single mistaken thought — I beg you, sir, to feel your own heart!’ Gong Zhuan was greatly startled, and knew that the wealthy merchant — whom he had pushed into the water and drowned in the Yangtze River twenty years earlier — had already been reborn as his son to take revenge upon him! So Gong Zhuan fled his home in terror, and in the end died an unnatural death.

From this one may know that any wealth obtained through scheming, one definitely cannot rest easy in enjoying it, for it will still be taken over by the resentful foe one has wronged; and what one gains for oneself is twenty years of living in fear and trepidation, and ultimately dying a bad death. Moreover, the judges of the underworld have not yet settled accounts with one; if the reckoning is made in the underworld, the torment would be even more unbearable to hear of!

In the past there was a yamen runner. One early morning he set out from home very early, and as he passed through the desolate wilderness, he was seen by an outsider who carried valuables with him. When this outsider saw the runner approaching with his weapon, he feared the runner might harbor ill intent toward him, so he immediately hid in the grass. The runner was then uncertain, and only heard a rustling sound from the grass; not seeing anyone nearby, he feared that a tiger or leopard might be hiding in the grass. So he thrust his long spear randomly into the grass, and struck the outsider. When he dragged him out of the grass, the man was already dead. The runner then realized that he had killed the man by accident. With no other recourse, he took the valuables the outsider carried, and discarded the corpse in the grass. This matter was never discovered. The runner thereby became rich, and his wife gave birth to a daughter. One day, at his gate, the runner suddenly saw the outsider whom he had accidentally stabbed to death. He immediately shut the gate and hid behind it to peek; the outsider actually entered the home of the cobbler across the street. Before long, the cobbler’s wife bore a son. The runner knew the karmic link and treated the cobbler very well, doting on and loving the cobbler’s son. When his own daughter grew up, he prepared to marry her to the cobbler’s son. The cobbler was overjoyed and asked his son to honor and care for the runner, just as he would his own father. One summer, the weather was very hot, and the runner, having drunk himself tipsy, lay asleep on the bed; his sweat kept seeping out. The cobbler’s son, attending him at his side, took a knife and gently scraped away the sweat on the runner’s body. Because the runner was drunk and befuddled, he felt something moving about on his body, and struck at it with his hand; so the knife went askew and stabbed into the runner’s belly. At that point the runner was not yet dead, so he called his family and told them the truth of the matter, immediately married his daughter to the cobbler’s son, and returned all the family property to him.
To frame others in order to seize their official positions.

Every rank and office in the world, though settled by destiny, can be attained if a subordinate is willing to endeavor to abandon evil and cultivate virtue, for he may be promoted to a very eminent position. An ordinary person so long as he does many good deeds also has a chance of obtaining rank and emolument. But if, in order to advance oneself, one stops at nothing to frame others so as to seize their positions — then because the cycle of cause and effect is clear and Heaven’s justice is manifest, the one who frames others will in the end be framed by others; and the one who seizes others’ positions will in the end have his own position taken away by others. Moreover, the retribution is so swift that it can almost be seen at once!

Mi Dechao, a great minister of the Song dynasty, seeing that the merit and prestige of the Grand Councilor Cao Bin were growing daily more prominent, framed Cao Bin before the emperor as secretly plotting treason and intending to rebel. The emperor, believing the slander of Mi Dechao, dismissed Cao Bin from office and promoted Mi Dechao to the important post of Grand Councilor. Not long after this happened, Chief Minister Zhao Pu did his utmost to defend Cao Bin and clear his name. The emperor finally came to his senses, and banished Mi Dechao to a very far place, while treating Cao Bin with the same honor as before. Seeing this story, is it not all the more clear that to frame others is to frame oneself? And yet such harm is still considered minor! As for Li Linfu, the chief minister of the Tang dynasty, who repeatedly framed others to secure his own position — at that time the marshals of the frontier were all renowned ministers of the court; those with outstanding merit could enter the court and become chief ministers. Li Linfu wanted to block this path to the premiership, so he said to the emperor: ‘Civil officials are timid and dare not resist the invasion of foreign troops; if one employs barbarians to serve as marshals, the barbarians will surely fight to the death to protect the great Tang.’ The emperor, misled, adopted Li Linfu’s suggestion. This led to the rebellion of An Lushan and the great chaos under heaven. This is an example of how the selfish thought of preserving one’s own rank and emolument caused havoc among the people of the world. In the end, Li Linfu was convicted by the court of colluding in treason, and even after death his coffin was opened and his corpse beheaded — a crime he had not committed! Yet because he framed the worthy to secure his own position and thereby employed An Lushan, so the court attached the crime of treason to him — is this not the case freely settled by Heaven in the unseen realm? Alas! One who enjoys the ruler’s salary, and serves as his minister, should repay the ruler and the state; how can he commit such deeds that defy Heaven and reason!
[Words of Worth]

The ancients said: ‘Since one has entrusted oneself to serve the ruler, then this body should no longer be one’s own; so one should think of the ruler and the state in every thought. How can one still attend to one’s own life and family? Would such a minister not be loyal to the state?’ These words of the ancients may truly serve as words of precious advice for the persons mentioned above!
When bandits have already surrendered and submitted, to instead kill them most greatly defies the principle of Heaven.

War is an inauspicious thing; combat is truly perilous, and the sage resorted to arms only when he could not help it. Therefore in ancient times, when many enemies had been killed in war, people would grieve for them and pity them for dying on the battlefield, and the victorious side would even hold funerals for the fallen. As for enemies who surrendered and came over, one should all the more pity, reassure and exhort them. If one kills enemies who have already surrendered and submitted, such a heart is truly too cruel and ruthless, and the evil karma created is also too great; so the calamity one will meet in the future is greater than any other!

Mr. Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty said: ‘A person with a heavy heart of compassion cannot lead troops to fight as a general! Does it mean that being a general is a road to certain death? Not so. If a general can save the people, quell upheaval and bring stability to the state, then being a general has a road to life. Therefore, because one saves the multitudes and kills only when one cannot help it, then no merit is greater than a general’s. Why? Because sacrificing a few lives to save tens of millions of lives is of course different from ordinary acts of virtue. If, in order to accomplish one’s own fame and merit, one uses slaughter to harm living beings, then no guilt is greater than a general’s. Why? Because if one loses a battle one kills many of one’s own troops, and if one wins a battle one kills many of the enemy’s troops; and if military discipline is not strict, one will recklessly slaughter innocent civilians — all of this is the responsibility of the commanding general! Therefore the appointment of a general must not be taken lightly; and the general’s appointment of his subordinates is especially something that must not be taken lightly! The ancients said: “To be a general for three generations is what the Daoists regard as taboo.” However, using killing to put an end to killing is also an unavoidable matter, but can it be done with ease of mind? Therefore in dispatching and employing generals, one must observe the following three prohibitions. First, one fears initiating trouble where there is none, sacrificing the lives of a million soldiers in order to gain for oneself the seal of a feudal lord. Second, one fears replacing violence with even greater violence, slaughtering innocent civilians and cutting off more heads in order to compete for merit. Third, one fears exhausting and bitter fighting between the two armies, each killing many of the other’s troops. Those who personally undertake this combat mission will say: “Killing is up to me — in this way the goal of establishing authority can be achieved!” They will also say: “Killing is done by others — I let them recklessly slaughter and plunder, bluffing and posturing, and then I may take that as my own combat merit!” One should know that the most important thing in the way of a general is to strictly forbid the army to kill; and with strict governance of the troops the soldiers will not be harmed and will be able to accomplish merit in whatever direction they advance. This is the principle of carrying out killing by means of the way of life!’

The great Han general Li Guang, skilled in martial arts and excellent in archery, was greatly feared by the Xiongnu, and so Li Guang was called the Flying General. The great Tang poet Wang Changling wrote a poem on the frontier, praising Li Guang’s valor, saying: ‘The bright moon of Qin and the passes of Han; those who set forth on the ten-thousand-li march have not yet returned. If only the Flying General of Dragon City were here, the barbarian horses would never cross the Yinshan Mountains.’ However, Li Guang’s official fortune was poor: though his military merit was outstanding, he was never able to obtain a noble title. Li Guang once said to the physiognomist Wang Shuo: ‘Since I, Li Guang, joined the army in my youth, in every battle with the Xiongnu I have never failed to be first, risking my life to kill the enemy and win merit. Whenever Han troops pursued the Xiongnu, I always participated. Yet those younger than I who joined the army later have all been enfeoffed; while I alone remain unenfeoffed. What is the reason for this?’ Wang Shuo said: ‘General, please think carefully — in your whole life, is there anything that you have done that makes you feel regret?’ Li Guang replied: ‘I once killed eight hundred surrendered barbarians, and afterward I deeply regretted it.’ Wang Shuo said: ‘No calamity is greater than killing enemies who have already surrendered. This is the reason you cannot be enfeoffed.’ Later, when Li Guang marched against the Xiongnu, he lost his way in the desert, and Li Guang took his own life in despair. His grandson Li Ling also became a general, and in one battle was captured and surrendered to the Xiongnu; and so Li Ling’s family, by imperial decree of the Han emperor, was beheaded in a mass execution.
To demote upright officials and send them away to distant regions; to push out worthy colleagues and strip them of their offices.

Upright men and worthy scholars are the pillars and beams of the state, and so they ought to be given weight and employment; only then will the court be rich in talent, and will those within the realm and without both know of it and stand in awe and watchfulness. But if, out of envy for their ability and integrity, and because they do not walk the same road as oneself, a man devises every means to push them aside and to banish and demote them to distant regions, then the sin of injuring the worthy and poisoning the state is truly too great, too great!

You must know that only when there is a Bo Le in the world does a thousand-li horse appear; the thousand-li horse is always to be found, but a Bo Le is not always to be found. The fortunes of men of talent follow the very same principle. If those who hold power in their hands were all like Bo Le, knowing how to discover talent and how to put it to good use, then a man of moral depth and breadth of mind could be made chancellor; a man of large understanding could be made a remonstrating official; a man of plans and strategy could be entrusted with command of the armies; a man of clean integrity could be given charge of money and grain; a man who loves the people could be made a prefect or a magistrate. In this way every office, great and small, would be filled by a fitting man, and no talent would be left by the wayside; and then the state would surely flourish!

The Ming scholar Yan Maoyou said: ‘Between the man who pushes out and demotes the worthy and the man who embraces and shelters the worthy, the original difference is in truth not great; it is only that both are swayed by the notion of a self. Suppose a man hears of a worthy’s reputation and admires him exceedingly; yet when the worthy comes before him, there are one or two matters he cannot endure, and in the course of time these harden into hatred. Hence it is comparatively easy to embrace a worthy who is far away, but harder to embrace a worthy close at hand; easy to embrace him for a short while, but harder to embrace him for long. Why is this so? Because each one’s temper clashes against the other’s, and each one’s ability grates against the other’s; and because their reputations press upon one another, each is wounded by the other’s influence. Moreover, such worthy men are not necessarily able to reach the stage of an impartial mind and no mark of self; and so, after long dealings with one another, they begin to see each other’s shortcomings. The virtue they once admired they now count as having been mistakenly revered; and today, when they envy the worthy, they rather feel that their own hearts have never swerved—when in truth it is simply that their own measure of mind cannot hold a gentleman. Thus it is that gentlemen meet, and in the end part as enemies; the fault lies exactly here. A man must therefore have, in ordinary days, the discipline of subduing himself and enduring insult, must not seek fame, must not cling to appearances, and must sincerely act for the sake of his country and his people; and toward all slander and all praise alike he must not let the least thing weigh upon his mind. Only thus can he lay up blessings for his descendants and his people!’

Xie Bi of the Song dynasty best understood how to know men. He never lightly promised to recommend anyone, and in all his life those he recommended to the court were no more than a few. Each time he sent a letter of recommendation to the court, he would invariably burn incense and pray, and bowing toward the imperial palace gates he would say, ‘Your old servant has again won a man of talent for Your Majesty!’ Fan Zhongyan and Wang Dan were both men he recommended. When Xie Bi was near the end of his life he was able to bathe and wash himself and burn incense, and then he died sitting upright; and after he had breathed his last, his head did not tilt even a little. Had he not had the power of long discipline, how could such auspicious signs have come about?

In the Spring and Autumn period of the Zhou dynasty, Yan Zi said to Duke Jing of Qi: ‘A state has three inauspicious things, and spirits and goblins are not among them. The first is that the state has worthy men, and the ruler does not know it—this is the first inauspiciousness; the second is that he knows the worthy but does not employ them—this is the second inauspiciousness; and the third is that he employs the worthy but does not trust them—this is the third inauspiciousness.’ This is what is meant by inauspiciousness; so how can upright and worthy men be pushed out and demoted?

Lu Qi of the Tang dynasty greatly disliked Yan Zhenqing, and was forever scheming to drive Yan Zhenqing out of the court. It happened that Li Xilie had just rebelled, and Lu Qi memorialized the emperor, saying, ‘Your servant believes that if one weighty minister of scholarly refinement were sent to set before Li Xilie the blessings and disasters of rebellion, the armies might be spared all toil and Li Xilie brought to submit to the court. Yan Zhenqing is a veteran minister of three reigns, loyal and upright, firm and resolute, and his name is heavy throughout the realm, so that all men revere him; therefore your servant believes he is the fittest man for the task.’ The emperor accordingly approved Lu Qi’s proposal and issued a decree sending Yan Zhenqing to pacify Li Xilie on behalf of the court. Later Li Xilie wished to keep Yan Zhenqing as his chancellor, and Yan Zhenqing defied him to the death and so gave his life for his country; and this affair was in truth brought about by Lu Qi. Afterwards Li Huaiguang memorialized the emperor: ‘Lu Qi has injured the loyal and good, and a treacherous minister has ruined the state.’ On this account Lu Qi was demoted and banished to Xinzhou, and it was in Xinzhou that he died.

The Ming scholar Yan Maoyou said: ‘The petty man is jealous only because he fears that others will attack him and do him harm; he does not know that cunning and scheming can never prevail against the principle of destiny. If it is fated that a thing shall fail, then though a man exhaust every device of his mind and every trick at his disposal, he is powerless. Men like Lu Qi were not ignorant of this principle, yet they could not help themselves; for at the outset a single thought arose, the wish to secure the emperor’s favor and trust for himself, and when the matter came to a head he was already riding a tiger and could not get down. Therefore one must be exceedingly careful and cautious at the very beginning!’
To bully orphans and oppress widows.

The general sense of ‘to bully orphans and oppress widows’ has already been touched upon in the annotations to ‘to pity orphans and to compassionate widows’ above. The Most High first admonishes us to pity and compassionate orphans and widows, and then admonishes us again not to bully and oppress orphans and widows, repeating the warning over and over with the utmost earnestness; for to be an orphan or a widow is a misfortune in human life, and such persons are therefore regarded with weight by Heaven and Earth. How then can one take advantage of their helplessness to deceive them and injure them? Still worse is it to seize and plunder their property, or to use treacherous means to send them off to labor service, or to rely upon power and influence to force orphans and widows into homelessness, so that their grievances have nowhere to be told! Let us set aside for the moment the clear scrutiny of the ghosts and spirits and the unfailingness of retribution; let a man only remember that the orphan is another man’s son, and the widow is another man’s wife, and put himself in their place, weighing his own son and his own wife in the balance against them; then he will no longer be able to do such a thing, which outrages Heaven and destroys reason, as to bully orphans and oppress widows.

In a place called Fangcheng there was a man named Gong Gu, who was neighbor to a wealthy man of the surname Zhou. In the wealthy man’s household the men and women alike suddenly died, leaving only an old woman and her young grandson. Gong Gu then took the occasion of inviting them to a meal to deceive the old woman, saying, ‘Your little grandson is too young and his body too frail; to live upon the property left behind is hardly the best of plans. Why not sell the property to me, and I will undertake to support the two of you, grandmother and grandson?’ The old woman was delighted to hear this, and at once made the contract, selling him the whole property for less than half its price. The moment Gong Gu had the contract in hand he forced the two of them to move out; and that night he dreamed that someone rebuked him, saying, ‘Gong Gu, you dared to scheme for my estate and drive out my wife and grandson! I have already laid this matter before the High God; next year your whole family will die to the last soul!’ In the following year a band of robbers came and plundered the Gong household, killing them all, so that not one living mouth was left; and the old woman and her little grandson, having been driven from the house the year before, were saved from that calamity. After the Gong family had all died, grandmother and grandson were able to return to their old home, and the property too came back to its rightful owners.
[Conclusion]

Seeing this tragedy, which brought ruin upon a whole family, those who dare to bully and oppress orphans and widows ought surely to be able to reflect and repent. And as for those who dare to bully and oppress orphans and widows even among their own brothers and clan, that is nothing less than the extinction of natural human feeling and the loss of every human bond; and the retribution they receive is correspondingly more severe.
To hold office and yet dare to cast aside the law and take bribes.

From ‘to cast aside the law and take bribes’ down to ‘to see a man put to death and add anger to it’, all is spoken with regard to officials who examine criminal cases. All yamen runners and clerks and scribes are included as well, and it is not meant to refer to judges alone. The Most High speaks first of ‘making the crooked straight and the straight crooked, the light heavy and the heavy light’, and of these he first takes up ‘to cast aside the law and take bribes’; for in the making crooked or straight and the weighing of light and heavy there is a fixed principle to be followed, and the one aim of such a man is to get money. Therefore he recklessly accepts whatever the briber asks, and turns the provisions of the law upside down. If a judge, a runner or a clerk disregards the provisions of the law, dares to cast the law aside, and by his own likes and dislikes alone decides whether a prisoner shall live or die, then the people will not know what to do, and will be utterly at a loss; and have such men never considered that by so doing they will surely bring down the wrath of Heaven and the resentment of men, and that they themselves will certainly meet with strange calamity?

The Ming scholar Yan Maoyou said: ‘Those who can pass the examinations and hold office are all men who have read the Odes, the Documents, the Rites and the Music thoroughly! How could they not know that integrity ought to be honored? It is only that they have grown used to the ways of officialdom, and in seeking office and asking others to recommend and promote them they do not shrink from borrowing money to make gifts; and if one has no money, how is it to be managed? When a man first begins to be corrupt he still keeps some measure and feels shame and unease in his heart; but as the days grow long the habit becomes hard to turn back, and the more he covets the worse he grows. By this time his very nature has been stained, until it is as foul and stinking as raw fish and mutton. And the human heart is insatiable in its greed: having coveted a hundred taels of gold, a man thinks, would it not be better if I could covet a thousand? And when he has got a thousand, he will certainly think, would it not be better still if I could covet ten thousand? Worse still, his power and rank blaze for a time and gold and silver are piled up all over the house, some of the treasure grown old from lying so long unused, and even then he feels unsatisfied. Those who look on all laugh at him, yet the man in the midst of it is blinded, and knows nothing of it at all; the truth is simply that he has come to love money as an addiction. Such corrupt men, for the most part, wish to secure lasting wealth and honor for their sons and grandsons, not knowing that many a foolish son of a great house has on this very account met with the ruin of his whole clan, while many a poor and honest man’s son has risen to wealth and honor. You must know that blessing and emolument have their fixed measure! If a man gains more than his due by unjust wealth, he leaves behind a debt of resentment for his sons and grandsons to repay, and this is no blessing. As for an official who wishes to build temples and shrines to aid his clan, and to relieve poor relatives, these are good works indeed; yet if in his heart he wishes to complete them quickly, he will only covet more and more fiercely, and it would be better to accumulate virtue and do good, which draws down auspiciousness; for when a man has held office long, he will naturally become wealthy, and then his blessings will flow further and last longer! Every official who loves wine, lusts after women and takes pleasure in killing does so because of greed for wealth; and the fault of greed too begins from indulging one’s own thoughts until it becomes a habit. When the habit is old, the very nature changes, and a man will cling to his greed even at the cost of his own life; and naturally he will not care whether the wealth he has grasped will in the end be of use or not. When a man has just entered office, some can still hold themselves in check and refuse to be corrupt; but when he is old and long in office, he can no longer keep his grip and drifts with the current. This is because he has gradually come to regard the yamen as his own home and wealth as his own life! Yet such a man is far better than one who, the moment he takes office, cannot wait to plunder on the grandest scale.’

Furthermore, a man who serves as a superior officer cannot think that it is enough merely to be himself clean and uncorrupt, and to keep his own safety and wisdom; he ought all the more to forbid corruption strictly among his subordinates. Why? Because a superior’s eyes and ears are after all limited, and almost all cases must be handled in the hands of the clerks and subordinates within the office, who therefore have many opportunities of contact with bribes. If the superior cannot, in ordinary times, lead by his own example and teach his subordinates the principle that ‘to be within the public gate is a good place for cultivation’, he is in effect abetting their corruption, and his own guilt is very heavy!’

Geng Jiuchou of the Ming dynasty, while serving as salt commissioner of the Two Huai, had a name for integrity that was known far and near. Once, as Geng Jiuchou sat by the riverside, a small child said to him, ‘The clearness of this river water cannot compare with the purity of your conduct!’ In the early years of the Tianshun reign the court wished to single out officials of clean integrity to serve as models for the officials and people of the whole realm, and so appointed Geng Jiuchou chief censor in charge of the discipline of officials throughout the empire, and afterwards appointed him a minister. His son Geng Ziyu kept his instruction, and his integrity too was of the highest; he rose to be grand guardian of the heir apparent and minister of personnel.

Formerly there was an official named Fan Guang, who while serving as assistant to the governor of Jiaozhi commandery was one day at work in his office when thunder suddenly crashed and a great wind arose. Fan Guang, his son and his dog were all struck dead by lightning; and his wife, at the moment of the thunder, saw a Daoist move her body and set it down elsewhere, and so she alone escaped, for otherwise she too would long since have been killed. Someone asked her, ‘What was the reason for this?’ Fan Guang’s wife said, ‘There were once two men who accused each other in a lawsuit, and both were thrown into prison by Fan Guang. The one who was in the wrong took money and bribed Fan Guang; and the man who had right on his side was therefore cruelly tortured and interrogated by Fan Guang, who forced him to confess to a crime. The food his family sent was all given by Fan Guang to his son and his dog, and the accused, having nothing to eat and being about to starve to death, was seen by someone with his hair unbound and hanging loose, accusing Fan Guang of his crimes before the Celestial Emperor. Only a few days after this matter, it came about that Fan Guang, his son and his dog were all struck dead by lightning.’

While Hou Jian was serving as magistrate of Jiangling, he was on very friendly terms with a monk, and whenever he had leisure he would certainly go to call on him. And each time he called, the monk had long since prepared the dishes and rice with which to welcome and entertain him. But on one occasion when Hou Jian went to visit the monk, the monk’s hospitality on this visit was so greatly diminished from before that Hou Jian asked him the reason; and the monk answered, ‘My lord Hou, each time you have come, the local earth god has always informed me beforehand, and that is how I was able to make ready in advance. But this time, when you came, the earth god gave me no notice, and so I had no time to prepare, and the entertainment has been poor.’ Hou Jian was greatly astonished at this, and begged the monk to ask the earth god the reason for the omission. That night the monk dreamed that the earth god said to him, ‘Hou Jian’s office might have risen as high as chancellor; but lately, because he accepted sixty taels of silver as a bribe from a man named Hu, and on that account wrongly decided a case, the High God has already struck his chancellorship from the record, and his office can go no higher than that of a supervising commissioner. He no longer stands under my jurisdiction, and that is why I gave no notice.’

Alas! Because Hou Jian accepted a bribe of sixty taels of silver, the High God altered and removed the official emolument by which he might have risen to chancellor. So then, in acting as he did, was Hou Jian clever or was he foolish? And the gods do not plainly inform every man of the causes of blessing and calamity in each of his affairs; and so those who take bribes and never know that their blessings have already been diminished are far too many to count!

Again, for example, there was a prefectural judge named Wei Zhao, charged with the hearing of cases, who because he had accepted a bribe of four hundred taels of gold deliberately acquitted a murderer, so that the dead man’s grievance found no redress; and the High God accordingly struck away Wei Zhao’s emolument and his span of life, and a year later Wei Zhao died. People today often suppose that to clear a man of a crime cannot be compared with deliberately making his crime heavier, and use this as their excuse; not knowing the principle that ‘the law may not be indulged, nor may a man be wronged’.
To turn the man who is in the right into the man who is in the wrong, and to hold the man who is in the wrong to be in the right.

When the parties on either side each bring their complaint before the authorities and accuse one another, at such a time the crookedness or straightness of their cases has not yet been made clear, and their life or death, their guilt or innocence all rest upon a single word from the judge. How then can a judge pronounce sentence carelessly and at random? Yet today there are judges who decide the man in the right to be in the wrong, and the man in the wrong to be in the right! If a judge thus turns crooked and straight upside down, either he has taken a bribe, or he is partial and plays favorites; for otherwise, how could a man so reckless and crude ever have attained the office of judge?

Formerly there was a man named Liu Anmin who worked in the county yamen; because he handled matters with fairness, everyone respected him. And so, when the common people wished to lodge a complaint, before ever they brought it to the yamen they would always first go to Liu Anmin and ask him to judge whether their case was crooked or straight and whether a suit could be brought, and only then decide whether to sue or not. Liu Anmin was most conscientious and served the people without payment; though it was very hard work, he never declined it. When the principle a man set out was right, Liu Anmin would agree with him, saying, ‘Your case is straight; you may bring suit.’ And when a man’s case was crooked, he would say to him, ‘Your case is crooked; if you bring suit, you will certainly lose.’ Thus the lawsuits of the whole county were reduced by more than half, because Liu Anmin judged crooked and straight so well and served the people; and afterwards both of Liu Anmin’s sons passed the examinations and won office, and the Liu family is a distinguished clan to this day!

While Zhao Shi was serving as instructor of Wuwei prefecture, one night he dreamed that a prisoner said to him, ‘I was unluckily done to death by Zu Xiang!’ Zhao Shi said, ‘Zu Xiang is a man thoroughly versed in the law, a man of clean integrity, exceedingly cautious in his conduct and dealings; how could he possibly have wronged you?’ The prisoner said, ‘My death was not Zu Xiang’s intention; but because he always harbored a suspicion in his heart that I was guilty, he made no distinction between crooked and straight and actually sentenced me to death! As the saying goes, every wrong has its head and every debt its master: if it was not Zu Xiang who killed me, then who was it? I have already laid my grievance before the King of the Underworld, and so Zu Xiang has not long to live!’ Sure enough, a little more than a month later Zu Xiang died.

In recent times the habit of attacking others and lodging accusations in the courts seems to have grown more and more widespread. If those in government cannot move the people by moral influence, then making the penalty for false accusation heavier may perhaps reduce the number of lawsuits among the people; and even when suits are brought, cases misjudged through suspicion will not be too many. What is most to be feared is a judge who manipulates the mind of the plaintiff and misuses the terminology of judgment in order to encourage and stir up a litigious temper; such a judge, I fear, has not long to live, and the justice of society will be corrupted with him!
To sentence to heavy punishment a man who ought to be lightly punished.

The Book of Documents says: ‘When a judge feels doubt in his heart as he passes sentence, he should sentence the lighter penalty.’ It also says: ‘Better to err on the side of a lighter sentence than to impose a penalty heavier than a man deserves!’ Yet there are actually judges who deliberately turn what ought to be a light sentence into a heavy one, gravely defying the intent of the sages, who pitied and compassionated offenders! Moreover, a human life is bound up with Heaven, and the question of life and death carries the heaviest responsibility of all; the official charged with hearing a case ought above all to take care, and to search out the evidence with caution, allowing not the slightest negligence; otherwise he may easily be made use of by slanderers and false accusers, and so be misled in the case!

While Li Ruoshui was serving as judicial commissioner of Huainan, it happened that five robbers, their affair having failed, were seized and thrown into prison. Under interrogation the robbers declared that they had once banded together with a monk to commit robbery; and afterwards all five robbers were sentenced to death, and the executions had already been carried out when the monk was discovered by the authorities. The monk said, ‘This poor monk truly has never been a robber!’ Li Ruoshui ought to have dealt with the monk leniently, since the robbers were already dead and could not confront him; yet Li Ruoshui insisted that what the robbers had said was true, and with a cruel heart he put the monk to death by savage torture. Unexpectedly, a little more than a month later the prison guard Li Neng cried out for no reason at all, ‘Monk! This is no doing of mine! It was entirely the judicial commissioner Li Ruoshui who threatened me and forced me to kill you!’ Having said this, Li Neng died. The next day the prefectural judge Liu Yuan also died. A day later Li Ruoshui dropped dead. And before long nearly all of Li Ruoshui’s family had died as well.

Zhao Qingxian, the iron-faced censor of the Song dynasty, while serving as prefectural judge of the Wu’an defense command, had before him common people who had forged and used seals, and his subordinates all said, ‘Those who forge and use seals ought by law to be sentenced to death.’ But Lord Zhao Qingxian alone said, ‘These people made the seals before the great amnesty, and used them after it; they neither used them before the amnesty nor forged them again after it. Therefore, whether before the amnesty or after it, by law they cannot be sentenced to death.’ In the end Zhao Qingxian, applying the rule that ‘where guilt is doubtful, the lighter penalty is given’, released these people suspected of forging and using seals. Later, when he was prefect of Chengdu in Sichuan, there was a man named Li Xiaozhong who gathered two hundred men and privately made ordination certificates in order to ordain men as monks; and someone brought an accusation against Li Xiaozhong before the authorities on the charge of plotting rebellion. The authorities sent men to arrest Li Xiaozhong and his followers and throw them into prison on the charge of plotting rebellion, to be judged and put to death. But Zhao Qingxian alone set aside the opinion of the crowd and decided that Li Xiaozhong alone should suffer death for privately making ordination certificates, while all the others were excused from the death penalty. Lord Zhao Qingxian’s handling of this case was nevertheless noised abroad; and when the news reached the capital, men said he had acted with reckless audacity, daring to clear men of the rebel party. The court sent men to examine the documents of his sentencing in this case and to check whether there was any perversion of the law; and in the end the court confirmed that his judgment had been correct. Afterwards Lord Zhao Qingxian rose to be grand guardian of the heir apparent, and his two sons Zhao Wan and Zhao Dou both became highly honored.
To see a man sentenced to death and put to death, and instead of grieving and pitying him, to add anger to it: such a man is truly cruel beyond measure!

Zengzi said: ‘If one has found out the true circumstances, one should grieve for him and pity him, and not be glad.’ This means that when a guilty man receives his punishment, one should still make allowance for the motive that led him to commit the crime, and must not recklessly and willfully make his penalty heavier; and moreover the dead cannot come to life again, and though it is he who has brought it on himself, and the guilt is his own to bear, yet one who stands there and watches him tortured and killed ought to feel grief unending in his heart, and should be covering his face and weeping for him and unable to do enough; how could he add hatred and fury to it? The heart of such a man is cruel beyond measure. And as for domestic fowl, beasts and fish, when they are slaughtered by men, one ought all the more to pity them for their innocence and their guiltlessness; and if a man sees them killed and adds hatred and anger to it, that man is surely a savage and a tyrant who takes pleasure in killing!

Lu Duoxun, a great minister of the Song dynasty, was demoted and banished to Zhuya, which is present-day Hainan. At that time Li Fu, a grand master of remonstrance, went on this account to see the chancellor Zhao Pu and put this proposal to him: ‘Zhuya, to be sure, lies beyond the sea, yet its soil and climate are good, and officials banished there for the most part keep their lives; while Chunzhou, though it lies within the interior, is a place where any official exiled to it is certain to die. I beg you to alter the earlier order and banish Lu Duoxun to Chunzhou: outwardly it will display your great magnanimity, while in truth it will put him to death.’ Zhao Pu heard Li Fu’s proposal and nodded his head in assent. A little more than a month later Li Fu fell into trouble and was himself demoted and banished to Chunzhou; and when Li Fu reached the seat of Chunzhou commandery, he died there.

Yang Daosheng was military adviser to the prince of Shaoling. He had an elder brother named Haizhen, who served as governor of Cuozhou. Once Yang Daosheng took leave to go and see his brother, and saw a man bound to a tree, who wept and begged him, saying, ‘The governor of Cuozhou means to put me to death; I beg you to have great compassion and save me!’ Daosheng asked him, ‘What crime have you committed?’ The man said, ‘I only wished to run away and desert.’ Hearing this, Daosheng was very angry and said, ‘The crime you have committed is the most infuriating of all.’ With that he took his own sword and gouged out the prisoner’s eye, and swallowed it in a single mouthful. Before long, when Daosheng’s brother arrived, he gave the order to behead the man. Then Daosheng felt that the eye he had just swallowed was lodged in his throat and would not go down, and by degrees he felt it swell and block him; and so Daosheng could take no food, and starved to death.

Liu Xizhi of the Ming dynasty once dreamed that someone came and bowed to him, begging, ‘I am Cao Han, a great general of the Song dynasty. Formerly, in the Tang dynasty, I was a minor official; and because I heard a master preach the scriptures and was moved to understanding, I made an offering of one vegetarian meal to that master. From that time on I drew down blessings, and life after life I was reborn as a human being, gradually accumulating good causes. In the Song dynasty I held the post of deputy general in the army; and because for a long time I could not take the city I was attacking, my heart was filled with fury, and after the city fell I gave the order to massacre it, killing every soldier and civilian within the walls. Because of that massacre my life after life I have been reborn as a pig, to repay the debt of killing I owe. Two years ago a tenant farmer gave me to you in payment of the rent he owed, and thanks to your compassion and pity I was able to live and was not killed. Today I am to repay here the debt of killing I owe from before, and shall very soon be killed by men; and so I have come especially to beg you for help!’ Liu Xizhi said, ‘Then by what means can you be saved?’ Cao Han said, ‘When beasts and birds are slaughtered and cut up by men, their suffering is truly beyond description; but at such a time, if they hear the sound of the Buddha’s name being recited, their pain can be released. Therefore I hope that whenever you see livestock being slaughtered or being boiled, you will bring forth a great compassionate heart; you should recite Amitābha Buddha, or else recite the Great Compassion Mantra and the Cundi Mantra, and dedicate the merit to living beings. Thus you will not only release me from the pain of being killed, but also bring about the great benefit of deliverance!’ When Cao Han had finished speaking, he took leave of Liu Xizhi with grief and deepest earnestness, and departed.
Story Four:

Formerly there was a man named Zheng Lin, who suddenly dropped dead. Afterwards the King of the Underworld discovered that the wrong man had been seized, and so sent Zheng Lin back, saying to him, ‘After you return to the world of the living, you should earnestly accumulate virtue and do good. When you see living creatures being killed, recite for them Namo Amitābha Buddha and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; then those slaughtered creatures will thereby be able to be reborn, and you too will gain blessings!’

From this we may know that Buddha-recitation can indeed deliver and rescue the dead, and that in this present life it can also increase one’s blessings and lengthen one’s years; and when the span of this life is exhausted, one will surely be reborn in the Western Pure Land. Someone may ask, ‘Why is it that the mere recitation of the Buddha’s name brings benefit both to oneself and to others?’ I answer: ‘Because living beings, through distant kalpas past, have been lost to and blinded to their own true nature, and to awaken them is truly a matter of remoteness beyond hope, too hard, too hard! Yet as soon as one hears the Buddha’s name, this blindness awakens. Moreover, when another man with cruel means takes a life, and I with a compassionate heart that draws out suffering recite the Buddha’s name for the slaughtered being, then right here lies the road of renouncing evil and following good! Therefore to recite the Buddha’s name for living beings when one sees them killed may be called merit without measure!’

Master Hanshan of the Ming dynasty said: ‘In ordinary times, whenever I hear the sound of livestock being slaughtered, I cannot help but feel a pain in my heart; and at once I recite the Buddha’s name and the Rebirth Mantra for them. In doing so I am only doing what I can, to the limit of my heart, for those slaughtered creatures.’ From the two cases above we know that when living beings suffer in being killed, if they can hear the sound of the Buddha’s name, then in truth they gain great benefit and joy. Therefore whenever we see or hear living beings being killed, or see creatures on the chopping block or in the boiling pot, we should at all times and in all places bring forth this great compassionate heart and recite the Buddha’s name for them; and thus we can truly be compassionate and draw out the suffering of living beings. If everyone could bring forth this samādhi of compassionate mind, then all of it would be the great work of bodhisattvas in delivering living beings, and the merit of it would be inconceivable!

The hearing of cases and the administration of prisons are among the great affairs of state, and the life and death of the common people are bound up with them directly. Therefore when the Most High set down his words, he first strictly forbade the taking of bribes; and in all that concerns crookedness and straightness and the lightness or heaviness of sentences, he laid his weight especially upon the officials charged with hearing cases, because they hold power in their hands and can easily do men a kindness. Yet the eyes and ears of one official are exceedingly limited; and so if the clerks and runners who serve as his subordinates could put away their own bad habits and follow their superior in doing good, saving men in the midst of trouble and hardship, then they could create merit boundless and without limit. You must know that the dividing line between good and evil lies in a single thought in one’s own heart; and to hoist the sail when the wind blows is the easier by far. Others say, ‘The public gate is no place to enter!’ but I say, ‘The public gate is a good place for cultivation!’ How could the words of the ancients deceive me? And as for killing men and killing creatures, whether another kills or I kill, it is killing all the same! Even if one cannot manage to save the lives of the creatures about to be killed, would it really cost one’s money or waste one’s strength to recite the Buddha’s name for them with sincere heart? This principle, I beg you all, should be thought over carefully!
Clearly to know one’s own faults, and yet be unwilling to reform.

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked the Buddha, ‘If a man commits evil in his youth and only begins to practice in old age, can he still attain Buddhahood?’ The Buddha answered, ‘The sea of suffering is boundless; turn the head and the shore is there.’ Chan Master Yuanwu said, ‘Who is it that has no fault? To be able to reform after a fault is the greatest good of all!’ Hence it is only the gentleman who can reform his faults and turn to good, and so his virtue is renewed day by day; while the petty man conceals and hides his faults, and even glosses them over, and so the evil karma he creates becomes more and more conspicuous. For when a petty man commits a fault he will certainly find many reasons to make a rationalized defense of it; and this is why the Most High admonishes us so earnestly and repeatedly! Mr. He Longtu said, ‘The faults men commit may be divided into three kinds: faults committed by the mouth, faults committed by the body, and faults committed by the mind. One who is good at reforming his faults need only be keenly alert himself, and earnestly rid himself of the habits of clinging and of stinginess; and as for principle, he must search it out deeply and probe it to the very bottom; then he will naturally arrive at sincerity of intention and uprightness of heart. The learning of the sages, the learning of the Buddha, and the learning of the mystery are all vast and profound, and not easy to set forth clearly; yet the most fundamental method of learning, and the one that can penetrate the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism alike, is the reforming of faults.’

Sima Guang of the Song dynasty, when he was five years old, once tried to remove the skin from a walnut. He worked at it for a long time but simply could not get the skin off. Later a maidservant in the household saw this and helped him by soaking the walnut in hot water, so that the skin came off very easily. Just then his elder sister came in from outside and asked him, ‘Did you peel the walnut yourself?’ Sima Guang replied, ‘Yes, I peeled it myself!’ His father heard this and scolded him, ‘A child must not speak falsehoods!’ Sima Guang was startled, and from then on repented and reformed; for the rest of his life he never dared to lie again.

Xu Jiexiaoji of the Song dynasty, when he first paid a visit to Mr. Anding, tilted his head ever so slightly. Mr. Anding said sternly, ‘Your head should be held straight; it must not be crooked.’ Xu immediately repented and understood, saying, ‘If the head must be held straight and not crooked, how then can the mind be allowed to be crooked?’ From that time on, Xu’s mind was never in the least bit slanted. When someone asked him, ‘What is the essential secret of conducting oneself in the world and cultivating oneself?’ he would always write the two large words ‘upright and honest’ for the one who asked.

The great Song dynasty writer Zeng Zigu (Zeng Gong) was on good terms with Wang Anshi. Emperor Shenzong asked Zeng Gong, ‘What do you think of Anshi’s character?’ Zeng Gong replied, ‘Anshi’s writings and conduct are not inferior to those of Yang Xiong of the Han dynasty, but because he is niggardly, he falls short of Yang Xiong.’ The emperor said, ‘Anshi does not set store by wealth and rank; how can you call him niggardly?’ Zeng Gong said, ‘What I call niggardly is that, though Anshi is bold in undertaking affairs and accomplishing things, he is nonetheless stingy about correcting his own faults.’ Hearing this, Emperor Shenzong nodded in agreement with his view.

Alas! Wang Anshi, with the talent of a prime minister, ended by covering up his faults and refusing to acknowledge them, until at last he brought calamity upon the whole realm, harmed the common people, and left behind a name reviled for ten thousand generations. How much more so for those today who are obstinate and self-opinionated and yet without talent, who live amid their faults every day and do not even know to reform!
Though good deeds are plainly before one’s eyes, yet one refuses to go and do them bravely.

The ancients said, ‘By taking what is small one attains the great; by accumulating ones one reaches the myriad.’ Therefore in doing good, what matters most is daily accumulation and steady storing up. When you know a thing is good, do it at once, and do it earnestly and diligently. Laozi said, ‘A nine-story tower begins from a mound of earth piled up bit by bit; a journey of a thousand li begins from a single step.’ If a person can correct one fault each day, he can dissolve one karmic offense; if he can do one good deed each day, he can add one foundation of blessing. The Purple Void Perfected Lord said, ‘The Way is born of stillness, virtue is born of humility, blessing is born of frugality and purity, and life is born of harmony and ease. Calamity comes from many desires, and fault comes from contempt and negligence. Therefore guard the eyes — let them not look at others’ faults; guard the mouth — let it not speak of others’ shortcomings; guard the mind — let it not indulge thoughts of greed and anger; guard the body — let it not follow evil companions. Life is like a candle burning in the wind; at any moment it may be blown out. So always think: after death, where will the spirit go? This body is only a temporary lodging in this dusty world; do not go and create offense upon offense. Know that good and evil both dwell in the mind and never err by a hair’s breadth; and if a person is clever at schemes and contrivances, then Heaven is all the more clever at requital.’ From this we see that if in one day a person hears one word of good, sees one good deed, and does one good act, then that day is not wasted in vain. But if a person plainly sees a good deed before his eyes and will not do it, one knows not what sort of heart, liver, or intestines he has; it is nothing but self-abandonment, self-degradation, wasting one’s life, and cutting oneself off from the world. How foolish indeed!

In the Tang dynasty there was a man named Su Cheng, of a most vicious and intractable nature, who in his whole life never did a single good deed. Whenever he saw in books words of virtue and meritorious conduct, he would surely say, ‘This must be false!’ When he saw others diligently doing good, he would surely laugh and say, ‘This man must be a crafty and wicked villain!’ When Su Cheng reached middle age, his body gradually shrank, until he had to crawl on the ground on his two hands. He ate and slept with the dogs, and so a year passed before he died.

Toward the end of the Zhou dynasty, Duke Huan of Qi once passed by the ruins of the Guo clan and asked an old man living nearby, ‘How did the Guo clan come to decline and perish?’ The old man replied, ‘Because the Guo clan loved what was good and hated what was evil.’ Duke Huan said, ‘To love good and hate evil — how could that lead to decline and ruin?’ The old man said, ‘Because the Guo clan loved good but could not practice it, and hated evil yet could not keep themselves from doing it. For that reason they declined and perished.’

Judging from this story, the people of today have lost their own spirit and cannot awaken to their true nature; moreover, with the myriad conditions crisscrossing and interfering, their minds are weary with running about all day, hard-pressed to cope. One thought comes, another thought goes; in a single day and night there are eight hundred and forty million thoughts. This is like the wind dancing in the sky with nothing to rest upon, or a stone pressing on grass — it stops for a moment, then springs up again. Where is there any day given wholly to doing good? Therefore though one knows that good deeds should be done, one is changed by one’s own desires; even if one preaches the sutras all day long, it is often mixed with fame and gain, like a tree whose leaves flourish on the outside while its roots have already rotted, till at last it destroys and overturns itself. Is this not a great pity?

A fine admonition. The Chan master Tianru Weize of the Yuan dynasty earnestly urged the people of the world, saying: ‘The ancients of virtue often said, “When I see another person die, my heart burns with anxiety as if on fire — not because I am anxious for that other, but because I see that soon it will be my turn.” Such words — who does not know them? But though one knows them, one simply is unwilling to practice. And yet to say you are unwilling to practice is to wrong you; the worthies present here have for the most part begun with earnest effort. It is only that you have not yet reached the point where everything is settled and complete. Where is the fault? The fault lies in not being fierce enough, not being diligent enough, not being firm enough, not being enduring enough. You merely rouse a resolve for a while, and soon after you retreat. Hence it is said, “The Buddha-dharma is not much; it is the long-lasting person that is hard to find.” If practitioners of the Way were as earnest as on the day they first resolved, even becoming a Buddha would be more than enough. Therefore it is said that he who is unchanging from beginning to end is truly a great man. How many people today can be unchanging from beginning to end? Often ten people yield five already fallen away from their resolve for the Way! If we examine the causes of their falling away, each has his own encumbrances. What then are the encumbrances? There are three. First, whether monk or lay, man or woman, everyone is encumbered by body and mouth. Next, those with family are encumbered by their families, and those with a livelihood are encumbered by their livelihood. These three encumbrances — they are what kill the people of the world! All the people of the world suffer these three encumbrances, and so they are busy for a lifetime, bustling for a lifetime, toiling for a lifetime, slaving for a lifetime, and passing by a lifetime in emptiness. Moreover, because of these three encumbrances they give rise to measureless greed, anger, and delusion, and thereby create measureless great and small evil deeds. Through such karmic retribution they fall into the bitter sea of the three realms and the eight difficulties, transmigrating in birth and death, suffering measureless misery, unable to attain deliverance. Though they suffer measureless misery, they never awaken; and those who do not awaken are so because they are not enlightened. What is it they are not enlightened about? They are not enlightened that body, family, and livelihood are not their own. Now as to your body not being yours, you do not yet believe it. Let this mountain monk now, with all candor, spell it out for you from the beginning. When you first entered your mother’s womb and took on this life, you were but a single consciousness-spirit; where was there ever a body? This body is nothing but a lump of dull flesh formed by the union of father’s essence and mother’s blood, originally without perception; it knew neither pain nor itch, neither cold nor heat, neither hunger nor fullness, neither bitterness nor joy. When this consciousness-spirit attached itself to that lump of dull flesh, from then on it knew pain and itch, cold and heat, hunger and fullness, bitterness and joy; and after it left the mother’s womb it simply took this as its own and called it “my body.” The principle and the fact I have just set forth — that this body is not my own — you thereupon absolutely refuse to believe. Therefore the Buddhas and patriarchs, in compassion for the foolishness of living beings, again earnestly and kindly say to you: “This is not your body! It is a stinking skin-bag formed of essence and blood. It is not under your control, not at your command; even birth, aging, sickness, and death are not arranged by you. How do we know this is so? Just as after you first entered the womb and dwelt in your mother’s belly, you changed every seven days, developing in due order into the five organs and six viscera, the hundred limbs and nine orifices, the four limbs and six sense-roots, sinews, bones, skin, and flesh, gradually taking shape; and even your coming forth from the womb was borne along by the warm wind and driven by karmic power — while you knew nothing of it, and it was never commanded or arranged by you. After birth, when you grow to thirty or forty, your hair turns white, your teeth loosen, your face turns sallow, your flesh becomes thin; all these come gradually, and the signs of old age then appear. Next sickness arrives; and since sickness has come, death follows in its train. So change upon change and ruin upon ruin — each and all are beyond your control. You too were unwilling that it should be so, but you simply cannot manage it. Consider that from birth to death you have spent upon this stinking skin-bag no small measure of love and affection, tending it in every way, cherishing and pitying it in every way, treating and settling it in every way; yet it is ungrateful and repays you with such loathsomeness. And there is that which is even more repulsive: for example, on a hot summer day a strong and hale fellow suddenly takes an acute illness at dusk and dies; by the second or third watch of the night his corpse reeks and overpowers those nearby, so that none can approach. In haste they place the body in a coffin, close it up, and before the bell of dawn they hurriedly carry it out and burn it. Even his dearest and most beloved family do not allow him to linger a moment longer.” Judging by this, last night he was still a hale man, and this morning he is a heap of bone-ash; and no one knows where his consciousness-spirit has gone. So sudden is the change, and it is not in your power. Since it is your body, it ought to be governed by you; since it is not governed by you, how can you falsely take it to be your body? This is only to be burdened by it for nothing and to retreat from your resolve for the Way. Your family is likewise: each drags along a stinking skin-bag, each is unfree, each is beyond the other’s control; and once impermanence arrives, none can take the place of another. While alive, they are bound together by affection and are called “family”; but once their eyes are closed, they do not recognize one another. How can you falsely take them as your family, be burdened by them, and retreat from your resolve? Your livelihood is likewise: while your eyes are open and your legs are strong, you scheme and manage, hoard and guard your property, thinking that for a hundred thousand years you will enjoy its use. Who would know that when one breath fails, not a hair’s worth can be carried along! How can you falsely take it as your livelihood, be burdened by it, and retreat from your resolve? Since you have now heard these truths, you should turn back the light and break through, awaken to yourself with sorrow. With regard to these three encumbrances, do not grasp them, do not cling to them, do not covet them. Dwell in your allotted portion, be content with your lot, and pass the days as they come. You must turn your thoughts and, with regard to the great matter of birth and death, rouse yourself to fierce and vigorous diligence. And let your resolve for the Way be firm and enduring, and in this matter strive to fathom it thoroughly.’
Having committed a crime oneself, one refuses to acknowledge it; instead one drags in others, hoping to cast off the responsibility for one’s own offense.

The crime was committed by oneself; but when the affair comes to light, one drags in others to bear the blame and shifts it upon them. This is what the proverb calls “pulling a man down into the water.” The motive is either to cover up one’s own wrongdoings, or to take revenge by framing one’s enemy. One does not realize that one’s own fault can never be concealed, and that to falsely accuse another can never succeed. It only adds to one’s own sin. Even if by luck one escapes the punishment of the law, one cannot escape the judgment of Heaven.

Zhao Ye once stood by and watched Jia Yi slaughter an ox. After Jia Yi died, he said to the judge of the underworld, ‘When I slaughtered the ox, Zhao Ye was also beside me helping me kill it.’ He said this hoping that Zhao Ye would share the burden of his guilt. When Zhao Ye’s soul was seized by the ghostly soldiers and brought to the underworld, he could scarcely recognize Jia Yi. Soon he saw a great mirror, about a zhang across, hanging in the air; and in it was clearly visible Jia Yi holding a knife and slaughtering the ox, while Zhao Ye leaned by the door with a look of pity and reluctance in his heart. Only then was Jia Yi willing to admit his guilt, and Zhao Ye’s soul was able to return to the world of the living.

According to the Buddha’s words: ‘All living beings in the world are subject to birth and death in succession. At the moment of death, before the warmth of the body has departed, all the good and evil done in one’s lifetime suddenly appear before one.
