As a rule, the states that appear at death are precisely the states of one’s ordinary mind.’ Therefore the jewel of guilt held by Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha is my own jewel of the mind, and the mirror of karma before King Yama is my own mirror of the mind. Moreover, when we do an unwholesome deed, an impression is left in our minds, lingering and haunting us and never wearing away. How then can one recklessly drag others in and falsely accuse them?

To deliberately obstruct such arts as medicine, divination, astrology, physiognomy, or any single skill or profession, so that those who practice them cannot use their learning to support their families and help the world.

Medicine, divination, astrology, and physiognomy, as well as any single skill or craft, may all be counted as practical arts. Those of shallow skill may use these arts to support their families; those of deep skill may use them to save and help others. If one deliberately obstructs and blocks such arts so that they cannot be practiced, this shows one’s mind is not broad and generous, and it will result in many in the land being cold, hungry, and out of work. As for heterodox teachers and unskilled physicians who harm right teaching and ruin lives, and such practices as refining elixirs and calcining mercury, these cannot be excused by this principle and should instead be forbidden. The households of scholars must strictly guard their doors; all such women as the three nuns and six matchmakers should be refused all contact; and even if there must be contact, one should pay attention to the uprightness of their character. This too is a method of straightening the root and guarding against trouble at its very outset.

While Zhai Qianyou was alive, he was quite renowned for his ability to summon spirits. Whenever he thought of the commandery of Yun’an, there were as many as fifteen places where the river currents were dangerous. So he summoned the spirits of the rapids, planning to level these perilous shoals so that they would no longer be dangerous. Fourteen of the rapids’ spirits answered his summons. Alone there was a female spirit of the rapids, wearing a tall hat and a long robe, who boldly admonished Zhai Qianyou, saying: ‘From what I observe, your intention in leveling the shoals is merely to make it convenient for the boats coming and going. But you do not know that those who ply the boat trade reap extremely rich profits; even if they spend a bit more, it is no loss to them. Yet there are three or four hundred poor households living along the river. They have no fields to till and no mulberry trees on which to raise silkworms; all of them depend on the labor of towing boats through the dangerous shoals to make a living. If today these shoals are leveled, it will indeed be more convenient for the boatmen; but for those poor people who live by the river and depend on towing boats for their livelihood, on what will they rely to get by in the future? The intention of the Most High is surely not like this. I fear that you, Sir, will in the end incur blame because of this; I cannot but worry for you, and so I make this suggestion, hoping that you will change your decision.’ The celestial master Zhai sighed and said, ‘Your consideration is so thorough and far-sighted that I am not able to equal you.’ Thereupon he again commanded the fourteen spirits of the rapids each to restore the shoals to their former danger.

From this story we can see that not only must the practical arts not be obstructed and blocked, but even the small trades by which people earn their food through their own labor should be allowed to circulate and flow; one should leave them some room in every case, so that their lives are not trapped by cold and hunger. This is how a benevolent person uses his heart.
Toward the sages and worthies of antiquity one does not offer respectful veneration, but instead dares to slander them at will.

There are two kinds of people who delight in mocking and slandering the sages and worthies. One kind, through their own folly, does not know the great and far-reaching influence of the sages’ teaching upon the world. Such people are like one hiding in a jar and looking at the sky through the jar’s mouth, yet complaining that the sky is so small. The other kind are those of worldly cleverness and eloquent wit, who rely on their intelligence and persuasive speech to incite and mislead others into slandering the sages; these are like grasping for the moon in the water, laboring in vain. And the sages are not in the least affected by their incitement and slander. The sages and worthies referred to here are the sages of the three teachings: Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism. Confucianism teaches by means of uprightness, Buddhism teaches by means of greatness, and Taoism teaches by means of reverence. We see that all three teachings are skilled at protecting living beings and abhor killing them. All are manifestations of a benevolent heart; all require that one treat others as one treats oneself; all are equal, impartial, and selfless, curbing anger and moderating desire, forbidding faults and preventing error; all require the inner cultivation and discipline of the self; and all can, like thunder, shake living beings from their confusion and awaken their wisdom. Likewise all can serve the function of transforming customs and enlightening the people. In a word, the principle of the world consists of but two paths, good and evil; and the original intent of the three teachings is nothing other than to teach people to correct their faults and follow the good. If we speak of the inner cultivation of the mind, then the three teachings all return to the One. Therefore Emperor Xiaozong of the Song, in reply to Han Yu’s essay that rejected Buddhism and Taoism, said: ‘Govern the mind with Buddhism, govern the body with Taoism, and govern the world with Confucianism.’ Emperor Xiaozong truly understood that mind, body, and world are alike of equal importance, and that not one of them may be left ungoverned. If this is so, then how could the three teachings tolerate one of them being absent? They should all exist together at the same time!

The Confucians of today either cite the sages to refute and deny Buddhism, or consider Buddhism as excelling the sages. The monks and Taoists of today either destroy Taoism for the sake of Buddhism, or criticize Buddhism for the sake of Taoism. In short, they are all led astray by the attachment of their own views and are wrongly discriminating the great Way. How could they understand that the three teachings are in the end not at all different? What is most to be feared is that people form mistaken ideas and, by their own intention, make conjectures and dispute with an agitated mind. Whereas a person of truly great wisdom, able to calm his mind and thoroughly fuse these principles, tracing them to their root and straight to their source, will know that Buddhism’s teaching to illuminate the mind and see one’s own nature, to cast off delusion and seek awakening; Taoism’s teaching to purify the mind and reduce desires, to accumulate merit and practice virtue; and Confucianism’s teaching to rectify the mind and make the will sincere — all are able to gather, receive, and transform living beings without conflict. In a word, they all but lead people to the Way. What further names and forms are there to cling to? Hence we know that the three teachings are all the right teaching, and for a million years together the eyes of all sentient and intelligent beings, and the standard of truth. Why be so foolish as to slander the sages and worthies, creating the evil cause for falling into the hell of the pulled-out tongue in the next life? As for the scriptures, books, and written papers, these are where the spirit of the sages and worthies is entrusted; and those who trample upon scriptures, books, and written papers bear the same guilt as those who revile the sages.

Gao Zhishou did not believe in the immortals or the Buddha, and exerted every effort to vilify them. He once pasted his wall with the Lotus Sutra. When someone presented him with a Buddha image, Gao Zhishou said: ‘This Buddha image can be made into utensils for use!’ So he sawed it up and made it into ten ring-shaped ornaments. Later, because he ridiculed and criticized the policies of the imperial court, the emperor issued a decree sending him to the Ministry of Justice for trial and sentencing. He was finally sentenced to be cut in two at the waist, and the sentence was carried out in the marketplace.

The great Ming-dynasty general Qi Jiguang recited the Diamond Sutra in his daily practice. One day he suddenly dreamed of a dead soldier who begged him to recite one roll of the Diamond Sutra to increase his merit in the netherworld. When Qi Jiguang arose in the morning, he recited a full roll of the Diamond Sutra for the deceased soldier. Yet again he dreamed of the soldier, who said to him: ‘I am indebted to you for your great kindness, General, in reciting a roll of the Diamond Sutra for me. But I obtained only half a roll’s merit, because there were mixed in the two words “not needed”!’ Qi Jiguang thought for a long time before he understood where the two words ‘not needed’ came from. It turned out that while he was reciting, his maidservant brought him tea and cakes; he waved his hand to decline, and though he did not speak it aloud, in his mind there were the words ‘not needed.’ So the next morning he shut his door and recited the sutra. Later he again dreamed of the deceased soldier, who thanked him, saying: ‘Reporting to you, General, I have now attained deliverance!’
From this story we can understand that in reciting the scriptures of the sages one may not even mix in a single wandering thought; much less may one slander the sages.
When one meets a man of the Way and of virtue, one does not respect him or draw near him, but instead violates and bullies him.

People of virtue in the world — such as Confucian scholars who read books and understand principle, or monks and Taoists who practice austerities assiduously — their words can serve as a model for the world, and their conduct can serve as an example for the world. These virtuous people stand out above the crowd because they are the very condensation of the upright energy of heaven and earth. If we love and respect them, it is already not enough; how can we violate and bully them?

The Chan master Guoqing expounded the sutras and preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. But a certain official, who had never believed in Buddhism, bound the master and struck him twenty strokes with a plank. That night the official dreamed that his dead father was very angry, and weeping, said to him: ‘How dare you insult a Chan master! Because of this, King Yama has also struck me twenty lashes of an iron whip, and even your official rank has been stripped away.’

When Chunyu Chongde was twenty years old, he entered the school palace to study. His nature was exceedingly strange and perverse, and whenever there was a virtuous scholar he would surely subject him to great bullying and denigration. One night he suddenly saw a deity, who said to him: ‘You have made every kind of effort to violate and bully virtuous men, so I have come to take away your intelligence!’ When the deity finished, he drew his knife and struck; and Chunyu Chongde fell senseless to the ground. After he woke, he was as dull as an idiot, and within a few years he died.

When Zhang Liang of the Han dynasty was young, he once traveled to Xiapi to amuse himself. There was an old man on a bridge whose shoe fell down to the foot of the bridge. The old man said to Zhang Liang: ‘Young man, go under the bridge and pick up my shoe for me.’ Zhang Liang, considering the old man’s age, reluctantly repressed his temper and went down beneath the bridge to pick up the shoe. After he had picked it up, the old man raised his foot and said: ‘Young man, put it on for me.’ Zhang Liang knelt and put the shoe on for the old man. The old man said: ‘You are a lad who can be taught!’ Then he brought out a scroll and said to Zhang Liang: ‘If you read this scroll, you can become a teacher of emperors.’ Having said this, the old man left without ever turning his head. Zhang Liang looked at the scroll; it was the military classic of the Grand Duke Jiang. Thereupon he studied it earnestly, and later helped Emperor Gaozu of Han, Liu Bang, win the empire, and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liu.

From this story we can learn that people of virtue can bring about the success of many talented persons; those who violate and insult men of virtue are like one throwing dust against the wind, or stretching out a hand to block the sky — they only let others see how utterly they overestimate themselves.
To shoot and kill flying birds, and to hunt and capture running beasts.

‘To shoot’ does not refer only to shooting with bow and arrow. All that is done with firelocks, bird-guns, poisoned crossbows, pellet bows, sticky poles, snares, and nets also counts as shooting. Whether to make money or to satisfy the appetites of mouth and belly, one sets traps of killing all around, so that the flying birds lose their lives — some with heads cut off, some with breasts run through. How great is their suffering! We ought to double our loving-kindness in delivering and protecting them. Those who eat their flesh — how can they bear to forge this enmity that is certain to be repaid hereafter, and to use them as dishes that could be reduced or dispensed with? And those who make a living by trapping and killing birds and beasts — why would they take the trouble to create this endless enmity in order to earn these limited profits?

A certain Mr. Dong delighted in catching flying birds with nets, and after catching them, ran a bamboo stick through the birds’ heads, burned their feathers with straw, and sold them for money. The number of birds he killed was beyond counting. When Dong grew old, he fell ill with a strange disease. His whole body broke out in a thick skin, coarse and wrinkled like tree bark. When it itched, he used straw to burn the thick skin to stop the itch; when his head ached, he had people beat it with a bamboo stick. In the end he died from this strange illness. And Liu Dong’er made a speciality of shooting flying birds with a crossbow; there was no counting the birds he shot down. One day, leaning by the door to shoot sparrows, he happened to feel an itch in his ear and used an arrowhead to scratch it. Then suddenly a gust of wind slammed the door, which struck the hand that held the arrow; the arrowhead pierced through his ear and the blood gushed out like a stream. And so Liu Dong’er died.
Alas! Shooting oneself with the arrow, burning oneself with the straw — each and every one is the evil karma that one has oneself created. How wondrously exact is the retribution!

In the Tang dynasty, Wei Gao kept a parrot. Whenever this parrot heard the recitation of the Buddha’s name, it would become extremely excited and listen intently; and when told to recite, it would loudly chant Namo Amitābha Buddha. One day the parrot stood upright and passed away. After cremation there were found ten relics, and Wei Gao erected a stupa to bury it. Again, during the Yuanyou era of the Song dynasty, there was a monk who kept a mynah bird that always recited the Buddha’s name along with the monk. One day the mynah lowered its head, folded its wings, and stood up and passed away. The abbot of the temple, taking pity on it, buried it. Suddenly there grew from the place where it was buried a blue lotus flower, of extraordinary fragrance. Everyone, greatly astonished, dug open the mound where the mynah was buried, and found the lotus had actually grown from the mynah’s tongue-root! All the people of the prefecture came to see it, and the prefect composed a special verse in its honor: ‘Heaven produced this wonder-bird, eight-eight its name; it learned the monk’s mouth, chanting Amitābha the same. If this feathered creature could the unborn patience gain, how can we who are human fall short and feel no shame?’

Observing these two stories, the creatures of the world, great and small, are all sentient beings; and our Buddha, in his great compassion, receives and cherishes them all impartially. Why then should people still slaughter the lives of creatures?

Mr. Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty said: ‘The people of today all say that Heaven produced the myriad things to nourish mankind, and so these flying birds and running beasts were meant from the very beginning to be eaten by people. They do not know that man too is one of the creatures growing between heaven and earth. If a person can cultivate his true nature and kindly protect living beings, then he is worthy to be called “the most spiritual of all creatures”; otherwise, what difference is there between him and the beasts? Moreover, if a person does not practice according to the right teaching, he cannot escape the six realms but still transmigrates within them. The animal of this life may have been a human being in a former life, and the person who gains a human body in this life may have been an animal in a former life. Thus greed, anger, and slaughter, devouring one another along the road of birth and death, are things to be most feared; and once one enters the netherworld, how does one know that the one who today hunts and captures the running beast will not in turn be pursued by the beasts he has slain?’

Someone may ask: ‘If people did not kill living beings or eat meat, would not the birds and beasts then fill the world? For example, wolves, jackals, tigers, and leopards would eat people — would this not be raising beasts to harm mankind?’ I answer him: ‘The Buddha said: if a person possesses loving-kindness and merit, then all weapons, fire, water, and soldiers cannot harm him, and all fierce beasts and venomous insects cannot harm him. In former times there was an evil king who drove a herd of fierce elephants toward the Buddha, seeking to kill him; but the Buddha’s mind gave rise to loving-kindness, pitying the evil king and the elephants for their ignorance. At that moment the herd of elephants saw the Buddha’s five fingers transform into a lion’s roar, and the elephants all fell prostrate before the Buddha. This is why the Nirvāṇa Sutra so greatly praises the merit of loving-kindness; for when loving-kindness reaches its utmost, it can transform even the most savage beasts of the world!’

In the time of Emperor Guangwu of the Eastern Han, within the jurisdiction of Hongnong commandery there were many tigers. The governor ordered the people to set many traps and take up bows and arrows to guard against the harm the tigers caused; yet the harm wrought by the tigers became even worse. When Liu Kun became the governor of Hongnong commandery, he said: ‘The menace of the tigers has been brought about by tyrannical government.’ Thereupon he ordered the people to fill in all the traps and snap their bows and arrows, and actively to practice benevolent governance and to feel for the hardships of the common people. The tigers thereupon crossed the river in droves and left the commandery of Hongnong.

The governor Liu Kun had not cultivated the Way or realized sagehood; it was simply by a single thought of benevolence that he was at once able to quell a raging tiger menace — how much more so for one who learns the compassion of the Buddha! Again, take the case of enlightened holy monks who tamed tigers and subdued dragons, and of the modern ‘tiger-taming monk,’ the Elder Guangqin — his deeds too are familiar to everyone, and were even witnessed with their own eyes; they are by no means fabrications. If everyone could learn from the Buddha and from the holy monks, then even if fierce and cruel beasts such as tigers and leopards filled the world, they could do no harm! Why then worry that birds and beasts will injure people? For when violent men are all transformed into the compassionate, the beasts that harm people are likewise transformed into qilin and phoenixes! Hence we know that though some creatures are exceedingly fierce and venomous, there is still a place where they may be moved and transformed — the only fear is that we ourselves may fail to be compassionate!
To dig out the insects that lie dormant in the earth, and to disturb the birds roosting in the trees.

When the weather turns cold, the insects all lie dormant in the earth; if they are dug out, they will surely freeze stiff and die. Therefore the Most High wrote this out here especially, to forbid people from doing so; and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in particular cherish and pity these small insects. How can people fail to take this principle to heart, and carelessly dig out the insects that lie dormant in the earth?

The great Song general Cao Bin would never repair his houses or walls in wintertime. Someone asked him why. Cao Bin replied, ‘To repair house walls in winter would likely injure the insects lying dormant inside!’

Cao Bin and his grandsons were enfeoffed as kings by the emperors generation after generation; such was the greatness of his blessings. Yet he was unwilling to plant the evil cause of digging out dormant insects. And now there are people who wantonly burn mountains, forests, and grass, and even dare to make a game and amusement of it, giving free rein to a moment’s pleasure while injuring billions of living creatures. Why do we not take the story of Cao Bin’s care for dormant insects and warn and remind one another by it? If we come upon someone burning grass, woods, or mountains, we should put the fire out at once; and as for villagers and children who do such things out of ignorance, we should especially counsel them well. If someone pours hot water on the ground, or burns paper money on the earth as an offering to the ancestors, in all these cases we should give timely attention and gentle counsel, so as to preserve the dormant insects beneath the ground from harm. Such a mind is truly most compassionate!

Since the birds have already settled in the trees, it is just as when a person has already gone to bed and fallen asleep; if at such a time one suddenly startles and disturbs them, would not the whole household be thrown into confusion? The Most High’s admonition not to disturb the birds roosting in the trees is the same in meaning as Confucius’s saying, ‘He would not shoot a bird at roost.’ The Scripture of the Immortals likewise says, ‘Whoever is able to practice skillful means at any time and in any place to save and protect the lives of living beings will surely receive the reward of merit and long life.’

Long ago there was an old woman who lived in the mountains, named Li Xizi. Whenever the great snows came, the branches of the trees were all covered with snow, so that the birds had no place to roost; they came flying to gather at her house, and the old woman would feed them grain, not daring to startle them. The Lord on High said, ‘Li Xizi has a benevolent heart; she may live to be five hundred years old.’ And in the end Li Xizi truly lived to be five hundred.

There was a man surnamed Yang who made his living by catching birds and selling them for money. One day he saw a winter magpie roosting on a branch, so he took a bamboo pole smeared with glue and climbed the branch to catch it. The branch broke and he fell from the tree; the pole he was holding in his hand pierced his head, and he bled to death.
To stop up the burrows where insects and ants live, and to overturn the nests where birds roost.

A burrow is the gathering place of all the tiny creatures that hold a spirit. From a human’s point of view it is merely a hole in the ground; from their point of view it is the home on which they depend for shelter. It is no different from the home a person lives in — how can one fill up and stop such a burrow? To do so is to cut off their gate of life, block their way out, and even wipe out their whole clan! How can human beings bear to do such a thing!

Formerly there was a bhiksu who had attained the six spiritual powers through cultivation and lived together with a young novice monk. In his meditative concentration the bhiksu saw that the novice had only seven days left to live; so he found a convenient pretext and told the novice to go home and visit his parents. Eight days later the novice returned, alive. The bhiksu was astonished, and entering concentration again he observed: why had the novice not died? Then he understood. On the road home the novice had seen an anthill, and the water running over the ground was about to flow into the ants’ hole. The novice hurriedly took off his robe, and with earth he dammed the water so that it could not flow into the ants’ burrow. Because of this cause of saving the ants’ lives, the novice’s lifespan was extended by twelve years; and for this reason he practiced even more diligently and attained the fruit of the fourth-stage arhat.

In Hangzhou there was a woman who delighted in killing living creatures, and above all hated ants for dirtying her food. So she often burned ants to death; whenever she found an anthill, she either stopped it up or poured boiling water into it, killing countless ants. Later she bore a child, still at the nursing stage; one day this child was bitten all over by a great swarm of ants until his whole body swelled up, and in the end his flesh rotted and he died.

Mr. Zhu Ji said, ‘A woman loves her child as she loves her own life; so when urging a woman to abstain from killing, one should use this case to persuade her — it is more effective, for the woman being urged will feel afraid.’ Therefore in Zhu Ji’s vow to abstain from killing there are the two lines, ‘If I raise the knife again, it is as though I were killing our own children’ — on the one hand to caution himself, and on the other to caution his wife.

A nest is the place where birds of every size rely for shelter while they suckle and give birth, and where they can also escape the onslaught of frost and snow and the danger of being caught in nets or struck by pellets. If someone overturns a bird’s nest, it is no different from a human being whose house is destroyed and whose home is burned — is that not to put them to death? The Most High says in the Chapter on Preserving One’s Offspring: ‘Whenever a person’s descendants decline and are cut off, it is because in a former life he overturned birds’ nests, destroyed birds’ eggs, burned mountains and forests for hunting, drained ponds to catch fish, or caused abortions and destroyed children, thus violating the one thousand six hundred and twentieth precept; and only for this reason does he bring down upon himself the retribution of his descendants being cut off.’

The Buddha said, ‘If you see someone climbing a tree to take birds’ eggs, or entering the water to catch fish, then you should silently recite the holy name of Ratnasikhin Tathagata several dozen times, and the eggs and the fish will thereby escape their calamity. This too is a way of saving lives.’ Someone may ask, ‘One ought first to be kind to people and afterward to love creatures; why is it that now people are taught only to love creatures — what is the reason for this?’ We should answer, ‘Because being kind to people is comparatively easy, while loving creatures is comparatively difficult. If a person dares to harden his heart and harm creatures, then he will surely also dare to harden his heart and harm people; and if a person cannot bear to harm creatures, then his heart toward others may be known as well.’ Hence the Avatamsaka Sutra says, ‘I cannot even bear to make an ant do hard labor; how much less a human being!’

In ancient times King Tang, the founder of the Shang, himself taught a hunter to spread his net on three sides only, so as not to take all the game at one cast; his benevolent heart moved the hunter deeply. King Tang extended this heart that loved creatures to the common people, and so his benevolence covered all the living beings under heaven. Once King Xuan of Qi could not bear to see an ox trembling with fear as it was led past the hall, looking as though it had committed no crime yet was being taken unjustly to its death; so he ordered a sheep to be substituted for it. The common people, however, misunderstood, thinking that King Xuan begrudged an ox and used a small sheep to replace a big one; but Mencius praised King Xuan for having a benevolent heart sufficient to practice kingly government, and said that if King Xuan could extend that heart, he would be able to keep the empire. Had Bai Qi, the great general of Qin, been able to hold a heart that loved creatures, he would not have buried alive four hundred thousand soldiers of Zhao at the battle of Changping! So loving creatures and loving people are one and the same benevolent heart. When the Tathagata was practicing on the causal ground, out of pity for a dove pursued by a hawk he protected the dove; and the hawk reproached the Buddha for being too cruel, since in saving the dove he would let the hawk starve to death. Thereupon the Buddha cut flesh from his own arm to feed the hawk, without the least regret in his mind; and at once the flesh on his arm grew back again. The Buddha’s great compassion and great pity in giving his arm’s flesh to the hawk not only filled the ten directions but overflowed throughout ten thousand kalpas. Who says that one who loves creatures cannot love people? Therefore one who can save beings from suffering with every thought is a manifestation of Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara; and one who can practice kindness with every thought is Bodhisattva Maitreya descending to be born in the world!

In the Song dynasty Su Shi built a dwelling at Dongpo and lived there, and so he called himself the Layman of Dongpo. In front of his study he planted many bamboos, cypresses, flowers, and grasses; in time the whole courtyard was filled with bamboo, cypress, flowers, and grass, and many birds came to build nests in the trees before his house. Dongpo therefore forbade his children and servants to catch the birds; and after a few years the nests the birds built on the branches were made lower and lower, so that even with the head bowed one could see the eggs in the nests!

I have heard it said of old that birds build their nests close to human dwellings, for the very purpose of keeping away from the harm of snakes, rats, and hawks. Yet people today go so far as to eat their fledglings and overturn the nests they have built — are human beings then less compassionate than snakes, rats, and hawks?

In the Song dynasty there was a man surnamed Zhu who liked to overturn birds’ nests and especially hated bees. Whenever he saw a bees’ nest, even if it was built in a very high place, he would find a way, bring a ladder, climb up, and destroy it. Later he had two sons; when the children were born, their anuses were blocked, so that they could not excrete, and before long they died. Mr. Zhu in the end was left without descendants.

The Chan master Cishou said: ‘Men take much life; hence come the sword-swept years. You took a life — your own life disappears. You owed a debt — your house is burned to clay. You broke a nest — your wife is torn away. Each deed its own exact requital earns; so wash your ears, and of the Buddha learn.’ The meaning of this verse is: ‘The many killings of the people of the world are the cause, and so there is the retribution of the kalpas of sword and soldier. Because you killed another’s life, he comes to kill you, demanding that you repay his life. Because you owed another’s money and did not repay it, he comes to burn your house and make you lose your property. Your wife and children are scattered from you because in the past you destroyed the nests and burrows of birds and bees — this is retribution. And the retribution is exactly matched; so we should wash our ears and listen well to what the Buddha says!’
To injure the unborn young of animals and to destroy their eggs is the act of killing.

Though the birds and beasts have not yet been born, the womb and the egg both contain life, just as when a human being is with child; so to injure their young and destroy their eggs is nothing other than to kill. The Buddha said, ‘If a person is fierce and cruel, not believing in the principle of cause and effect, and dares to catch newly hatched fledglings and eat their eggs, causing the birds to lose their young and cry out in grief, even to the point of weeping blood from their eyes, such a person will receive the retribution of being lonely and without a son.’

Formerly Bai Guinian went into the mountains to seek the immortals and study the Way, and obtained a book of the immortals; by it he learned to understand the speech of every kind of bird and beast. One day as he passed through Luzhou, the governor learned that he had this special ability, and so invited him to come and sit with him. It happened that the governor’s subordinates were driving a flock of sheep past the courtyard; among them was one sheep that would not move no matter how it was whipped, and that kept bleating pitifully. Seeing this, the governor asked Bai Guinian, ‘Master Bai, can you tell what this sheep is saying?’ Bai Guinian replied, ‘This sheep says that it is with young and about to give birth; when it has given birth, it will be willing to die.’ The governor, greatly amazed, ordered his subordinates to keep the sheep and not kill it; and before long the sheep indeed gave birth to two lambs.

Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty paid great attention to food. Once, while the imperial kitchen was boiling eggs for him, there suddenly came from within the pot a faint sound, as though a multitude were crying out together the holy name of Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and the sound was exceedingly mournful and sad. The officer supervising the kitchen reported the matter to the emperor, and the emperor sent people to inspect the kitchen, and it was indeed so. The emperor sighed and said, ‘I did not know that the awesome spiritual power of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas could respond in such a way!’ Thereupon he ordered that from that day on no more eggs should be boiled.

We should know that to save beings from suffering and distress is the original vow-power of Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara. Even the eggs boiling in a pot could cry out together the holy name of the Bodhisattva — how then can we human beings fail to recite the Bodhisattva’s holy name with reverence?

In the Liang dynasty there was a man who washed his hair with egg white mixed with water, in order to make his hair black and glossy; for this he broke many eggs. As he lay dying, he heard from within his hair the chirping of several thousand chicks.
Always to wish others failure and to take delight in their calamities.

When another person meets with failure, it is truly a most unfortunate matter; not to grieve for him and pity him, but instead to wish that he fail utterly — this is what is called rejoicing in another’s calamity. Since such a person considers calamity something to be rejoiced in, how could calamity fail to follow after him? Then the failure will not belong to another, but will fall upon himself. However foolish a person may be, he should not do such a thing!

Li Shiheng was ordered to go on a mission to Goryeo, and Yu Ying served as his deputy, accompanying him on that mission. All the gifts Li Shiheng received he handed over to Yu Ying to handle. Yu Ying, fearing that there would be dampness when the ship crossed the sea, put all of Li Shiheng’s gifts at the bottom of the ship and placed his own goods on top. Unexpectedly they met a great wind in mid-voyage, and the boatmen asked that the ship’s cargo be lightened to ensure the safety of the people and the vessel; so in the hurry and confusion many goods were thrown overboard at random. When the wind stopped, they checked what had just been thrown away: it was all Yu Ying’s things. And of Li Shiheng’s gifts, because they were all at the bottom of the ship, not a single one was lost.
Who does not have a selfish thought like Yu Ying’s? It is simply that because one’s own mind cannot be impartial, in the end one harms oneself!

The Nirvāṇa Sutra says, ‘A practitioner should, by the power of wisdom, apply the six methods impartially in order to subdue his own mind; he must cause his mind, in its application, to be equal in all things.’ (The six methods are: conduct of body, conduct of speech, conduct of mind, rightful gain and support, upholding the precepts, and the ability to give rise to right views.) The Song dynasty gentleman Shao Kangjie wrote in a poem: ‘At dawn of every day one stick of incense burn; to Heaven, to Earth, to throne due thanks return. I only ask that every field bear grain, and every man long years of life attain. May the state have wise ministers to keep it strong, and no rebellious son at home do parents wrong. May the four quarters rest, all weapons cease; though I be poor, at heart I shall be at ease.’

From what has been said above, we may know that the mind of the three teachings — Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism — is to teach people to be impartial; therefore we should hold this measure of mind to master ourselves and govern our minds, and never, because of the selfish thoughts of each passing moment, create heavy sin upon heavy sin!
To wreck another’s success and cause him to fail when success is within his grasp.

The word ‘wreck’ has two meanings: one is to destroy, the other is to slander. One who wishes to accomplish merit — whether great merit or small — spares no effort in striving for success; yet I insist on obstructing him, wrecking him, causing him to fail. Such cunning of mind is as venomous as a snake or a scorpion! Mr. Zhen Xishan of the Song dynasty said, ‘When we hear that someone has done a good deed, we should praise him and second his good deed; when we hear that someone has done an evil deed, we must do our utmost to cover it up for him.’ To enable another to succeed, without any loss of one’s own virtue — such was the mind of the ancients; how much less should one dare to wreck the success of one who has already succeeded!

Zeng Xian of the Ming dynasty was in charge of frontier military affairs and wished to recover the Ordos region. The prime minister of the day, Yan Song, who monopolized power and was corrupt, feared that Zeng Xian might recover the Ordos and win great merit; so he seized the opportunity to slander Zeng Xian and Xia Yan before the emperor, saying that they had stirred up conflict on the frontier without authorization. As a result both Zeng Xian and Xia Yan were put to death by the court. Later Yan Song was impeached and reduced to a commoner; and his son Yan Shifan was beheaded.

In the Song dynasty there was a man named Xuan Qiying, of a sinister disposition. When his neighbor’s house was nearly finished, Xuan Qiying, envious that the neighbor’s new house was about to be completed, took advantage of the darkness of night and broke the base of the pillars of the neighbor’s house; at that moment the great beam suddenly fell, and Xuan Qiying was crushed to death on the spot.

Alas! One who wrecks others is in truth wrecking himself! People today, in a matter of business, or in some object, or in affairs such as trade and lending, are ever fond of showing off a quick tongue and wrecking another’s success; such a mind is truly contemptible, and we should know that such a person is destroying himself!
To make others bear the danger while seeking only one’s own safety.

Thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises discuss only one word: mind. Now when I am in the midst of calamity and chaos together with others, I actually want others to bear the danger while I dwell in safety; such a mind has truly lost its original conscience! Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, ‘To avoid danger and seek safety is the ordinary way of human feeling; why then is it detested by Heaven? Heaven does not detest a man’s seeking safety for himself; it detests his making others bear the danger. In the many situations a person passes through in life, there is none without the distinction of safety and danger. If one knows only to seek safety for oneself and pays no heed to the danger of others, then a killing intent has already lain hidden within, and at any time and place there will be the danger of its bursting out. If such scheming could succeed, then all the crafty and deceitful could sleep undisturbed on their high pillows, while those with a kind and generous heart would have no way to live. How could this be the mind of Heaven and Earth? Moreover, the pivot of safety and danger turns like a revolving ring; in the end it will not let those with selfish minds see through it. So what they move toward may instead be the place of danger, and what they avoid may instead be the smooth road. If one can be impartial in mind between self and others, then wherever one goes, one will be safe.’

Li Xu of the Song dynasty was in charge of the military affairs of Yong’an. At that time a band of robbers of great strength had just begun to stir up trouble. Li Xu, fearing that he himself would meet with disaster, used a scheme to recommend his good friend Fan Xing to act in his place in charge of the Yong’an army; so after Fan Xing took up the post, Li Xu was able to leave his residence in Yong’an. Later Fan Xing’s whole family was killed by the robbers. Not long after this, Li Xu was transferred to Lin’an; on the road to Lin’an he met robbers, and Li Xu’s whole family too was killed by them.

Alas! Seeing another in danger, a gentleman will still think of every means to rescue him from his peril; how can one make others face danger while keeping oneself safe? This is the conduct of a mean and ungenerous petty man; and what he obtains is the greatest calamity!
To cut down another’s profit and seek only one’s own gain.

In all the world, only one who benefits others can benefit himself. If a thing benefits oneself while not benefiting others, it is still not true benefit; how much worse is it to diminish another’s profit while taking a greater profit for oneself! Such a person is what is called ‘one who cares only for his own wealth and not for the poverty of others.’ Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, ‘People today, in matters of money, land, houses, and property, often diminish others to benefit themselves in just this way; how could they know that in doing so they are only borrowing a debt from others without writing out an IOU! Though their wealth increases day by day, the term of their life draws nearer and nearer; seen in this light, where is the profit?’

In the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty there were two men, A and B, who were on very good terms. At that time the court was holding the examination to select military candidates, and local officials might recommend one military candidate to the court. A asked the county magistrate to recommend his man, and B asked the assistant prefect to recommend his; and whoever was recommended, if he passed, had to give a gift of fifty taels of gold as a thank-offering. Later A reflected that the magistrate’s prestige was not great enough, and that the man he recommended would certainly fail, whereas the assistant prefect’s prestige was sufficient and the man he recommended would certainly succeed. So, wishing to cut down B’s profit for his own advantage, A devised a plan and said to B, ‘Since the two of us are of one mind, we should share both sweet and bitter. If in the recommendation of military candidates only one of our two men is taken — whether it be your man or mine — we should divide the thank-money equally between us.’ B agreed to A’s proposal. When the results were posted, the man recommended through the assistant prefect had unexpectedly not been taken, while the man recommended through the county magistrate had unexpectedly passed. And the thank-money, which had been sealed up and deposited before the recommendation, was all in B’s keeping, with B responsible for it; A could not go back on his word, and could only mope in silent gloom.

From this story we see that A meant to benefit himself but instead benefited another; and by this principle we know that whenever officials exploit the people, or the rich squeeze interest out of the poor, seeking to fatten themselves by lining their own pockets, in the end there is no one who does not suffer loss himself!
In the exchange of goods, to secretly substitute bad goods for good.

What is called ‘exchanging the bad for the good’ is, for example, taking iron to exchange for gold, using stone to exchange for fine jade, or exchanging cloth for silk and satin; in the eyes of a broad-minded person it is not worth a laugh. But the mind and motive of such a person come close to theft. The Fourth Patriarch said, ‘Outer states, in themselves, have no distinction of fair and foul; the distinction of fair and foul arises from the mind. If the mind did not insist on discriminating, deluded thoughts and attachment would have no way to arise.’ In the Tang dynasty, Dharma Master Wonhyo of Goryeo traveled on foot a thousand li to come to China, wishing to find a master of high understanding to study the Buddha-dharma. One night, because he was hurrying on the road, he slept in a desolate heap of graves. At that time he was both thirsty and weary and wanted to drink water; he saw beside him a pool of clear water, and scooping it up with his bowl he drank it all at one draught, and it felt wonderfully refreshing and good. When day broke and he looked, it was a pool of liquid oozing from a corpse! Dharma Master Wonhyo was at once seized with nausea and vomited up all the water he had drunk the night before; and in that instant he was greatly awakened, saying, ‘The three realms are mind only, the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only; the three realms and the six paths of rebirth are all made by our own mind, and the appearances of all dharmas in the universe are discriminated by our own consciousness. So the feelings of beauty and of repulsion are all our own mind making distinctions; they have nothing whatever to do with the water!’

The great Song literary master Su Dongpo once treasured a piece of fine jade. An official named Zhang Chi came to visit Su Dongpo at his home and asked to see the jade; and seizing the opportunity while admiring it, Zhang Chi secretly substituted a piece of Yan stone for the fine jade. Su Dongpo did not notice at the time; only when he arrived at Huangzhou did he discover that the jade had long since been swapped by Zhang Chi; yet Su Dongpo merely laughed it off. Not long after this, Zhang Chi was demoted by the court and exiled to Taizhou, where he died. Who knows into whose hands that fine jade has now passed!
To set aside public principle for the sake of one’s private mind.

To set aside the right and wrong, the crooked and straight, of public justice for the sake of one’s personal likes and dislikes, favors and grudges: if those in high station set aside the public for the private, then the crooked and the upright cannot be distinguished; and then among friends and neighbors there will be the suspicion of forming cliques, attacking dissenters, and excluding those of different views. If a person sets aside the public for the private, and goes further to love and hate improperly, then even his own family, father and son, the nearest flesh and blood, will become enemies. The harm of being blinded by human feeling is nowhere greater than this! Whether worthy or foolish, noble or base, everyone has this failing, only in different degrees. Knowing the harm of this failing, one should understand principle in order to dissolve one’s own biased temperament, and calm the mind in order to dissolve the guarded depths within one’s heart; one who can do this is a person of great learning and great capacity!

The Song dynasty ministers Zhao Bian and Fan Zhen had come to nurse a grudge against each other because of disagreements over court policy. When Wang Anshi became prime minister, he hated Fan Zhen for having once pointed out his faults to Emperor Shenzong; so when the emperor asked, ‘What sort of man is Fan Zhen?’ Wang Anshi replied, ‘Zhao Bian understands Fan Zhen’s character best of all!’ So the emperor asked Zhao Bian, and Zhao Bian said, ‘Fan Zhen is a loyal minister.’ The emperor asked again, ‘How do you know he is loyal?’ Zhao Bian said, ‘Once when Emperor Renzong was ill and bedridden, Fan Zhen was the first to submit a memorial, requesting that Emperor Renzong designate the crown prince to settle the realm and the people’s hearts. The memorial was presented to Renzong on the nineteenth day, and Fan Zhen waited altogether a hundred days before the memorial was approved. Over this matter Fan Zhen’s hair and beard turned white with anxiety; so if Fan Zhen is not a loyal minister, what is he?’ When Zhao Bian had audience with the emperor and finished speaking, he withdrew; and Wang Anshi reproached him, saying, ‘Are you not at enmity with Fan Zhen?’ Zhao Bian said, ‘I dare not set aside public justice for the sake of private grudge.’

Formerly Kong Yi, the magistrate of Luoyang, placed a brazier in the courtyard of his office, and every letter seeking a favor or intercession he threw into the brazier to burn, without even looking at it. He said, ‘The magistrate is closest of all to the people, and in official life there are bound to be many requests and intercessions. If I comply, the people will suffer harm; if I do not comply, I cannot avoid offending people. The only way is that when a letter of intercession reaches my hands, I do not open it but at once throw it into the brazier to burn. For my part, I do not know what the request concerns; and for the one making the request, he will not be offended either. For the right and wrong, the crooked and straight, of public principle all have a fixed standard, and the judging of cases has the basis of law — how can one set aside the public for the private?’ Later Kong Yi’s son passed the imperial examination as a presented scholar at the age of nineteen.
To steal another’s skill and take it as one’s own.

For example, to steal another’s essay and think it one’s own essay; to steal another’s plan and think it one’s own plan; to steal another’s merit and think it one’s own merit; to steal a teacher’s instruction and think it one’s own insight — all these are acts of deceiving oneself and others, and will surely bring condemnation.

In the Zhou dynasty, when Mount Liang collapsed, the ruler of Jin summoned the grand officer Bo Zong to learn the circumstances of the landslide. On his way to audience with the ruler, Grand Officer Bo Zong met a cart driver and asked him, ‘Have you heard any news lately?’ The driver replied, ‘Mount Liang has collapsed, and the earth and rocks that fell have dammed up the river, so that the water no longer flows! I hear that the ruler of Jin is about to summon Grand Officer Bo Zong over this matter to discuss how to solve it.’ Bo Zong asked the driver, ‘Then how should it be solved?’ The driver said, ‘Very simply: if the ruler of Jin himself leads the civil and military officials to Mount Liang to weep and make offerings, the river water will flow again.’ Bo Zong took the driver’s suggestion and reported it to the ruler of Jin; and after the ruler adopted and carried it out, the river water began to flow. The ruler of Jin asked Bo Zong, ‘How did you come to know this method?’ Bo Zong replied, ‘I thought of it myself!’ When Confucius heard of it he said, ‘Bo Zong, that man, is about to have his line cut off! For he has stolen another’s good deed and made it his own.’ In the end Bo Zong indeed met with a violent death, and his office of grand officer was cut off.

Alas! Bo Zong merely stole a single sentence from another, and even so suffered such a severe chastisement from Heaven; how much more so for other, worse deeds — their retribution need not be spoken of to be known!
To conceal another’s good deeds so that others do not know of them.

The Buddhist sutras say, ‘The one word “good” is the most able to bring to fulfillment all the vows and aspirations of people in the world.’ Therefore if a person has even one good word or one good deed, we should praise it; and we should even fear that our praise is not enough, that we may fail to make his good words and good deeds shine abroad. By doing so we not only accomplish his own fair repute, but can also stir the good thoughts of others; and we can cause everyone to spread and encourage one another, so that those who do good will be more and more numerous. This is truly a joy — why should one conceal and cover it up? Therefore the person who conceals another’s good deeds must have no love of goodness at all in his heart, and may even harbor jealousy; and only for this reason is he unwilling to make known another’s virtue in doing good, fearing perhaps that it would throw his own wickedness into relief. Such a person is an inauspicious person in the world!

Chen Shou, the historian of the Jin dynasty, when he was compiling the Record of the Three Kingdoms, said to Ding Liangzhou: ‘If you will lend me a thousand hu of rice, I will write a fine biography for you.’ Ding Liangzhou would not agree to Chen Shou’s request, and so Chen Shou did not write a biography for him. After the Record of the Three Kingdoms that Chen Shou wrote was completed, everyone mocked and reviled him for harbouring partiality and for writing what was amiss; in the end Chen Shou unexpectedly met with a violent death.

Long ago there were two scholars who were ordered to compile and arrange the gazetteer of Jiangyin county. They happened to see that the old gazetteer recorded the deeds of two women who had kept their chastity; judging the matter to be commonplace and unremarkable, they struck out the records of these two chaste women. That very night the Daoist priest of the City God’s temple heard two women weeping and complaining to the City God: ‘The two of us endured hardship all our lives to keep our chastity, and after we died our keeping of chastity was recorded in the gazetteer; now for no reason at all it has been deleted by others!’ When the City God heard this he said: ‘These two scholars ought originally to have been able to pass the examinations and win rank; since they have concealed the chastity and good conduct of others, their official emoluments should be struck from them.’ Hearing these words of the City God, the two women wept, bowed in thanks to the City God, and departed. Afterwards the two scholars heard of this matter and retorted: ‘This is simply nonsense, nothing but wild talk!’ The next year the two scholars, because their examination results were so poor, were indeed stripped of their status as stipendiary students; and so in grief and resentment they died.
To describe the ugly deeds of others, and moreover to spread them far and wide.

The ugly deeds and ugly conduct of others are what is called ‘words of shame that may not be heard by others.’ Yet some people dare to describe the ugly deeds of others and expose their ugly conduct. In doing so they not only injure their own magnanimity, but all the hidden virtue they have accumulated vanishes along with it! The Record of Panshan says: ‘What a cultivator most dreads is to speak of others’ right and wrong, good and ugly, and even of all the affairs of the world; whatever is not one’s own concern, not only may the mouth not speak of it, the mind may not even think of it. Whenever the mouth speaks or the mind thinks of it, one has obscured one’s own true nature. If a person can devote himself single-mindedly to the work of the mind, constantly searching out his own faults, what leisure would he have to mind the affairs inside another man’s house? Even should he be crushed to powder and his bones ground up, he must not let his mind be stirred! One should sweep and cleanse one’s own mind until it is utterly clean, and at every moment earnestly seek to fathom and examine the very place from which one’s own nature arises.’ From this we see that a person should take governing himself as the urgent task, and in every thought fear only that his own body and mind may have faults—what leisure would he have to mind other people?

Long ago there was a man named Xi Kuang. He met a physiognomist whose readings were marvellously accurate, who told him that he would die in a certain year; when Xi Kuang heard this he was deeply grieved. Later Xi Kuang happened upon someone who was discussing the ugly scandals between men and women within another family’s inner chambers; and he showed himself very angry at the man who was talking. The talker accordingly felt ashamed in his heart and stopped speaking of it, and so the ugly matter was hidden and covered over. When that year came, Xi Kuang not only did not die, he fell ill with nothing and met with no disaster; afterwards he entered official life and rose to be a chief minister.

The ancients said: ‘If in one gathering someone is talking and alluding to the ugly deeds of others, and I simply sit upright in silence until he stops talking of it, this is the teaching without words; men like Xi Kuang may serve us as a model to follow.’

Zheng Xuan was a man of plain simplicity and few words, and he said: ‘In the midst of a great crowd one must not talk extravagantly; doing so not only invites envy, it also wounds others. For among the crowd there are bound to be some who have done ugly things, and if one speaks of them, then although such a man says nothing, he feels pain and regret in his heart. For instance, if one says to an official, “When you hold office, be clean and honest!” then the dishonest official who hears it will be angry. If one says to a friend, “Friends should deal with one another with upright hearts,” then the crooked friend who hears it will be angry, for he will think that I am purposely saying it for his benefit. Therefore the only course is to speak little and keep a mild and cheerful countenance; if someone asks me a question, then I answer just the question he asks. In this way perhaps one may avoid the fault of the mouth and giving offence.’ These words of Zheng Xuan truly grasp the essential secret of the way of dealing with the world.
To expose the private secrets of others, and moreover to spread them everywhere.

People are not sages and worthies—who among them has no private matters? We ought never to pry into the private affairs of others! Yet if in some place where no one is present one sees another’s private matters and then spreads them everywhere and makes them public, so that the person cannot face anyone and has no place to stand in society—such a mind is the most insidious and poisonous of all, and is certain to bring down the wrath of Heaven and the resentment of men.

When Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty was emperor, she issued an edict forbidding slaughter. A certain Zhang De, who held the office of Reminder, had just had a son, and privately slaughtered a sheep, inviting his colleagues to a meal in celebration. Du Su stealthily took some of the mutton from Zhang De’s feast for his colleagues, and denounced Zhang De to Wu Zetian for violating the court’s prohibition of slaughter. The next day Wu Zetian said to Zhang De: ‘We hear that you have had a son; We are exceedingly glad!’ Zhang De bowed in thanks to the emperor. Wu Zetian then asked: ‘Zhang De, from where did you get the mutton with which you feasted your guests?’ At this question from the emperor, Zhang De at once knocked his head on the ground and confessed his crime. Wu Zetian consoled him, saying: ‘We issued an edict forbidding slaughter, but weddings and funerals in the home do not fall within the scope of the prohibition. From now on, if you invite guests, you must also choose your guests with care!’ When Wu Zetian had finished speaking, she brought out Du Su’s memorial denouncing Zhang De and showed it to him. At this Du Su felt so ashamed that he wished he could hide himself; and the civil and military officials of the whole court, utterly despising Du Su’s character, all wanted to spit in his face. Afterwards Du Su fell into ruin, and his end was quite desolate.

In the Liang dynasty there was a man named Dao Gai, whose family for three generations had made a living by carrying night-soil for others; afterwards Dao Gai passed the examinations and rose in office to be Minister of Personnel. A certain He Jingrong asked Dao Gai to do him a favour in some matter, and Dao Gai would not agree; thereupon He Jingrong said to others: ‘In former days Dao Gai’s household lived by carrying night-soil for others; that is why to this day he still has the lingering stench of night-soil about him! And yet now he has taken to putting on the airs of a great man!’ When Dao Gai heard these words he hated He Jingrong to the marrow of his bones. Dao Gai’s younger brother Dao Qia one day asked Liu Xiaochuo: ‘I very much want to buy the plot of land belonging to our eastern neighbour, but the owner keeps making difficulties again and again, which leaves me quite helpless!’ Liu Xiaochuo replied: ‘All you need do is haul a cartload or two more of night-soil past his house; when the stench becomes unbearable to him, he will move away.’ When Dao Qia heard Liu Xiaochuo’s words he was very angry, and actually used some other affair to do Liu Xiaochuo harm and take his revenge.

[Conclusion] Alas! People often, for the sake of a single sentence, wound the harmony between Heaven and earth; and for the sake of a single matter, brew up a calamity that lasts a lifetime. Therefore in dealing with the world we must not use violent words or jesting words, for these make others hate us to the very marrow. As the proverb says, ‘When you strike a man, do not strike his knee; when you speak of a man, do not speak his sore truth’—this is just what it means!
To consume the goods and wealth of others, and to seek profit for oneself thereby.

This refers to those wicked petty men who entice other people’s sons and brothers, or delude the foolish into visiting brothels, gambling, going to law, and refining elixirs and the like, while they themselves seize the chance to profit from it. Thus unworthy sons, made fools of by these wicked petty men, give no thought to the hardship their ancestors endured in founding the family, but squander and waste the family estate; and when the family fortune is gone, the home is broken and its people destroyed. If we trace the matter to its cause, whose fault is it after all? Can such a man escape evil retribution?

Mao Qizong of Jiangsu in the Ming dynasty once wrote an essay to warn the world, saying: ‘I have often seen the sons and grandsons of powerful and noble houses, of great families and mighty clans, turn out unworthy, given to brothels and gambling and debauchery, doing every kind of mischief. Though such people are not yet dead, their property has secretly all been sold to others; or before their bones are cold, others have already come to the door and taken possession of their houses and lands. Their forebears toiled so hard, saving and accumulating wealth bit by bit, while their descendants waste and trample it, flinging it away like mud and sand without the least regret. And most of these unworthy sons and grandsons are clever men—what cause can there be for this? The reason is simply that in those earlier days, by flaunting their power and working their schemes, sparing no means, they ruined the family fortunes of many people and pieced together a fortune for their own single household. This is to have begun by consuming the goods and wealth of others, and later to have one’s own goods and wealth consumed by others! As the proverb well says, ‘What comes by crooked means goes by the very same road.’ This is just what it means. From this we may know that those whose goods and wealth are consumed by others today are the very men who consumed the goods and wealth of others in days gone by; and so those who consume the goods and wealth of others today will before long certainly have their own goods and wealth consumed by others!

In the Ming dynasty there was a man named Xu Chi, exceedingly rich, yet very greedy and domineering. He wanted to get hold of Xu Ba’s house and land, so he set someone to tempt Xu Ba’s son into visiting brothels and leading a dissolute life; Xu Ba fell deep into debt because of it, and Xu Chi indeed obtained Xu Ba’s house and land. Afterwards Xu Chi’s two sons and five grandsons all contracted a strange illness, and the shaman said: ‘This is Xu Ba working his mischief!’ Xu Chi was terrified, so he set up an altar, invited Daoist priests to perform rites, and begged the City God’s temple for a way to resolve it. Just then a beggar came up to him and asked: ‘Are you Xu Chi? Last night I slept in the temple and heard someone calling your name before the god, saying you had done him harm; and when the god heard his accusation he too was greatly angered!’ Hearing the beggar’s words, Xu Chi was utterly terrified, and after he returned home he died; before long his sons and grandsons had all died out as well.

You must understand that the brothel and the courtesan’s house are truly the karmic cause of paying off debts, and that painted beauties are the sea of sin that ruins a family—everyone knows this truth. From visiting prostitutes one contracts disease, and when the sores and poisons break out, even the features of the face are distorted and disfigured; and even if such a disease is cured, its lingering poison will reach down to three generations of descendants! Why then are there still men who dare to visit prostitutes and take no heed?

In Wuxi, Jiangsu, there was a man of the surname Qian who banded together with more than ten accomplices to lure the sons of wealthy families into throwing dice and gambling. The dice Qian used had been tampered with beforehand, so that he usually won money at play. Later he gambled with a young man in that young man’s own house and won several hundred thousand; suddenly the dice flew out of the bowl and vanished, and Qian fell to the ground and died with blood pouring from his mouth and nose. At that very moment a Daoist priest was at his altar performing rites to invoke the divine general, and Lord Guan, the Emperor of Sagehood, descended with this instruction: ‘Just now I was at such and such a place rooting out evil, and I placed the three dice on the great beam of that house.’ The Daoist priest at once paid a visit to Qian’s house, where he saw everyone standing about stupefied and much astonished; he told them to fetch a ladder, and having climbed up to the great beam they found the three dice that had just flown away and vanished. He then explained to them in detail the sacred instruction of Lord Guan; and when these gamblers who set up traps to swindle others heard the Daoist’s words, they were all greatly shocked. Before long every one of them in turn fell ill with plague and died. There was also a man named Ding Shi, of whom a physiognomist said that he would one day be first in the whole realm and take the place of zhuangyuan in the imperial examination; later he met that physiognomist again, and the physiognomist, seeing him, cried out in great alarm: ‘What evil have you been doing of late? Your emolument as first in the realm has been stripped from you!’ Ding Shi reflected that he had lately set up a gambling trap and won six million, and he told the physiognomist the truth of the matter. The physiognomist said: ‘It is because of this very thing! Your destiny as zhuangyuan has been taken away!’ When Ding Shi heard this he was filled with repentance, and he hurriedly returned all the money he had left from his winnings to the other party, hoping thereby to atone for his crime; in the end Ding Shi only passed at the very bottom of the list.

Today those who commit this kind of fault are to be found everywhere; and the local gentry and the educated are mostly absorbed in it and never tire of it, which is especially hateful. As the proverb says, ‘A xiucai is like a maiden, and must fear others; a jinshi is like a daughter-in-law, and must support others; a scholar who has not yet won rank is like an old grandmother, and must teach others.’ If one cannot support others and cannot teach others, that is one thing; but why would one still want to harm other people’s sons and brothers? What kind of mind is that?
Appendix: Ten Rules for Quitting Gambling
First:

Gambling ruins the mind. Once one enters the gambling house, it becomes a place of contending for profit; the mind schemes in a hundred ways, and all of it comes down to a single greed; one thinks only of winning the other man’s money, and in the mind there arise endless evil thoughts. Even if one is gambling with one’s closest kin, one is certain to have secretly set spears and halberds between them; even if one is gambling in the same room with a dear friend, one is exactly like an enemy. One cares only for winning one’s own money—how could one care that another is being ruined? Is not one’s mind thereby utterly ruined?
Second:

Gambling destroys character. Men differ in whether their character is base or noble, high or low; but in the gambling house one asks only whether there is little money or much—who would reckon who is noble and who is base? In the seating there is no order of elder and younger, and a servant becomes a friend; in seniority there is no distinction of honoured and humble, and slave and master actually call each other brother. Moreover they mock one another at will and address one another as they please—what kind of propriety is that? Naturally one loses all character!
Third:

It harms life itself. Those who win money go off in high spirits and gamble day and night without distinction; those who lose money struggle on desperately, heedless of their own hunger and cold. From this they wear themselves down without cease and exhaust their spirit; and if this goes on long, it is certain to ruin their health and may even cost them their lives. Once their gambling debts pile high beyond their power to repay, they feel they have lost face before those they meet; they can only swallow their shame and hold back their anger, and so they become a body full of sickness. In the end, driven to the last extremity, they can only use death to put off their responsibility and settle their gambling debts. Therefore the road to the City of Wasted Death is truly the homeland to which gamblers return! Is this not gambling harming life itself?
Fourth:

It defiles one’s ancestors. Gambling not only gives one’s money to others, it also makes one laughed at as a wastrel and a fool; gambling not only breaks one’s family estate, it also makes one spoken of as a fool’s son or grandson doing mischief. Not only can one not bring glory to one’s ancestors, one rather shames one’s own house. Relatives and neighbours all blame his forebears for not having accumulated virtue, which is why such a wastrel was born into the family; and so after his grandfather and father died, they must below the nine springs hold their grievance and never clear their name!
Fifth:

It destroys family instruction. Gambling is the easiest thing of all to be drawn into. In the home, where the space is small, it is the easiest thing to see and hear and learn. Ordinarily when one instructs one’s own sons and brothers one says: ‘You must learn good examples!’ Yet when the sons and brothers secretly watch their father and elder brothers at home, they say: ‘I am willing to learn according to this present rule and pattern.’ And so it comes about that father and son gamble, elder and younger brother gamble, and slaves and servants gamble. What kind of family rule is such a performance? In the end it comes to gambling by day, gambling late into the night, and hiding in a secret room to gamble; and the gambling habit further fosters the habit of sexual licence, so that family instruction is utterly ruined—truly this chills the heart!
Sixth:

It ruins the family and scatters the estate. When one first begins to gamble one’s spirit is bold, and one flings gold about like dirt without changing countenance; later, having lost much, one grows desperate and stakes the property left by one’s forebears. The household that grandfather and father built up through a lifetime of toil is ruined in the space of a moment’s squandering by their descendants, and the family’s good name is destroyed with it; even one’s clothes are all pawned, leaving nothing but one’s bare body. At such a time which relative or friend will come to cherish one? The fields and houses are all sold, and still the gambling debts are not paid. Where under heaven is there a place to which one may return? To think of this—is it not pitiable!
Seventh:

It gives rise to calamitous events. Gambling often goes on from dusk to dawn, the whole night long; and since the doors and gates are not properly shut, thieves seize the chance to break in and rob; and since the lamps and candles are not put out, fires often break out because of it. Worse still, ruffians take the opportunity to work their schemes, and scoundrels spy about to do their villainy; lights are put out to knock at the door, so that host and guest cannot tell who is who; men and women take the chance to strip off their clothes, and without regard for propriety they commit indecencies. This is what is meant by the lurking seed of disaster—why will people not think it over carefully?
Eighth:

It estranges the affection of kith and kin. Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants each have their own calling, and all work diligently; parents, wives, and children cherish and care for one another and look after one another—this is the joy of the natural bonds of kin. But once one enters the gambling house to gamble, the joy of the family’s natural bonds is lost, and it turns into a sea of suffering. One takes one’s wife’s ornaments to pawn them; the wife, helpless, can only swallow her anger and hold her tongue, daring to be angry but not to speak. One sells off the fields and houses, and one’s parents grow anxious and frown with worry. One cares only for one’s own swagger and pays no heed to the resentment of the family. Search your heart and ask yourself—can your heart be at peace?
Ninth:

It violates the laws of the state. The laws of former times forbade gambling far more strictly than do the laws of today. For the lighter offence a man was beaten with a hundred strokes of the great rod and moreover made to wear the cangue for two months; for the heavier offence he was shut up in prison for three years and moreover had to leave his home and native place and be exiled to the savage wilds three thousand li away. Whatever your station or rank, you would suffer the same punishment. And so when a local gentleman of standing is imprisoned or exiled for gambling, with what face can he come back and meet his relatives and friends again? If a constable or an official gambles, because he knows the law and breaks it he must be punished twice over; and he loses his post, his rice-bowl is smashed, and his wife and children are suddenly deprived of the support on which they depended for food and clothing. Rather than repent after the event, why not give it up beforehand?
Tenth:

It surely brings down the condemnation of Heaven. Let us simply observe that from ancient times to the present those who opened gambling houses have invariably met with sudden calamity, while those who won money by gambling have afterwards, of all things, been exceedingly poor. This is always because they drink men’s blood and eat men’s flesh to fill their own bellies, and gather up others’ resentment and grief to supply their own laughter and delight. Therefore the ghosts and spirits feel a special wrath against such men; and so their vengeance will never be relaxed even a little! You must know that Heaven’s way returns, and that the retribution of cause and effect is not off by a hair’s breadth. Why then must people destroy one another together?

So if we see through to the truth of it, what good is there in gambling? As the ten rules above set out, the principles they state are not only incisive, their purport is also exceedingly earnest. Here I earnestly hope that the people of the world will think calmly and wake with a start; that they will cut the bad habit of gambling clean in two with a single stroke and vow never to commit it again. Then the pit of gambling, which traps and harms men like a jackal or a wolf, can be leapt out of at a single turn—and that is indeed a great blessing. Alas! The harm gambling does to men is even fiercer than flood, fire, and thieves; yet men feel for it a special fondness, and cling to it in delusion, and even when it costs them their lives they are willing and content. This is truly too pitiable, too sorrowful! This is why I shed tears and set out this explanation for everyone. And if there are those who hear these principles and still will not turn back, then they are truly too foolish!
To separate or set at odds the flesh and blood of others.

This word ‘separate’ has two meanings. The one is pressing men for debts, and the extortion of officials and yamen runners, forcing people to sell their sons and daughters; the other is sowing dissension, so that father and son fall out and brothers contend. Both are the conduct of one who separates the flesh and blood of others and extinguishes all conscience. Such men do not know that between flesh and blood there is the bond of kindred born of the same blood, and naturally there dwells the affection of the natural bonds of kin. Therefore when the benevolent and the noble see the flesh and blood of others in poverty and unable to survive, they all use their wealth to help them through the difficulty, so that they may be kept safe and not separated; and where flesh and blood are at odds, they counsel and reconcile them, dissolving the misunderstandings between them so that they may dwell together in harmony. This too is an important path of cultivation.

Zong Chuan, in the night, heard the wife of the neighbour next door holding her child and weeping the whole night through. The next morning Zong Chuan asked the woman: ‘Why did you weep the whole night long last night?’ The woman answered: ‘Because my husband has committed a crime and is shut up in prison, I mean to sell myself and so buy my husband back!’ When Zong Chuan heard this he was deeply moved, and he brought out money to help the woman, so that husband and wife and children could be reunited as before. At that time Zong Chuan had long been distressed at having no son, yet that very year he had a son; and to this day Zong Chuan’s descendants are still quite flourishing!

An Tingbo was a man of ready eloquence, but he loved to sow discord among people. Even the closest flesh and blood, once he had stirred them up, would at once turn from affection to enmity. The brothers Li Zhongfu had originally lived together in great harmony, but because An Tingbo sowed discord between them, the brothers began to contend with one another. Cai Lun and Zhang Yi were intimate friends, and the affection between them was very good; but because they gave ear to An Tingbo’s troublemaking, in the end they actually broke off all relations. There is no knowing how many instances there were of An Tingbo sowing discord among others.
