Afterwards his life grew more and more wretched and more and more poverty-stricken, and poisonous sores broke out on both his cheeks, while his throat and tongue festered and suppurated, so that he could not get down any food; and in the end, amid cries and wailing, he gave up his breath.

After Emperor Yingzong of the Song dynasty came to the throne, he did not treat the palace eunuchs with enough generosity and seldom bestowed favours on them. And so the eunuchs constantly sowed discord in the presence of the Empress Dowager, causing discord between the two palaces of the Empress Dowager and the Empress. One day Han Qi and Ouyang Xiu were reporting matters before the Empress Dowager’s curtain; the Empress Dowager suddenly began to weep, and told Han Qi in detail of the discord between the two palaces. Han Qi said: ‘This is perhaps because the emperor is ill; when the emperor recovers, he will certainly not be like this!’ At that time the emperor was ill from fright and suspicion. Ouyang Xiu then advised the Empress Dowager: ‘Your Majesty served the late emperor for several decades, and the image of Your Majesty’s benevolence has long been made known throughout the realm. In former days Wencheng enjoyed the late emperor’s favour to the utmost, yet Your Majesty could take it calmly and live with her in harmony. Why is it that today, between Your Majesty and the emperor, mother and son, there should instead be no tolerance?’ Han Qi then said to the Empress Dowager again: ‘Your Majesty has no children of your own flesh; the emperor was raised by Your Majesty in the palace from childhood, and the Empress is moreover Your Majesty’s own niece. These are the son and daughter-in-law that Heaven arranged for Your Majesty! How could you not cherish and care for them?’ When the Empress Dowager heard this her mood grew a little more gentle. Han Qi feared the Empress Dowager might change, and so he used grave words to move her, saying: ‘We who are ministers cannot enter the palace freely to have audience with the emperor, and so the protection within the palace all rests upon Your Majesty! If the emperor is deprived of care and guidance, Your Majesty cannot shift this responsibility away!’ The Empress Dowager heard this and said in astonishment: ‘Prime Minister, what words are these you speak? My heart to cherish and guide them is all the more earnest!’ Those who had audience with the Empress Dowager together with Han Qi, hearing her words, were all so tense that the sweat ran down their backs. Some days later Han Qi had audience with the emperor alone, and he memorialised: ‘That Your Majesty could ascend the throne and become Son of Heaven is entirely the grace of the Empress Dowager! Knowing grace and repaying grace, Your Majesty cannot but repay the Empress Dowager! I beg Your Majesty to serve the Empress Dowager with added care, and then naturally all will be well.’ The emperor said: ‘We will accept your instruction.’ Some days later Han Qi went again to have audience with the emperor, and the emperor said: ‘The Empress Dowager still does not treat me well!’ Han Qi said: ‘From ancient times there has been no lack of sage and worthy emperors! Why is King Shun alone praised for his great filial piety? Were all the other emperors then unfilial? That parents should be kind and children filial is the ordinary thing and not worth speaking of; only where the parents are not kind and the children can still fulfil their filial duty is there enough to merit great praise. But I fear that Your Majesty in serving the Empress Dowager today has not yet reached the point of doing all that is in your heart and strength! Under heaven, what parents are there who do not love their children?’ When the emperor heard these words of Han Qi he was greatly moved and awakened. At that time many incidents arose at court; many of them came from petty men secretly sowing discord; but in the end it was by the efforts of Han Qi and several wise ministers of the day, working from within, that the Empress Dowager, the emperor, and the Empress were brought into harmony.
To seize by force the things that others love.

The things that others love—fields and houses, books and curios, vessels and clothes and ornaments, and the like—if one thinks up every means to seize them by force and make them one’s own, such conduct is not far from the ways of a robber! Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: ‘In the things themselves there is no such thing as beauty or ugliness; but if a man loves them, they will be prized by him as treasures. If another person were to seize by force the things I love, what would my own feelings be?’ Lu Zijin said: ‘At such a moment, if one considers the thing one loves as being seized by another, one need not fear that the greed in one’s heart will not be extinguished!’

Long ago Zhang Gai had a grand and imposing house. Because he was short of money, he mortgaged the house to Zhang Jun for a thousand strings of cash. Zhang Jun was exceedingly fond of Zhang Gai’s house and thought up ways to seize it and make it his own; so he took a generous gift of money and gave it to the broker who had acted as intermediary in the mortgage of the house, and moreover forged a contract of sale for the house. Later Zhang Gai became even more hard pressed, and came to beg Zhang Jun to end the mortgage arrangement and change it to an outright sale, so that he could get a little more money to tide himself over. At this point Zhang Jun brought out and showed Zhang Gai the contract by which Zhang Gai’s house had already been sold outright to him. Zhang Gai looked and was speechless; he knew that the contract had been tampered with by Zhang Jun, and with tears streaming down he vowed to Heaven: ‘May your sons and grandsons be as wretched as I am!’ Afterwards Zhang Jun’s sons and grandsons all lost their voices and became mute, and died of grave illness.

Alas! Fields and houses are things outside the body; and to seize them by force and make them one’s own, one uses one’s own dearest sons and grandsons to repay this sinful debt—what folly is this! Those who love to seize by force the things that others love should take this as a warning.
To help others do wrong, and to join with them in doing evil.

To help a man do wrong, to bring another’s evil deed to completion, and to be unable to guide others toward good—all of this counts as helping others do wrong. The Buddha said: ‘To expound the right Dharma and teach and transform living beings is called the gift of Dharma; the gift of Dharma enables living beings to hear the Buddhadharma, and by this cause and condition one may obtain immeasurable good retribution.’ The Ledger of Merits and Demerits says: ‘To teach a man to do evil—if another commits one evil deed because of it, one has one fault of one’s own; and if the evil deed committed is great, the fault must be reckoned according to the greatness of the deed. And having accumulated such evil causes, one will obtain immeasurable evil retribution.’ I hold that when one urges men toward good and to do good deeds, then the good deeds others do are all as though done by oneself, so that one’s own good conduct will grow daily purer; whereas when one helps others do evil, then the evil deeds others do are all as though done by oneself, so that one’s own evil conduct will increase day by day! In the end the reckoning of one’s own good and evil will be as far apart as heaven and earth, and the retribution of calamity and fortune will differ as much as cloud from mud! So everyone should understand this and know how to choose.

Yang Kai was the magistrate of Danyang county, and by nature exceedingly violent and overbearing; Yang Xun was his staff adviser, and loved to guess at other men’s intentions, hoping to win their favour. Thus although he plainly knew that Yang Kai had done wrong, he did not dare to oppose him. Whatever Yang Kai did, Yang Xun merely praised it as very well and very rightly done. Once, on a very hot summer day, Yang Kai ordered that the officials in the yamen who had not done their work well, and the prisoners in the jail, be beaten with rods—more than forty men in all, two of whom were beaten to death—and Yang Xun even praised him from the side, saying: ‘Beaten to death—very good!’ That night Yang Xun dreamed that a spirit rebuked him, saying: ‘You helped Yang Kai do evil, and you should be punished with the same crime as Yang Kai!’ Before long Yang Xun contracted a terrible disease and died. Seeing this story, those who serve as staff advisers today should know to be on their guard, and must not help others do wrong!

In Suzhou there was an old man of the surname Wu. His family was very poor and he had no occupation; he often went to the houses of the rich and noble and urged them to practise convenience and do good deeds, and when he met men of greedy disposition or violent temper he would certainly exhort and transform them earnestly and with skill. When he saw others do good deeds he would certainly praise and rejoice in them and bring their good deeds to completion; and so the good virtue he accumulated was very great, beyond all counting. His son Wu Congzhou won rank in the examinations while still young, and old Mr. Wu lived happily to a great age.

Among the Ten Great Vows of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra there is one vow called rejoicing in the merits of others, which means: ‘When one sees others create merit, one should rejoice in it and praise it.’ The sutras say: ‘The blessed reward of rejoicing in the merits of others is like one man selling incense and another buying incense, while those standing nearby catch the fragrance of the incense; and for these two, the seller and the buyer, their merit is not diminished because of it. Since the fruition of rejoicing in the merits of others is so supreme, then those who help others do wrong should turn their gaze inward and examine themselves well!’
To arbitrarily assert one's own authority and bully others.

A noble person is upright in his conduct and severe in his self-discipline, yet generous, gentle, and amiable toward others, so that people naturally come to feel awe, love, and admiration for him. But if a man is forever flaunting his power and bullying others, even though he can make them cower in fear, they will never submit from the heart, nor will they remember his kindly virtue. How can such a lover of showing off his authority rise above others?

During the Ming dynasty there was Shi Liangzuo of Nanjing, who served as censor of the western quarter of the city while living in the eastern quarter. Whenever he left his home or returned to it, the villagers who saw his carriage come by would not rise to show their respect. Shi Liangzuo was greatly angered and ordered that several of these villagers be seized and sent to the eastern censor for questioning and punishment. The eastern censor asked them, “Why did you not rise when the western censor's carriage passed by?” They replied, “We were all misled by Minister Ni!” The eastern censor asked, “How did Minister Ni mislead you?” They said, “Minister Ni is a native of Nanjing. While he was in charge of the Ministry of War, people would scatter and flee when his carriage went by, and he often had his attendants stop them and say, 'We are all from the same district; I cannot get down at the village gate to send you greetings, so how could I put you to the trouble of rising to greet me?' We were too foolish and took Minister Shi's conduct to be like that of Minister Ni, and so we did not rise to salute him. We never thought it would so offend him!” The eastern censor, hearing this explanation, laughed and released them. Minister Ni was the Duke of Wenyi, Ni Yue. Alas! When word of this reached Minister Shi, he too should have felt ashamed and stung with remorse.

In these latter days the evil of leaning on rank and power to swagger and treat others with arrogance is not confined to this alone. Some bring cruel laws and harsh punishments to poison the innocent; some let private likes and dislikes decide the weight of a sentence; some take bribes so that a just punishment is allowed to bend; some use public office for private ends and avenge personal grudges. Some even shield criminals, corner the marketplace, and collude with merchants. Though the forms are many and varied, all are cases of gratifying one's own will and strength in order to oppress the people, and such conduct has already offended Heaven. Yet dallying with power and influence can only domineer for a moment; the resentment it builds up, fermenting without cease, will bring its retribution the very moment the power runs out, at which point it is too late to repent. Would that one could bring this heart of regret into play a little earlier — how excellent that would be!

Lord Kou of the Song dynasty said, “The official who bends the law mourns when he loses office; the rich man who does not economize mourns when he grows poor; the craftsman who learned too little mourns when time has passed him by; he who will not study when he can mourns when the need arises; the drunkard's wild talk mourns when he is sober; he who takes no rest in health mourns when he falls ill.” These words are indeed the very key to lessening regret. Everyone should hold them fast in his heart and remind himself of them constantly.
To insult others in order to win one's own victory.

Even when one overcomes a man by reasoning, one may thereby stir up in him the very desire to win, until the reasons on both sides collide and refuse to be accepted. How much worse when one's own reasoning is not even adequate, and one forcibly storms, beats, and insults others in order to prevail! Lu Zijin said, “The sense of shame dwells in everyone; who would willingly accept another's insult? Yet there are those who insult others in order to win their own victory. Know that Heaven's way returns upon itself like a wheel — to slight another is in the end to slight oneself!”

Minister Lin Tuizhai, as he lay at the point of death, admonished his descendants, saying, “So long as you are willing to learn to take a loss, you will be right. Alas! Since antiquity many heroes ruined no small number of undertakings precisely because they could not take a loss. And since antiquity, too, many heroes accomplished no small number of undertakings precisely because they could bear insult and take a loss. Han Xin, for instance, endured the humiliation of creeping beneath a rascal's legs — one may say he took loss to the very utmost — and only thereby was later able to ascend the altar and be invested as general, and was enfeoffed by Liu Bang as the Prince of the Three Qis. The very young men of Huaiyin who once humiliated him all afterwards became his subordinates.”

From this we may see: the one who is humiliated today — can we be sure he will not be rich and honored tomorrow? And the one who humiliates others — can he guarantee that he will not be humiliated by others in days to come? Those, then, who delight in winning should think carefully over this principle.
To destroy the seedlings and grain that others have planted.

The common people rely on grain to sustain their lives. Moreover, the farmer's spring ploughing and summer weeding in planting rice are laborious in the extreme, and the payment of taxes and the support of the household all depend upon the harvest. How then can anyone block the irrigation works so that the fields go dry, breach the dikes so that the paddies are drowned, or let cattle trample the fields and eat the grain? When the grain produced by Heaven and Earth is left unreaped and the farmer's toil comes to nothing, such a man is cruel beyond words! Nor is that all. If those in high places do not value the farming season, take no care for irrigation, and thereby harm the peasants' harvest, this too is a deed that ruins the crops of others, and they may be condemned under the same crime.

In the ding-wei year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, a villager of Huguang named Li Jia made his living by selling cattle. Every harvest season, at the fourth watch of the night, he would turn his herd loose to graze on the rice planted in the fields of others, sometimes over an expanse several li wide, and he did this habitually; because the district was vast and thinly settled, no one could easily detect it. Then one day Li Jia was struck dead by lightning, and upon his back there appeared four red characters, “The Cattle Let Loose to Harm the Crops,” meaning that Li Jia had loosed his herd to destroy the rice that others had planted.
To break apart another person's marriage.

Only after the relation of husband and wife exists does the relation of father and son arise, and so the way of marriage becomes the more weighty. There are several ways of destroying a marriage. Some contrive every sort of slander to break it before it is made; some raise every kind of obstacle to break it on the very eve of making; some stir up trouble out of clear sky to break it after it is made. How could they know that marriage is determined by Heaven — how can any man destroy it? As for marriages that bear to be broken, it simply was not meant to be a marriage after all. Yet partings and unions are fixed by Heaven, and a man who stirs up his heart to destroy the marriage of others incurs a guilt equal to that of taking life. Alas! Why must the evildoer needlessly cast away his own conscience and commit so great a wrong? As for husbands and wives who were of themselves harmonious, when the wife's family resents the husband for his humble birth and stirs up division, or when the parents-in-law distrust the daughter-in-law for her poverty and take heed of slander — these are cases of kinsmen murdering each other, worse in cruelty than killing with staff and blade, and all should be taken as a warning. To renounce an engagement because one scorns poverty, or to force a marriage on the strength of one's power, especially offends the natural order. If a judge perverts the law and wrongfully rules for a divorce, he gravely damages his hidden merit and will certainly draw Heaven's punishment — this is what a judge ought especially to guard against.

Ge Dingnai of Siming, while he was studying at the local academy, passed by the Temple of the Earth God every day on his way to school. One day the temple keeper dreamed that the earth god said to him, “Whenever the top graduate Ge passes here I must rise and salute him. I hope you will build me a low wall to screen me from his sight.” The keeper accordingly set about building such a wall; but no sooner had he hired the workmen than he dreamed again, and the earth god said, “There is no need to build the wall. Ge Dingnai has written a divorce for someone, and his name has been struck off the rolls of merit entirely by Heaven, so I need no longer rise and salute him.” It turned out that a villager at the time meant to abandon his wife but could not write, and so had asked Ge Dingnai to draft the document for him. When Ge heard the keeper's words he was filled with regret, and devoted himself wholly to mending the couple's marriage. In later years he passed only the provincial examination, the examination conducted by the province for selecting candidates for office, and his rank never rose above that of deputy commissioner.

When Zheng Shutong was small, his parents betrothed him to a young girl of the Xia family. After he grew up and passed the examinations, that girl had by then become mute through illness. His uncles therefore urged him not to marry her, but Zheng held firm, saying, “If I do not marry the Xia daughter, she will have nowhere to turn. Moreover I was betrothed to her before she became mute; now that she is mute, to cast her off would be more than my heart can bear.” So he married the Xia girl after all. Later his rank rose to that of an attendant of the palace, and his son, too, passed the examinations.

The family instructions of Minister Sima Guang of the Song dynasty say, “In arranging a marriage one should first examine the character of both the young man and the young woman together with the standards of their families, and make it all clear; one must not merely envy the other side's wealth and rank. If the intended son-in-law is truly worthy, though he be poor and lowly now, how do we know he will not be rich and honored in days to come? If he is unworthy, though honored today, how do we know he will not be poor and lowly tomorrow? The wife, above all, is the pivot of a household's rise and decline. If one takes a wife merely out of envy for her family's momentary wealth, she will lean on her family's position to slight her husband and show no respect to her parents-in-law, growing into pride and jealousy, so that the house will never know peace again. Even if one grows rich through the wife's wealth and rises in office through her family's influence, can a man of true spirit fail to feel ashamed? The vulgar, too, delight in making careless betrothals while the children are still in arms. By the time they grow up, the boy may have turned to vice and become a scoundrel, the girl may be stricken with some foul disease, or the family may be so poor as to suffer hunger and cold, or go off to office in a distant land. Then, breaking faith with their vows, they end in lawsuits — of such examples there are very many. Therefore, whether it be a boy or a girl, wait until they are grown before arranging the marriage. Then, after the letters pass back and forth, and the young man's family sends gifts to the young woman's home to announce their wish to take her as a wife, and after some months of coming and going and mutual observation, the marriage may be consummated. In this way there will be no regret after the wedding, and this standard is what later generations should take as a model.”
To grow rich by whatever shabby means, gain wealth by mere chance, and then give oneself airs.

The word hu — from the Analects phrase “if he be rich” — means this: that without being greatly rich, having merely grown rich by shabby means is enough to swell him with pride, and it plainly portrays the petty man who, the moment he comes by money, acts heedlessly and at random. For having money breeds pride, pride breeds extravagance, extravagance breeds wastefulness, and wastefulness breeds the seizing of unjust gain — exploiting others to enrich oneself. Such a man is certain to trust in his wealth to be fierce and stubborn, to ride roughshod over his fellows in the village, and to slight his relatives and friends. On his own pleasures he will scatter a thousand pieces of gold, while toward others he will begrudge a single coin. Yet power, however dazzling for the moment, is easily worn away; and besides, Heaven's way abhors what is full and overflowing. So before his pride has been visited on others, calamity has already fallen on himself, and such things have proved true again and again without exception.

In former days there was a rich man named Yang Xi, greedy of nature, shallow of insight, and narrow of spirit. The gold, silver, treasure, cloth, and grain he hoarded and piled up increased day by day. His friend Chen Dongtang urged him, saying, “A man who only accumulates wealth and does not know how to give away will surely meet with some strange calamity. Why not perform some acts of charity, so that in this way you may long preserve your wealth?” But Yang Xi would not listen. Two or three years later Chen Dongtang told another, “From my observation Yang Xi's disaster is near. Before, he was merely greedy and miserly, a man to be held in contempt. Lately I hear he has grown more and more arrogant and violent, treating people harshly and heedless of all reason, until he will venture any wickedness. Is this not bringing calamity upon himself all the faster?” Not long after Chen said this, Yang Xi was indeed killed by robbers.

The ancients said, “Reverence and frugality are the beginning of a man's blessings; pride and stinginess are the omen of his calamity. Therefore he who is willing to cultivate his blessings may gradually obtain all that is auspicious and happy, while he who ventures to do evil deeds is often brought down all at once. From ancient times to the present, of such examples there are countless numbers!”
To seek escape when one ought not to be spared, and to do so without a trace of shame.

The Buddha said, “I have two white dharmas by which I can save and ferry across all living beings. What are the two white dharmas? One is called shame, and the other is called remorse.” Confucius said, “In his conduct a man should have a sense of shame,” meaning that he should feel compunction for his own wayward behavior. The Book of Rites says, “In the face of peril, do not seek to be spared.” It means that when a man faces calamity he must not harbor the hope of escaping it by chance. Now there are many who set aside the principles of being human and the provisions of the law in order to gain some lucky reprieve from disaster, and who show not even a trace of shame. Such people are utterly without character and have sunk very low indeed!

In the Tang dynasty Geshu Han and An Lushan were both great generals, and the two forever quarreled and fumed over this matter or that. When An Lushan rebelled, Geshu Han was seized by his troops and brought before him. An Lushan said, “You used to slight me often. Now what do you have to say?” Geshu Han, prostrate on the ground, replied, “Your servant's vulgar eyes could not recognize a sage.” An Lushan laughed heartily and enfeoffed him as Minister of Works. Afterwards, when An Lushan put all the Tang generals who had surrendered to the sword, Geshu Han too was killed.

The Song minister Fan Chunren, the son of Fan Zhongyan, once debated the affairs of state with Sima Guang, and the two were of differing minds. Later, when petty men held the reins at court, they sought to punish Sima Guang and his party of upright gentlemen. Another minister, Han Wei, had happened to be at odds with Sima Guang in the days when Sima Guang was in power, and so he was spared and left unpunished. Someone urged Fan Chunren, saying, “You may follow the precedent of Han Wei and ask the court to spare you from punishment.” Fan said, “When I formerly discussed state affairs alongside Sima Guang, even where our opinions differed, it was right to speak. If today I sought my own escape so as not to be punished by the court, that would be wrong. Better to die with an unburdened conscience than to live with a guilty one!” Thereupon Fan Chunren was degraded and banished to a very distant place.

Master Lu Zijin said, “To be spared when one ought not to be spared is what is called a lucky reprieve, and such a man should feel the deepest shame and self-reproach.” Yet now there are those who, relying on their power and position, sneer at the slaughter of the loyal and good, and mock at the destruction of men of integrity and principle. Such petty men, though they scramble through with their lives, have first let their consciences die. What face have they left to show the world? We need not even speak of the retribution they shall reap after death amid the curses of all. As for the rabble of the marketplace who commit every wrong and yet manage to evade the punishment of the law, they do not understand that this is precisely Heaven deepening their calamity. So they go on habitually in their wickedness, with not a shred of shame and no wish to reform, and in the end cannot escape the net of Heaven's justice. To die without once awakening — how pitiful it is!”
To claim another's kindness as one's own in order to curry favor, and to shift one's own faults onto others in order to escape blame.

To claim as one's own a kindness one never bestowed is at best a scheme to win the other's good will for a moment. Let him make the slightest investigation and the truth will surely come to light; then the other will not only feel no gratitude toward you, he will despise you for conjuring facts out of nothing. In the same way, to wish to shove one's own faults onto others is at best a scheme to dodge responsibility for a moment. Let them make the slightest investigation and the truth will surely come to light; then they will not only refuse to forgive you, they will all the more loathe your craftiness. Thus the petty man is truly wronged in being a petty man.

The Song prime minister Wang Zeng, whenever someone came with a request begging to be promoted in office or moved to a better post, unfailingly refused with a stern expression. And to those whom he did promote and employ he would never once mention the matter. His grandson once said to him, “Sir, why do you not tell those whom you have promoted?” Wang Zeng replied, “Child, the appointment of worthy men is the emperor's affair. If I were to tell them, so that they learned who recommended and promoted them, that would be showing private favor and selling personal kindness.”

In the county office of Xingshan there was a clerk who was a past master at deceiving people. Whenever the magistrate conferred a kindness on someone he would say, “It is all thanks to the influence I brought to bear on the magistrate.” And when the magistrate forgave someone and no longer scolded or punished him, he would say, “It is all the merit of my speaking up and preserving him.” Whatever good order the county office brought about, he took to be a kindness of his own, and everyone praised him for possessing a power that could turn the world around. Later the magistrate committed an offense and got into trouble, and the officials above arrested the clerk along with him, saying to him, “The magistrate did everything you told him; whatever he did was of your prompting, and so you cannot escape your share of the crime.” They had him beaten alive with the whip until he died.

There was a Ming dynasty top graduate, Wang Hua, who, while holding office, was falsely accused by someone. Others urged him to clear himself, but Wang Hua said, “This is the doing of a friend who passed the same examination with me in the same year. If I defended myself, I should be accusing a friend.” And so he refused on that account to clear his name. Later his son Wang Shouren, known as Master Wang Yangming, held office in the capital. Hearing the scholars of the capital discussing the matter on every side, he wished to submit a memorial to the emperor to redress his father's being slandered. When Wang Hua learned that his son meant to clear his name, he immediately sent a fast letter to stop him and said, “Do you take this matter to be your father's disgrace? I have nothing shameful about me at all. If today you would groundlessly accuse and expose my friend, you would instead bring a great disgrace upon me.” Wang Yangming, listening to his father's words, no longer submitted a memorial in his father's defense.

To be willing rather to own one's own fault than to advertise the errors of a friend — is not such cultivation of character a hundred thousand times beyond that of the ordinary man? How could a man of such refinement ever push his own faults onto others?
To shift one's own calamity onto others, and to unload one's own sins onto others.

To shift calamity onto another is like marrying off a daughter to another — the other must be willing to take her. To sell blame to another is like selling goods to another — the other must be willing to buy. So the deep-laid cunning of such a man, and the wickedness and crookedness of his mind, are far too great. Thus the retribution awaiting him must be very dire. In the end the calamity he shifts falls upon himself, and the blame he sells returns to his own person. Shifting calamity and selling blame therefore bring no benefit to oneself whatever.

During the Song dynasty, while Guo Huangzhong was in charge of the military affairs of Yun'an, he one day visited the Qixia Palace to pay his respects and offer incense. That very night he dreamed that a deity told him, “Your honor Guo, your services to Yun'an are very great, and every one of its people has received your kindness. Yet there is one wicked affair, done in deep secrecy, that I dare not fail to set before you. Tomorrow a man will escort nine men accused of killing oxen to your office. I hope that, besides these nine, you will look all the more carefully into the matter.” The next morning Guo asked the Inspectorate whether any case had been accepted. He found indeed that a single soldier had brought in nine suspects, saying of himself, “It was I who captured these men who killed the oxen, and I have brought them here to beg your honor's reward.” In truth the oxen had been killed by the soldier himself, and he was fastening the offense on those nine men, seizing them and escorting them to the officials to ask a reward. When Guo questioned him thus, the soldier bowed his head and confessed his crime.

In Zhejiang there was a man named Cheng Qi who had always given himself to blackguardly conduct. Whenever quarrels or fights broke out in the village, he would be sure to say to the parties, “Which of you can bring wine to make me drunk, and money to pay me, and I will win justice for him?” When someone met his terms, he would then, in his drunkenness, go and settle the account with the other party, cursing and beating him and stopping at nothing. He also devised schemes for men to bring ruin upon their enemies; so long as there was profit in it, there was no villainy he would not risk. One day, having been hired to go to the yamen and take another man's beating in his place, he was beaten there into mortal injury and died, his body being laid out by the roadside. Those who saw him all cursed and mocked him, saying, “Cheng Qi! Evil may be sold, but can one sell one's life as well?”
To purchase a hollow reputation, so that others will praise one.

Mencius said, “That which is within must show itself without.” And Zhuangzi said, “Fame is the guest of substance.” How then can one buy reputation? To buy it is to spend money on it, or to contrive schemes, using every art to draw it to oneself. We constantly see that from ancient times down, loyal ministers, filial sons, chaste women, and upright gentlemen, at the very moment they enjoyed a glorious name, were sure to meet with straitened adversity. Why is this? For fame, too, is a kind of blessing, and Heaven and Earth, gods and spirits, will not let one man enjoy a fullness of blessing. So one who is abundant on one side is sure to be lacking on another — this is a fixed principle. Moreover, for a man who has no real practice and sets out to purchase reputation, the rebuffs that await him are past all imagining. Master Yu Tieqiao said, “At present there are scholars whose essays may be carved and circulated in the world, and yet every time they sit the examinations they fail and fall back. There are officials who enjoy a fine name among the people, so that the folk sing of their virtuous governance, and yet in the same post they often go ten years without promotion. I fear these are one and all caught in the failing of purchasing reputation.”

The high-minded recluse Chen Xiyi of the Song dynasty once warned Zhong Fang, saying, “Fame is a fair and lovely thing that men of every age delight in, yet it is deeply dreaded by Heaven and Earth, gods and spirits. For this reason no one under heaven has ever enjoyed a flawless reputation. Now your name is about to rise, but there must surely be something that will come to shatter it and bring you low, so you must be especially careful and cautious.” Afterwards Zhong Fang's later years did not hold firm, precisely because the carriage he rode was adorned in too extravagant a fashion, and by that means he lost the fine reputation he had won.

If Zhong Fang, worthy as he was, could still be undone by the fame that redounded too much upon him, then how far beyond imagining will be the ruin and the exposed feet of those in our day who are sham men of letters, sham essayists, sham moralists, and sham upholders of honor, each still trumpeting the others and making their names known! We constantly see that the calamities which overtake the very famous are often crueler than those of ordinary men, so those who chase after empty fame have all the more reason to take warning. For chasing after empty fame does not merely cut away one's blessings; it draws down upon oneself a grave calamity. Therefore, in doing good, the precious thing is that it remain unknown, so that one may store up hidden merit, and then Heaven's reward will surely be a different thing.
To put on an appearance of smiling, welcoming, and gracious charm, while within the heart conceals a cunning and malicious intent that harms others.

The Surangama Sutra says, “When the mind-ground is made even, then the ground of the world is everywhere even.” This means that one should know that all phenomena are made by the mind alone. When our mind-ground is brought to a state of true evenness, it can attract even the earth of this world to become level. For if a man's heart is vicious and his breast conceals a mind that harms others so that men cannot detect it, then even amid laughter and chatter he plants his spears in secret, and in the very act of paying court to a man he sets his snare. The craft and treachery of such a mind outdo even the perils of lofty crags, deep rivers, and rushing rapids. Master Yuan Liaofan said, “The thing Heaven and Earth, gods and spirits most detest is a man of scheming and treacherous heart. Therefore Heaven, in requiting those of exceedingly sinister mind, will sometimes strike with special severity. This is true indeed.”

The Tang minister Li Yifu served as a chancellor, an office as exalted as that of prime minister. His countenance was gentle and deferential, and in speaking with a man his face was sure to wear a smile; yet in truth he was exceedingly crafty and sinister, envious and cruel, and skilled at laying false charges. To the men of his own day he was called “the knife smiling within the smile.” And because his art of harming men was so dexterous and so soft, they also called him “Li the Cat.” In the end Li Yifu fell into trouble, was degraded by the court and banished to Junzhou, where he died, and his descendants, too, sank into obscurity.
To thwart the strengths of others, so that they cannot give them full play.

The noble man delights in speaking well of the good deeds of others and will not cover up another's strengths. The strengths of others ought precisely to be nourished and fostered, so that he may be drawn on to still greater heights and have his talents brought to fullest flower. If one thwarts and suppresses him, so that he droops his head and his heart grows cold and he can no longer enlarge his strengths, this is brought about by nothing but one's own envy.

The Song poet Mu Xiu wrote excellent verse and was very well known. He often went to the capital on pleasure, and someone wrote one of his poems upon the wall of the palace. When Emperor Zhenzong saw Mu Xiu's verse he praised it greatly and asked, “Whose poem is this? The man writes so skillfully — why do the ministers not recommend him to me?” The treacherous minister Ding Wei said to Zhenzong, “This man's conduct falls short of his writings.” From that time on the emperor asked no more.

Ding Wei's intentions were indeed so sinister that he later came to no good end. Alas! Those who thwart and oppress others think only of covering up another's strengths, and give no thought to the fact that in doing so they ruin their own virtue.
To screen one's own faults and not know how to reform.

The petty man would rather, at whatever cost to Heaven's principle, dress up his faults and screen his shortcomings, and fancies besides that he is wiser than others and has come out ahead. How could he know the principle that Heaven's way cannot be escaped? The word “screen” here means to gloss over from every direction and firmly refuse to acknowledge the fact. It is like a man who falls ill and must be treated at once; if he conceals his illness from the physician and puts off the chance to be treated, it will turn into a serious disease and injure him for the rest of his life. Master Zhu Zai'an said, “To screen faults does not mean only to screen one's own. Whoever among descendants, household, or retainers commits an offense or sin, if I fail to guard against it in advance and instead let them grow into faults and sins — this too is screening faults. As for a father who teaches his children too sternly while the mother constantly shields the children's misdeeds and keeps them from the father, this too is a great failing of screening faults.”

Li Shuqing held the office of clerk of works in the commandery and was most upright in integrity and most prudent in word and deed. His colleague Sun Rong, however, was a petty man of sinister mind and sycophantic slander. Fearing that Li Shuqing might expose his faults, Sun Rong grew jealous of him and, striking first, traduced him. Li Shuqing could not clear himself and so, brooding and dejected, sickened and died; his wife, in her grief and fury, hanged herself. Before long Sun Rong was struck dead by lightning, and at the ribs beneath his arm there appeared eight characters: “He screened his own faults and recklessly destroyed a good man.”

Xu Jie, Duke Wenzhen of the Ming dynasty, was once ordered to superintendent the schools of central Zhejiang. A candidate, in the closing words of his essay, wrote the phrase “Yan lamented the preeminence of Confucius.” Duke Xu struck out those five characters, wrote the comment “invention,” placed the essay in the fourth grade, and meant to punish the candidate. The candidate reported to Duke Xu, saying, “The phrase 'Yan lamented the preeminence of Confucius' comes from the Fa Yan of Master Yang; it is not something I invented.” Hearing this, Duke Xu rose and said to the candidate, “I had only the good fortune to win my degree a little earlier than you; in truth I am quite without learning, and so I came near the grave error of punishing you.” And at once he changed the essay to the first grade. The men of his time all admired Duke Xu's broad-mindedness, and later he rose to be a grand secretary.

Whoever has merit and virtue is sure to have a great breadth of mind: he can embrace and contain all things, and will never shield his own shortcomings. Reading this story, one may understand the principle. And one who studies the Buddha's teaching must first rid himself of the notion of a self; the Confucians, in treating of benevolence, begin at once with the discipline of subduing the self. All of this is aimed at uprooting the fault of shielding one's own shortcomings.
Using authority and power to coerce and oppress.

The phrase “giving free rein to his will and putting on airs of authority” discussed above means no more than wantonly assuming a posture of power for oneself; but to coerce and oppress is actually to use force to threaten and crush others. For instance, an official may extort a confession by harsh torture, or compel the common people to labor on public works and set them a deadline for completion; he may press for the collection of taxes and grain as urgently as though sparks were flying; or the rich and noble may insult and bully women, force a man to sell his fields, demand repayment of a debt by force, and press for rent—all such things are “trading on authority to coerce and oppress,” and they must surely call down the wrath of Heaven and the resentment of men; there is no one who escapes retribution.

The history of the Han dynasty records that Shao Feng, the governor of Xuancheng Commandery, was greedy, cruel, and tyrannical. One day Shao Feng suddenly turned into a tiger and came into Xuancheng to eat people. When the common folk saw this tiger they called it Lord Feng; and strange to tell, whenever the tiger heard anyone call it Lord Feng, it would meekly wag its tail and go away. So a ballad arose in that place, which ran: “Learn not from Lord Feng, who in life misruled the people and in death devours them.” The meaning is: “In holding office, never imitate Shao Feng! While he lived he did not govern the people well, and after death he turned into a tiger to eat them.” This old tale may serve as a mirror for officials who have no pity for the people.

In the Ming dynasty there was a country gentleman in the Huguang region who, after taking office, saved up a thousand ounces of gold and then sent men to redeem his ancestral property, saying to his son, “At the current price it is worth several times what it was originally; so redeeming it is the cheapest way for us.” His son was only twelve at the time. Hearing this, the boy said nothing, and did not answer his father at once; only after a while did he slowly ask, “Father, how many years is it since our ancestral property was sold to others?” His father said, “Thirty years.” He asked again, “How many households bought it from us?” His father said, “Some twenty-odd families.” The son said, “I have seen the law of the Great Ming: once ancestral property has been sold for more than five years, it may not be redeemed. Why does Father not keep the king's law?” A retainer of the household said, “To redeem one's ancestral property is a matter of family honour!” The son said, “You know only how to flatter. If Father has taken office and can buy better property besides, is that not honour too? Why must these fields be redeemed?” His father said, “If I insist on redeeming the ancestral property, would the villagers dare to disobey me?” The son said, “It is precisely because I fear the villagers stand in awe of our family's power that I say this forced redemption will injure our hidden virtue.” His father said, “It is very good that a child should understand the principle of accumulating hidden virtue. Then today I shall refund them a little more of the incidental expenses they paid when they bought the land.” The son said, “The fees and paperwork are a small matter. Our family can easily buy land, but for those small households buying land is far harder. Suppose a family lives by farming ten acres; now that we redeem the land, and they must buy elsewhere, they can only buy back five acres. How can we bear to let half of that family go hungry?” So he urged his father not to redeem the ancestral property, but to store up hidden virtue for the sake of his descendants. After a long while his father answered, “My son, what you say is very reasonable; only the eighteen acres beside our ancestral graves must be redeemed, to serve as sacrificial land.” The son then begged his father to draw up the contract at the current price and make an honest purchase, and his father followed his advice. The villagers, moved by gratitude for his kindness, prayed for him at the shrine of the Fierce General, beseeching peace for him. Later, when the son was eighteen, he passed the examinations in one success after another, and the court promoted him to be prefect of Yanzhou. One day, as he rode out to receive an imperial decree, his horse stumbled on a bridge and fell into the river; and in that moment of utmost peril the Fierce General suddenly appeared and caught the son with his hand, setting him upright at the bridge's edge. Only then did they know that this was the response to the villagers' devout prayers and blessings. The son afterwards lived to be more than eighty.

Of the rich and noble who use their power and influence to threaten others, the cases are too many to count. How could such a family ever produce a son who understood how to extend the compassion of that young man of Huguang; who in every matter urged his parents to refrain from trading on authority and oppressing others, and to store up hidden virtue, that blessing might come to the household? This is rare indeed! One cannot know what hidden virtue that Huguang gentleman had stored up, that he should beget such a son.
Giving free rein to violence and savagery, and taking human life.

Giving free rein to violence and savagery is an offense that generals, chancellors, officials, and commoners alike may commit; but the gravest form is to use an army to slaughter at will. Next comes the passing of judgment, which easily falls into excess and reaches the innocent. Violence is already impermissible—how much worse to give one's own heart free rein to commit it? This is the most conspicuous and greatest of evils. And yet one who holds the power to unleash violence, if he refuses to unleash it and instead exercises a benevolent heart, saving the lives of many, has thereby performed the greatest and most conspicuous of benevolent deeds. “Taking life,” moreover, includes the taking of the lives of creatures as well; this too one must understand.

In the Yuan dynasty, Huang, the assistant prefect of Guangzhou, and his wife both fell ill, and lay on separate beds in the house to rest and recover. His wife dreamed that an underworld official, holding a document and leading several jailers with cangues and chains in their hands, drew open her mosquito netting and was about to seize her, when he said, “Eh! It is not this one!” He then went to the bed opposite, lifted the netting and looked, and said, “Right! This is the one!” Husband and wife woke in terror at the same moment, and Huang said to his wife, “I am certainly a dead man. When I was ordered to pacify the rebels, I killed many innocent people over and above; today they have all come to demand my life.” The next day Huang died.
Cutting cloth or silk for no good reason.

In ancient times, before the loom was invented, cloth and silk were woven by women with their own hands, thread by thread and strand by strand, through untold hardship; so unless there was no other way, one could not bear to cut them. As for fine damask and satin, they are made at the cost of countless silkworm lives, and all the more should they be treasured. To cut them without cause and make them into garments is likewise an offense.

A few days after the death of Wang, the wife of Zhao Shizhou, she possessed her maidservant and said, “All my life I loved to use silk and cloth wastefully, and when I washed my hair and my feet I used far too much water; the underworld has judged me guilty of this, and every day I am punished with the whip. I beg you to convey my meaning to Shizhou.” When Zhao Shizhou's family heard this, they were filled with grief.

Zhu Wuyou's household was exceedingly wealthy; his wife and concubines all wore garments of the finest, brightly figured silk, and even their stockings were made of damask and satin. The several concubines he kept were yet more extravagant still. Later, after Zhu Wuyou died, his wife and concubines went about in broken stockings and worn shoes, and could not obtain so much as a foot of cloth from anyone.

Looking through the emperors of past and present: Duke Wen of Jin, however cold the day, would not wear two fur garments; the ruler of the Liu Song would always wear a worn cotton coat hidden beneath his outer robe; the consort of Emperor Wen of Han wore dresses whose skirts never trailed upon the ground; Empress Ma, wife of Emperor Taizu of Ming, always wore a plain cloth skirt; Emperor Wenzong of Tang once held out his sleeve for the assembled ministers to see, saying, “This garment I wear has already been washed three times”; and Emperor Taizu of Song, seeing a princess in a short jacket of bright colours, admonished her, saying, “Those who are rich and noble must learn to treasure their blessings.” These emperors, empresses, consorts, and princesses, in their exalted stations, were yet so sparing of their blessings. How is it, then, that ordinary households today vie with one another in dress, striving in novelty and splendour, and waste and squander as they please? Having begun by creating the evil karma of waste, they must in future suffer the calamities that extravagance brings. Consider the people today who are clothed in rags and suffer cold and hunger—were they not the sons of rich households who once wore gorgeous raiment?
Slaughtering and cooking creatures contrary to ritual propriety.

The Book of Rites says, “The Son of Heaven does not kill an ox without cause, nor a great officer a sheep, nor a scholar a dog or a pig.” Mencius says, “A man of seventy may eat meat.” For the sages had the virtue of cherishing life, and would not slaughter living creatures at will; even when at times they slaughtered fowl and fish for the ancestral sacrifices, for the entertainment of guests, or for the support of parents, it was done only because there was no other way. They did not teach the people to slaughter living creatures every day and give free rein to the cravings of the belly and mouth; to do so is contrary to propriety. Taishang, whose heart is compassion itself, long ago declared, “Even insects, grasses, and trees may not be harmed”; yet now, expounding the Dharma for the people of the world, He is compelled to descend a level, and sets before them the two words “contrary to propriety,” hoping only that they will not overstep the rule. This too is the sages' intent, adopted because there was no other way.

The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says, “If all people ate no meat, then no one would kill living beings.” If people today cannot give up meat altogether, they may for the time being take a gradual course and rid themselves of the mind to kill, learning the ancient rule of abstaining from four kinds of meat. First, meat from an animal one has seen killed—do not eat it. Second, meat from an animal whose death cry one has heard—do not eat it. Third, meat from an animal killed expressly for oneself—do not eat it. Fourth, meat from an animal one has raised oneself—do not eat it. Keeping these four rules, one's ordinary fare need not be affected, and toward living beings one may be reckoned to have no intent to kill them. As for oxen and dogs, they have laboured on man's behalf and above all should not be eaten; if this can be done, then slaughtering and cooking contrary to propriety may perhaps be somewhat reduced.

In the region north of the river there was a man who shot down a male wild goose and killed and cooked it to eat. Then the female goose came and hovered over it, refusing to leave; and when the pot lid was lifted, she flew down into the pot and was cooked together with the male. When the people of that region heard of it they were deeply moved, and afterwards ate no more goose. Yuan Haowen, the great poet of the day, buried the two geese together, and the place of burial was called Goose Mound. The man who had shot the goose died not long after the burial.

In the Tang dynasty there was a man named Xu Yan who made his living selling fish. Suddenly his body turned as red as fire, and the pain was as though he were being fried in a pan. He said, “I see fire burning my body, and ten thousand fish pressing in to devour my flesh.” Someone urged him, saying, “You must at once do deeds of merit and transfer the merit to them.” So he took out money and had two images of Guanyin made; he also vowed to change his trade and sell fish no more, and his whole family gave up meat and wine. Only then did his illness pass.

In the region of Jiangsu and Anhui there is a custom of cooking eels by putting them alive into boiling water, so that some time passes before they die. In the Tianbao era, a fishmonger of Dangtu in Anhui told his son to cook an eel for them to eat, and the eel suddenly changed into a snake several feet long; when the son turned to look again, all the other eels had likewise become snakes—and having become snakes, they all departed. The son fell ill from this, and after a single day of illness he died; and within one month the seven members of the fishmonger's household died one after another.

Zhao Bi of Sizhou once dreamed that his dead wife came to him, saying, “Husband, while I lived I loved to take life, and above all I loved to eat drunken crab, and by this I killed a great many crabs. After I died, King Yama ordered his ghostly attendants to drive me to Crab Mountain; a multitude of crabs gathered round and dug out my eyes with their claws, and my whole body streams with blood as I suffer there day and night without cease. I beg you to write out for me seven scrolls of the Diamond Sutra, and I may then rely on the merit of the Diamond Prajñā to pull me free of the pains of hell.” Zhao Bi granted his dead wife's request and wrote out the seven scrolls of the Diamond Sutra for her; and when he had finished, he dreamed again that his wife said to him, “Husband, by the merit of the sutra you have written I have been raised up to the heavens.”
Story Five:

There was a scholar of Xin'an who went to Mount Huang to study. He was fond of catching the monkeys of the mountain to eat; and afterwards, when his wife gave birth, the labour was so painful and hard that she brought forth a monkey.
Story Six:

In Chuzhou there was a butcher who, whenever he slaughtered an ox, would have his son stand beside him and watch him use the knife, learning his way with it, in the hope that the son might carry on his trade. One day, while the butcher slept, his son took him in his sound sleep for an ox, and taking up the knife he killed this ox and even cut off its head. Everyone who saw the sight was greatly shocked, and asked the son why he had done it. The son answered, “What I saw was an ox, not my father. My father is always teaching me to slaughter oxen, and today when I saw the ox asleep I thought I would try, for my father was teaching me the way to kill an ox.”
Story Seven:

When Guan Shiren was young, he once encountered several ghosts at dawn on New Year's Day, around the fifth watch, and loudly demanded of them, “What ghosts are you, and what are you doing here?” The ghosts answered, “We are plague ghosts, and we have come into the world of men to spread pestilence.” Guan Shiren said, “Will my household be visited by the plague?” The plague ghosts answered, “Your household, because it does not eat beef, will be spared the plague.”

Among the offenses people commit, the taking of life is the gravest; and among the offenses of taking life, the killing of an ox is the gravest; and one who eats beef is guilty equally with the man who kills the ox. Mr. Xiao Dongbai said, “I exhort the people of the world not to eat beef. For the ox plows the fields and draws the cart for man, and has done great service in the world, yet is slain instead. Consider whence comes the food we eat: most of it is owing to the ox's labour. How can we bear to kill the ox and cook it for food?” He said also, “When the ox is killed, its body is cut limb from limb, yet its two eyes remain open. Does the ox open its eyes after death for nothing, and to no purpose? It is watching to see how long those who kill it and eat it can keep their human bodies. With such karma of killing and such hatred, how could it fail to become an ox itself in the life to come?” As for the dog, it too has laboured for man and is most loyal and faithful to its master, and does no harm to man; therefore the sin of killing dogs and eating their flesh is very great. Not only do peddlers and servants greedily eat dog meat; even men of the upper classes and scholars, and those of high office, often take eating dog flesh for a dashing and free-spirited act, and prettify the dog with the name “earth sheep.” The purpose of study is to understand principle—how can one be so muddled about this matter? Mr. Song Jue said, “If in this life I do not sternly rid myself of this habit of eating dog meat, in the next life I shall have a tail.” In my view there is no need to wait for the next life: only look at those who kill dogs and eat dog meat—when they pass by, a crowd of dogs barks madly at them. What is the reason? Perhaps their bodily form has already begun to change.

Yet we are but one person, or one household, keeping the rule against eating beef, and the good it produces is still very limited. Why not make a subscription book, carry it with us wherever we go, and, meeting others, gently exhort and win them over, so that they too may give it up forever and eat beef no more? Would that not be better still? And when one appeals to people for contributions, those with good roots and faith will mostly give goods and money; whereas we ask of others only that they not take life and not eat beef—it costs the other not a grain of rice nor a single coin, yet the merit and blessing obtained are truly beyond telling. The Record of Responses says, “One who can persuade a hundred people to give up eating beef may lengthen his own life by twelve years.” Here again is a most plain and effective proof. May everyone arouse the resolve to exhort others earnestly—the merit is measureless.

The analysis in this section is especially detailed on the matter of not killing dogs; the analysis of not killing other fowl and livestock has been kept brief. Readers are asked to consult the explanations and analyses of the passages “with a compassionate heart toward creatures,” “insects, grasses, and trees,” “bearing to do cruel and injurious deeds,” and “shooting at birds in flight and pursuing running beasts,” and they will naturally see the matter yet more clearly.
Scattering and wasting the five grains at will.

From ancient times, those who scattered and wasted the five grains at will have mostly met with the calamity of being struck by thunder, for “food is Heaven to the people,” and the five grains are the indispensable sustenance on which mankind depends for survival. Even if the scattering and wasting be not grave, it is still a profanation of Heaven; hence the retribution is extremely severe. In ancient times the Son of Heaven himself plowed the fields, and the sages took the deepest concern in the production of crops and grain. How is it, then, that people today cast them away and waste them at will—whether scattering them in the fields and not harvesting them, or letting them rot from long storage in the granary and refusing to bring them out to relieve the poor; whether throwing them into water or fire, or casting them on the ground for people to trample; or eating only the fine and delicate part and throwing away the coarse; or preparing too much and then discarding what is left; or wantonly feeding fowl and birds with cooked food, or feeding livestock on beans and wheat? All these are cases of scattering the five grains and wantonly wasting Heaven's gifts. There is a poem that says: “At noon the hoe turns the millet weed, / sweat drips into the soil below; / who knows that on the plate indeed / each single grain tastes of pain and woe?” Let everyone try to imagine: in a year of famine every single grain is as precious as a pearl; how then can we bear, when we have enough and to spare, to scatter it lightly away? If everyone could treasure the five grains and set store by farming and mulberry, mankind would never meet with years of famine.

Feng Ji, a minister of the Song dynasty, often said to others, “In my youth I once paid my respects in person to Chan Master Xuedou, and Master Xuedou was always teaching people the principle of treasuring one's blessings, saying, ‘The length of a man's life is by no means fixed; once his blessings are exhausted, his hour of death has come.’ All my life I have kept this instruction, and so I will not waste or spoil any food.”

In the Ming dynasty, Zhang Yifang was exceedingly rich, with several hundred qing of good fields. Each year the rent grain he received from his tenant farmers was more than he could well deal with; heaped up in the granaries so long that it rotted, he would order men to sweep out the rotten grain and throw it away. He even fed sesame to his pigs and mung beans to his oxen. When others urged him to bring out some grain to relieve the poor, he would not. Later, in the sixth year of the Zhengde era, the Yellow River burst its banks, and the flood swept over Zhang Yifang's fields and turned them all into rivers; in a single night his family property was utterly gone, and Zhang Yifang in the end starved to death.

There was once an old woman who had worked in the kitchen of an official's household. She often cooked far too much food, and when it could not all be eaten she threw the leftovers into the drain. One day, after she had fallen ill and died, she came back to life again and said, “I saw two boatloads of discarded food, stinking and filthy, and a man beat me with an iron whip, saying that this was the food I had thrown away in my lifetime; and he forced me to eat it. I could not help but force down a few mouthfuls, and my belly swelled up and the pain was unbearable. I do not know when I shall ever finish it. What am I to do?” Having said this, the old woman died again.
Wearily troubling the people, driving them like oxen and horses without the least care for them.

“Living beings” here means all the common people. Who among men does not wish for peace, happiness, and security for himself? If a man seeks peace and happiness for himself, yet hard-heartedly drives and harasses the common people; or, already secure in comfort and happiness, gives no thought to the sufferings of the people driven and harried—such conduct is utterly unkind.

In the Spring and Autumn period, Yan Yuan, a disciple of Confucius, told Duke Ding, “The ancient sage-king Shun could put the people's strength to good use without making them weary and troubled. Therefore, when Shun was ruler, there were no idlers in the land enjoying ease with nothing to do. In the time of King Mu of Zhou, Zaofu was skilled at driving a carriage, and so not one of the horses Zaofu kept stood idle at rest. Know that a bird when hungry will peck everywhere, a beast when hungry will claw desperately at the ground, a man driven to utter poverty and hunger will turn crafty and treacherous, and a horse when wearied by running will stop and rest. From antiquity to the present there has never been a regime that could drive and harry the people without danger.”

From the founding of the Han dynasty, the court suffered from the Xiongnu on its frontiers. The minister Wang Hui, wishing to win the credit of pacifying the border, submitted a memorial to the emperor proposing: “We may take advantage of the excellent moment when the court has just concluded a peace marriage with the Xiongnu, first luring them with money and goods, and then striking with heavy troops lying in ambush in advance; thus we shall surely crush the Xiongnu army and remove the frontier threat forever.” The ministers of the court all disapproved of Wang Hui's plan, but Wang Hui insisted and contended for it, and the emperor agreed to adopt it. Three hundred thousand troops were sent out and hidden in the valleys, and spies were dispatched to lure the Xiongnu chanyu inside the frontier pass; then the order was given for the army to attack. But the plan was not kept secret and word leaked out, so the chanyu withdrew his troops beyond the frontier. The Han army could not overtake them, and several tens of thousands of soldiers and horses died in consequence, while the waste of money and provisions was beyond counting. The common people and the army alike were loud in complaint, and the emperor in great wrath issued a decree ordering Wang Hui to take his own life in atonement. From that time on, conflicts along the frontier never ceased; great generals such as Wei Qing and Huo Qubing led armies against the Xiongnu in unending bloodshed—and even in death Wang Hui could not escape responsibility.

In the Zhengtong era of Emperor Yingzong of the Ming, Song Zhang, assistant administrator of Fujian, troubled the people and extorted wealth, embezzling several tens of thousands of taels of gold, which he presented to Wang Zhen, the eunuch then holding power; and so he was promoted to be provincial administration commissioner of Fujian, the equivalent of a governor today. After taking office, Song Zhang calculated the money his promotion had cost him, and ordered that it be collected from every household in shares. Poor households could not pay, and were constantly harried and pressed by the runners, so that complaint was heard on every side. Thereupon a bandit chief named Deng Maoqi seized the opportunity to raise rebellion, and the scholars and common folk of Fujian who joined him in the plot were very many and their strength considerable. The government troops could not hold them off, and Song Zhang was plundered by the brigands, his whole household slain.
Destroying the homes of the wealthy in order to seize their treasures.

To damage another's property by carelessness is already to injure one's own virtue; how much worse to ruin another's household by every means, for the sake of seizing his treasures! One may use power to rob him openly and by force, or secretly employ cunning and treacherous schemes. Yet open robbery and force can hardly escape the penalties of the law—and the sin thereby created is all the heavier. How heavy, then, is it? It is five times severer than the penalties men inflict under the law that assesses stolen goods and assigns punishment. For hidden evil is graver than open evil, and so the punishments of the underworld must weigh heavier than the punishments of the world above.

Xue Hongren of Kaifeng in Henan was a greedy and treacherous man. His neighbour owned a pearl robe worth many cities, and many people tried every means to get this pearl robe into their hands, all in vain. Xue Hongren then plotted to accuse his neighbour falsely at law and ruin his household, and the pearl robe fell into Xue Hongren's hands. By some means unknown, word of this reached robbers, who gathered their band and broke into his house to rob it. In his panic Xue Hongren put on the pearl robe and climbed to an upper storey to hide, and pulled away the stairs behind him. Seeing this, the robbers were furiously angry and set fire to the house, and so Xue Hongren was burned alive.

In the Yuan dynasty, in the western part of Zhejiang, there was a very wealthy household whose two brothers fell to quarrelling over their father's death. Mi Xinfu seized the chance to incite the two brothers to bring lawsuits against each other; in the end he broke up their household and took their family property for his own. Only then did the two brothers feel the deepest regret, and they died of grief and melancholy; and Mi Xinfu was a rich man for twenty years. In the Zhiyuan era, Mi Xinfu was implicated in a rebellion and brought to the county court for questioning. When he saw the county magistrate, who closely resembled the younger of those brothers, he was filled with terror and dread. The magistrate forced him to confess and admit his crime, and pressed him until he had sold off his entire estate, and only then was he spared torture. Unable to bear his rage, Mi Xinfu went to the prefect to accuse the magistrate; but when he saw the prefect, he knew that the prefect was the magistrate's elder brother. So he was put to cruel torture again and forced to confess his crime, and in this way all eight members of Mi's household died in prison.

Alas! The craft and cunning of the man who incites others to evil is the most hidden, subtle, and unknown of things—why then is its retribution so bitter and violent? To sow division and incite estrangement between other men's brothers is to commit but five parts of hidden, crafty sin, and yet it is fully equal to ten parts of open and straightforward sin.
Breaking dikes to flood, or setting fires to burn, the dwellings in which people live.

If one is so unfortunate as to meet with the calamity of flood or fire, the suffering is already hard enough to bear; why then should anyone harden his heart to do the evil of breaking dikes or setting fires to harm others? Once the dwellings in which people live are destroyed by water or fire, the goods and wealth within are emptied out with them, and the lives of people and animals are for the most part hard to save. Such harm is truly too great, and the sin created truly too deep. Therefore the evil deeds of setting fires and breaking dikes are surely such as neither Heaven nor earth can tolerate.

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, “To dig a pond and draw off the river's water, when the torrent bursts forth beyond control, may wrongly break a riverside dike; or to light firecrackers, when the wind blows them down to the ground, may set a house ablaze. The fault is indeed unintended, yet in the end it harms the many; therefore one should sternly refrain—sternly—refrain!”

When Wu Fengshan was in Wuxing, he happened upon a fire in that place, and the flames spread far and burned the houses of several tens of families. Wu Fengshan at once brought out money and found men to fight the fire; he also knelt upon the ground, bowing his head and weeping, praying to Heaven in his grief. At that moment a great wind suddenly arose, and instead blew the fire out. That night Wu Fengshan dreamed that a deity said to him, “You once gave money and asked others to save people from drowning, and today you have truly saved others from fire. The sincerity of your wish to save lives has moved Heaven; the High God grants you two sons, who shall both rise to great honour, and twelve years are added to your span of life.”

The retribution for saving people from flood and fire is, after all, a small one. If those in high station could truly do good work in preventing floods, so that thousands upon thousands of common people need not suffer the calamities of water and fire, then their merit would be yet vaster, and the response they obtained would surely come faster and more abundantly than Wu Fengshan's.

Emperor Wu of Liang gave ear to the plan of his minister Wang Zu and built earthen dikes to hold back the waters of the Huai River so as to irrigate the Shouyang region; he also called out two hundred thousand soldiers and civilians to build the embankments. It was then high summer, and one cannot tell how many people sickened with plague and died. In autumn the Huai River rose in flood and burst the earthen dikes; the sound of the dikes collapsing was like a great thunderclap, heard clearly three hundred li away. More than a hundred thousand residents of the cities and villages along the Huai were swept by the great water into the sea. Wang Zu was afterwards put to death for his crime, and his clan was exterminated as well.

In Jiangdu in Jiangsu, which is Yangzhou, there was a man surnamed Ruan who had a feud with a man surnamed Ge. Ruan took advantage of the dark night to set fire to Ge's house, and the flames spread to more than a dozen other dwellings. One day Ruan's own house suddenly caught fire without cause and burned down, and his wife was burned to death on the spot; and Ruan, who had just escaped the flames, was struck by a ball of fire that flew at him, and in an instant was scorched to death.
Disordering the plans others have laid, so as to destroy the success of their undertakings.

“Plans” here means such things as all the measures of government, education, law, and ordinance, all of which bear upon the gain or loss and the safety or peril of the realm. When a petty man envies another's success, he ruins and disorders these established measures, not knowing that to destroy another's success is in truth to destroy the peace of the state and of society. The harm of this is exceedingly great, and so the sin is great as well. As for disordering and ruining the affairs of an individual or a household, that too offends against Heaven's principle and is no small sin.

In the Song dynasty there took place the Huanshuo campaign. The great general Yang Ye was ordered to lead his troops in company with his second-in-command Pan Mei to march against the rebel forces. When the army arrived, the rebels were attacking Huan Prefecture. Yang Ye said, “The rebel forces are at the very height of their keenness now, and our army must not join battle with them rashly. We should first lead our troops out by the Dashi Road and send word beforehand to the defending generals of Yun and Shuo to come out from Shijie Valley to support us; thus we may be sure of making no mistake.” Wang Shen, the army inspector, then reproached Yang Ye for fearing death and not daring to attack the rebels. Yang Ye had no choice but to cancel the battle plan already fixed and send his troops straight out against the rebel army. He therefore instructed his second-in-command Pan Mei: “Station the infantry and the archers at the mouth of the valley in left and right wings; and when I have fought the rebels back and forth to this point, come out and strike them from both sides, and we shall surely win a great victory.” Pan Mei accordingly encamped his troops at the mouth of the valley to wait. But Wang Shen, on the plea that the rebels were about to flee, sought to claim the credit for himself, and ordered the troops to march in pursuit of the rebel army. When Yang Ye fought his way back to the mouth of the valley, he found that Wang Shen had already led the troops away and had not followed the battle plan fixed beforehand. Yang Ye at once beat his breast and wept aloud, knowing that all was lost, and, reckless of his own life, he fought the rebels to the death, killing several hundred of them with his own hands, and at the last died a heroic death himself. Had Wang Shen not destroyed Yang Ye's battle plan in the Huanshuo campaign, Yang Ye would long since have won the victory in a single battle. When the court learned the truth, it convicted Wang Shen of the crime of disordering military discipline, and Wang Shen thereupon took his own life; and Yang Ye's subordinates at once swarmed forward and cut him to pieces and ate him, so that Wang Shen was devoured in a moment.
Deliberately damaging the tools and implements that others use, so that when they are needed, they cannot be used.

Such implements are, for instance, the scholar's brush and ink, the warrior's sword and spear, the farmer's plow and hoe, the craftsman's axe and chisel, and household vessels; even the smallest tool becomes essential the moment it is needed. To damage one so that another cannot use it when he must—how hateful is such conduct, and how corrupt is the heart of one who does it!

In Huainan there were two men who each made their living by ferry. One was surnamed Chen, the other Xu. Chen, being the more nimble oarsman, earned the more, and Xu grew jealous of him. He would often secretly damage Chen's oars and gear, so that his boat would not work well. One night Xu secretly snapped the oars of Chen's boat; but fearing that Chen would discover it at daybreak, he cast off and set out, only to capsize midstream. When Chen heard a cry for help from the river and hurried to the rescue, the broken oars made his boat unmanageable, and he could only watch helplessly as Xu drowned.
A petty man, seeing another's prosperity and honor, wishes him exiled, degraded, or banished to a distant frontier post.

Those who come by honor and wealth are never so by chance. It is because in past lives they stored up the causes of virtue, and because their ancestors likewise accumulated merit, that they enjoy this today. Therefore, when we see another in prosperity, we should feel admiration—yet not for his wealth and rank, but for the virtuous causes he planted in former lives. To wish instead that he be demoted and exiled is to look upon things from a hollow and empty place and to give birth to a venomous heart, hoping that others fare as badly as we do. This is the very mind of the petty man: jealous and foolish alike.
