Such wishing does no harm to the other at all; it only earns its maker idle evil karma, bringing him deeper poverty and baser station.

In the Tang dynasty, the banishment of Liu Zongyuan and Liu Mengde was engineered chiefly by Wu Yuanheng. Later Wu Yuanheng was slain by brigands, while the two Liu's returned safe and sound. Bai Juyi's demotion, in truth, was the work of Wang Ya's secret slander; yet Wang Ya was later killed by eunuchs, while Bai Juyi suffered no harm at all.

The man in power, holding the power of life and death in his single hand, looks upon exiled and demoted officials as lowly as ants; yet in the blink of an eye his own head is no longer safe, while those he once trampled as ants sit by and laugh at the fate that has now befallen him. As for the idle wishes of onlookers who hoped he would be exiled—of what use are they?

In the Song dynasty, Wang Bowen served as an official with fairness and generous kindness. He once said, “Since I took office, whenever I have had to sentence an official to banishment, I have secretly chosen for him a region whose climate and soil are suitable for dwelling.” The grand steward Tu Yong, whenever he had to send an official into distant, malarious wilderness, would set down his brush for a long while and say, “I have been to such places. The officials posted there mostly fell ill and died because of the fierce miasma. One must therefore choose a climate and soil fit for habitation before banishing a wayward official.” He even submitted this counsel to the throne, and it was made a standing rule for banishment. Such is the care of a truly benevolent heart.
Seeing another's household rich with money, he wishes him ruined and scattered, and brought to poverty.

The wealthy man, too, enjoys the fruit of merit stored by himself and of virtue accumulated by his forebears. If one is jealous of his wealth and wishes his household broken and his property scattered, consider what sort of heart this is! Even the dullest should grasp this truth. Let us briefly turn the matter about: suppose I were rich and another wished me ruined—how would my heart feel? If my heart would burn with indignation, then I know another's heart must burn as well; and if the hearts of others burn, how should the heart of Heaven not burn? For this matter, then, one should cultivate three contemplations. First: this man is certainly wealthy because in a former life he did many deeds that benefited others, planting virtue and good, and so enjoys today's fortune. This is worthy of our emulation—how can we envy him? Second: perhaps he amassed his wealth by toil of body and mind, and gradually built it up by frugality. Though he laid up the past cause of wealth, in this present life he has suffered no small hardship, and ought rather to be pitied—how can we grudge him? Third: perhaps his wealth was not righteously gained, and, rich, he is unkind. Yet wealth's gathering and scattering is ever impermanent. Floods, fire, thieves, grudges, prodigal sons, sickness, lawsuits—these are all means by which wealth is consumed. The ruin is his own making; why need we envy him? Whoever can make these three contemplations will naturally find his heart at peace.

In Hong County there lived one Zhou Yifu, extravagantly wealthy and improvident, of a violent temper and unreasonable in his dealings with others. His friend Sun Shizhi counseled him not to behave so, but Zhou thundered, “How dare you meddle in my affairs!” From that day Sun harbored a grudge and said, “Very well—I shall wait and watch you fail.” When Sun later passed the examinations and took office as a judge with jurisdiction over Hong County, it chanced that someone lodged a complaint against Zhou for publicly beating a man in the market in broad daylight, and Zhou was summoned for investigation. Unexpectedly the accuser died suddenly, and Sun condemned Zhou to death for murder. Within a few years Sun himself was transferred to Hebei, and his whole family perished at the hands of robbers—much the same fate as Zhou Yifu.

As for Zhou Yifu, relying on his riches to be overbearing and unreasonable, he no doubt deserved his downfall. But Sun Shizhi, out of private spite, broke up Zhou's household—and so Heaven in turn broke up Sun's household as retribution. Hence the saying: “To make things easy for others is to make things easy for yourself.” This is a great truth.
Seeing another's wife or daughter fair and seductive, he at once stirs up thoughts of lust, desiring to have illicit relations with her.

Lust is the offense a person most readily commits. It is a hundredfold harder to control than such evils as greed and killing, and so its ruin of virtue and its summons of calamity are a hundredfold more stern and bitter. Yet the Great One, in warning again and again against greed and killing and the like, has but this single sentence for lust, the foremost of all evils. Not that He meant to pass it by; rather, the evils of greed and killing are manifest and their principle plain, such as words can exhaust. The sin of lust, by contrast, is deeply hidden and its principle profound, such as words can hardly convey. So the Great One uses the words that destroy the very thought, calling beings back from their delusion at the first stirring of the mind, saying: “Seeing her beauty, let not your heart seek her in private.” For when the eye first lights upon beauty, if the heart stirs, then thoughts of longing, admiration, and craving entwine about it and will not be untied. Once such a thought is born in the mind, ere the body has done any wrong, one has already violated Heaven's principle and sunk into human desire; and at that moment the underworld has already inscribed an endless record of karma. Thus the Great One's compassion is truly measureless: He does not heap up words but wakes us with a single sentence, bidding us, at the moment the heart rises at the sight of beauty, to cut off at its very source this subtle and deep-rooted evil. For at the first sprout of the thought one must resolutely sever it with a single stroke of the blade, allowing not a whisper of hesitation nor a trace of affection. Heaven and hell are sundered in that very instant. If at this moment one's discernment is dim and one cannot see through, cannot plant one's feet with iron resolve, then in a breath the thought stretches and spreads, and before one knows it one has drifted into the realm of the rākṣasa ghosts—how great is the peril! Hence the meaning of the Great One's words is at once vast and profound, and His heart is full of care.
Words of Good Counsel (1)

The Hall of Precious Goodness says: “Once the lustful heart stirs, then deeds that lose all sense of shame, corrupt custom, and gravely harm hidden virtue all follow in its train. Once the lustful heart turns, then deeds that preserve reputation and chastity, plant virtue and bring blessing, and move gods and men all likewise follow. The pivot between being human and being a beast lies wholly here; how then dare we fail to awaken and reflect in earnest?”

The four characters “seeing beauty, stir the heart” are the very root of all the sickness that befalls people in this life. If one today would cut out this root of woe, he must labor over that first character, “see”: look not upon what is against propriety, and even when one does see, look as though one did not. This is the supreme means of prevention. The innate conscience we all possess is not easily deceived, and the rites of the world are not easily overstepped. To guard by strict prohibition and force is the lesser means. Failing that, once a thought rises in the mind and is not checked at the outset, in the end it will surely be carried into action and issue in lewd deeds. A single moment's slip, and ten thousand kalpas cannot redeem it—is this not cause for deepest sorrow?
Words of Good Counsel (2)

The Sutra of Forty-Two Sections says: “When you see an elderly woman, regard her as your own mother; when you see a woman older than yourself, regard her as your elder sister; when you see a woman younger than yourself, regard her as your younger sister; when you see a young girl, regard her as your own daughter.” This is the supreme method of nurturing the heart.
Words of Good Counsel (3)

“Fair beauty all men love, yet Heaven cannot be deceived; if I debauch another's wife, another will debauch mine.” This is an admonition taught to the world by the ancients. Yang Youqing, having recited it, said: “If you see another's wife or daughter as fair and are moved to a wicked thought of intimacy, then at once imagine another seeing your own wife or daughter, likewise stirred to wickedness and wanting to seduce them. When you thus trade places and view the matter from the other's side, the wicked thought will instantly die away.”
Words of Good Counsel (4)

The recorded sayings of the ancients declare: “When you catch sight of a beauty or meet one and your heart is stirred, hasten at once to think: the god who oversees our faults stands beside me; the star gods of the Three Terrace and the Lord of the Northern Dipper are above my head; the three corpse spirits dwell within my body, and the hearth god in my kitchen; sun, moon, and the three lights, the myriad true ones and holy beings, are arrayed across the sky—some recording my wicked thought, some glaring at me in anger, some watching me closely, some ready to strike. Think in this way, and your heart will tremble with fear, and of itself the passion will cool and die.”

In the Ming dynasty there was a man addicted to lust who asked Mr. Wang Longxi how to rid himself of the habit. “Suppose,” replied Mr. Wang, “there were a courtesan of rare beauty waiting for you in this room; when you opened the door you found it was your own sister, or your daughter. Would your lust at once vanish?” “Alas, yes, it would vanish!” answered the man. “So the lustful thought is in itself empty,” said Mr. Wang, “and only your error makes you take it for real.”

The ten rules on the Banana Window of Emperor Wenchang place first the prohibition of lewd conduct, saying: “Before you see, do not think; when you see, do not act amiss; after you have seen, do not recall.” Not to think before seeing is the work of daily nurture. When a man is alone, he must sweep his thoughts clean and remind himself constantly; with the principle of Heaven thus present, human desire is of itself held back, and no filthy or depraved notion can enter an upright and open breast. This is the learning of the gentleman who reveres his own mind. Once my heart is settled, even if a beauty stands before me and seduces me in every way, it will not stir a hair's breadth—what steadfastness is this! Yet such a state is won only through strict daily discipline and the honest nurture of a rectified heart. Hence the Emperor, in order to purify the very source, tells us that to rid oneself of lewd acts one must first rid oneself of lewd thoughts, and that to attain the power of not being disturbed in the presence of beauty and of keeping one's composure with a woman in one's lap, one must day by day train the work of a rectified and sincere heart. As for “when you see, do not act amiss” and “after you have seen, do not recall,” these are precisely the meaning of the Great One's charge not to let the heart seek her in private—the work of self-reflection at the very moment of contact. Look more closely: each of the Emperor's three sentences holds its own realm. To think is to think toward the future; to act amiss is to err in the present; to recall is to recollect the past. The immense sins of lust committed by people today are all brought to birth within these three realms. If one can sweep all three away, then lewd conduct will find no soil in which to grow.

Of all evils, lust is first—the gravest sin on the register settled before Yama's hall. For once the lustful mind is born it gives rise to all manner of wicked deeds. When the conditions of lewdness are not yet united, the heart conceives deluded, fanciful cravings; if one cannot entice the other, it breeds craft and cunning; if a slight obstacle arises, it breeds hatred and anger; when passion confounds and blinds, it breeds greedy attachment and defilement; envying another's gorgeous beauty, it breeds jealousy and malice; to seize what another loves, it breeds the thought of killing. Thus all sense of shame is lost and the bonds of ethics entire are broken, and from this all evil karma arises while all good thoughts perish. Know that once the lewd thought stirs, even though one has not done the deed, it is already as grave as accumulated wickedness—how much more when one truly commits the acts of lust!
Words of Good Counsel (5)
The statutes of the underworld declare: “To debauch another's wife brings the retribution of childlessness; to defile an unmarried virgin brings the retribution of licentious children.”
The proverb too says: “Oh, borrow no amorous debt; what is borrowed quickly is repaid quickly. The household will not want for one to pay it back—when you would welsh, he will not.”

The murderer takes but one body; the adulterer takes, as it were, her three lives. For lewdness does not merely destroy a woman's chastity; it brings shame and agony to her in-laws, parents, husband, and children, and may even drive them to death through that shame—whether a husband slays his wife, a father hangs his daughter, a son disowns his mother, or relatives meet her with cold faces, while decent families will never consent to a match with her. Why for a moment of stolen pleasure heap up a crime that fills the heavens? Even the retribution of childlessness is not enough to punish the sin of one who debauches another's wife or daughter.

It is after the bond of husband and wife that the bonds of father and son and of brothers arise. To debauch another is not merely to disorder the single bond of marriage; it disorders as well the bond of father and son and the bond of brothers, so that among the five bonds three are destroyed. It even brings grief to her ancestors that they should have such a lewd descendant, and pain that they must disdain the very sacrifices offered them. Hence one who debauches another cannot escape the calamity of being smitten by gods and slain by ghosts.

The murderer injures the acquired nature of his victim, that is, his body. But one who debauches another disorders her innately bestowed nature—the very moral order of her husband, parents, brothers, in-laws, and ancestors. Moreover, the killer slays only because of a grudge against the slain. What grudge does the adulterer bear against her husband, her in-laws, her parents? And what deep enmity does he hold against this woman herself, that he must defile her body and rob her of her chastity?

He who has many lewd thoughts will surely have few good ones; he who has few lewd thoughts will surely have many good ones. Hence one who has wholly eradicated lewd thought attains three of the five blessings: long life, health and peace, and a good end. He who is forever rising lustful thoughts must expect the distress of disease and the calamity of a violent or untimely death.

The desire that rises in a moment is easy to quell; the fame, rank, and life of a whole lifetime are a matter of utmost weight. Why for a single moment's confusion would one squander a hundred years of reputation and integrity, the promise of a whole career, the merit amassed by one's ancestors, and the fortune in rank and emolument that descendants might have enjoyed? Truly one cannot fathom such a heart! Worse, there are those who, after lewdness, fall ill from fright and flight, and neither medicines nor physicians can cure them; or who are dragged into lawsuits and prison, breaking up their homes—by which time regret comes too late. Some are caught in the very act and so trade their own heads for a moment's pleasure. And sooner or later that retribution circles round to one's own wife and daughter, repaying the amorous debt. The bitterness of such an outcome is beyond words.

The proverb says: “Lewdness draws on death.” How true it is. Yet to say it merely draws near to death is still a mild expression; I hold that lewdness never fails to kill. If the adulteress's husband learns of it, he will certainly fly into a rage and slay her with his blade. The rival lovers, from jealousy, turn their sharp weapons upon each other and kill. Through lewdness that leads to another's death, the law condemns him to die. If by chance he slips through and escapes the law's justice, he is slain by the vengeful ghost of the wronged. And if he escapes all these, then excess of lust brings an incurable malady, so that physicians stand helpless, and the god who governs destiny slays him. That a man—endowed with the most spiritual and noblest body that heaven and earth bestow, a body capable of great deeds—should place himself upon ground where death is certain, is folly enough to break one's heart.
Words of Good Counsel (6)

The Daily Course of the Early Divination says: “In ancient times there was a worthy man who, when his lust surged, would lay his hand in the fire. The unbearable pain would then extinguish it. If it still could not be stopped, he would quiet his mind and sit in stillness, beholding his own body as already dead; then, recalling the graves of the ancients, he would reflect within: ‘This man, while living, was like me; and when I am dead and buried in this grave, I shall be like him.’ Thinking thus, what pleasure is there in lust?”

To guard against the thought of lust, one must rely wholly on the power of wisdom. Di the Lord of Liang in the Tang dynasty once said: “When beauty stands before you, think at once: if this fair one one day dies of illness, her corpse will begin to rot and swarm with maggots, and its stench will fill the air and turn the stomach. Reflect thus, and the wicked thought is dispelled.”
Words of Good Counsel (7)

In the Liang dynasty, Bodhidharma, the first patriarch of Chan, composed his Song of the Skin Bag, saying: “A drain of urine, a swirl of gore—what grace or dalliance can it hold in store?” In the Tang dynasty Lü Dongbin said: “Boast not, young lord, of amorous chase—round rebirth you wheel in osseous trade; if you doubt me, search the mirror's face: beneath the skin a skull is laid.” Again he said: “A maiden sweet as curd in spring; at her hip a sword dull men must sever; though no head you see in falling, in secret she drains the marrow ever.”
Words of Good Counsel (8)

The Method of Quelling Lust says: “She lures me to the ruin of my body and the breaking of my home, she shortens my years and wastes my blessings—truly a matter that destroys my very life. I should regard her as a blade that slays, as a tiger or a wolf, as a poisonous snake, as a demon sent to snatch my soul, as an enemy from a former life. If I can look upon her thus, it is like pouring water upon fire, and there is no lust that does not die.”

Gao Zongxian of the Ming dynasty said: “This body is as white jade: a single stumble and it shatters. This deed is as poisoned wine: a single sip and you die.” People today so often ruin a whole life for the single word “feeling,” never understanding that this word “feeling” is bestowed by Heaven for loyalty and filial piety, for friendship and fraternal love, for benevolence to the people and compassion for all things. Used rightly, it enables one to become a sage or a worthy; used wrongly, it turns one into a beast. How then dare we fail to watch over it with caution, fear, and care?

The Daoist books say: “The sin of the lecher is several degrees heavier than that of the murderer.” They also say: “All the various offenses a person has committed in the past can be wiped away through austere practice and cultivation—except for one who has defiled a virgin. Though he later cultivates to the highest attainment and perfects his practice, he cannot be released; only after he has endured the evil retribution may his spiritual task be fulfilled.”

The Buddha said: “A person who in this world does not violate the wives of others, nor harbor in his mind thought of anything depraved, obtains for this reason five wholesome retributions. First, he does not lose his money. Second, he does not fear the authorities. Third, he does not fear other people. Fourth, after death he can ascend to heaven and receive a celestial maiden of the heavens as his wife. Fifth, when he is born from heaven down into the world, he is reborn among upright and well-favored women. Thus, some of those we see today of handsome and upright features have attained this through the destiny of a former life in which they did not offend against the wives and daughters of others. Conversely, if a person in this world indulges in licentiousness and offends against the wives and daughters of others, he incurs for this reason five evil retributions. First, husband and wife are discordant, and he repeatedly loses money. Second, he fears the authorities and is often punished with the staff. Third, he deceives himself and is ever anxious and afraid of people. Fourth, after death he is reborn in the hell of Mount Tai; there, when the iron pillar is scorched red, he embraces it as though it were a beauty and endures the torture of branding—for this disaster is the fruit of offending in this life against the wives and daughters of others; and these punishments, drawn upon himself by his own karma, require tens of millions of years to be exhausted. Fifth, emerging from hell, he is reborn as a cock or a duck, or as birds and fowl. Such fowl are wanton without regard even for mother and young, and know no restraint. Yet the horse knows propriety and the goose keeps its chastity—these are things everyone knows. But the wantonness of cocks and ducks knows no satiety; all because in a past life they sinned in lust and offended against the wives and daughters of others, and so received the body of cocks and ducks, and are forever butchered and cooked by people. Such suffering cannot be fully told.”

Among the Buddha's five precepts, one is the precept against illicit lust. Whoever can receive and uphold this precept will draw to himself, in this life and the next, a retribution of parents and kin long-lived, healthy and at peace, harmonious and joyful, and of a wife and daughters chaste and good. The Sutra of Retribution says: “A ghost once asked, ‘Since I have taken this ghostly form I am filled with terror and am ever afraid of being pursued, seized, bound, and burdened with all manner of pain and poison, so that I have not a moment of joy. What offense have I committed to come to this?’ The Venerable Maudgalyāyana answered, ‘This is because when you were a man you delighted in illicit lust and offended against the wives and daughters of others; being ever afraid of discovery, your heart was ill at ease. The suffering you know today is but the flower of this lifetime; your fruit is in hell—whether lying on the iron bed or embracing the bronze pillar, punishments so painful and terrible that they cannot be fully told.’”

The Record of Heaven's Warnings of Emperor Wenchang says: “One who debauches another's wife or daughter, or defiles a virgin of the inner chamber, suffers in hell for five hundred kalpas before escaping to be reborn as a mule or a horse; and after another five hundred kalpas may he be reborn in human form as a courtesan or an actor. One who fornicates with a widow or with a nun who has left the world, corrupting the conduct and ambition of another, suffers in hell for eight hundred kalpas before escaping to be reborn as a sheep or a pig for slaughter; and after another eight hundred kalpas may he be reborn in human form as a mute or a deaf person, or one with disfigured features or maimed limbs. As for the evil of the lowly profaning the honourable and the young disturbing the old, this destroys the bonds of human ethics; such a one suffers in hell for fifteen hundred kalpas before escaping to be reborn as a snake or a rat; and after another fifteen hundred kalpas may he be reborn in human form. Yet either he dies in his mother's womb or perishes in infancy, and at last never enjoys the blessing of long life. The retribution of the sin of lust is truly pitiful.”

The Admonition of the Inner Chamber says: “If a woman falls into the sin of lewdness, in a whole lifetime she can never wash it clean; even filial sons and kindly grandsons cannot cleanse it for her. Therefore a virtuous lady and a renowned beauty must guard her body as jade, and suffer not the least blemish or fault. If she meets a reckless wretch, let her refuse him sternly on the spot, and then he will not dare to approach again. This is what is called the ‘upright air of the fragrant chamber,’ and even ghosts and spirits will shelter her. But if a woman is wanton, is there no evil retribution? The law of the underworld dooms her to be reborn as a pig or a dog to punish her sin—how much more than merely being scorned and cursed on earth! This is spoken here specially as a warning to wanton women.”
A Further Discussion

The moment when people most easily stumble is that instant before beauty when the impulse of desire can hardly be restrained; for then arise three demons. First, when your eyes fall upon her, her bewitching form gathers into your heart, so that the very bones grow hot and the spirit leaps up, as smoke rises and flames blaze—this is called the fire demon. Then the root of desire begins to stir and the two channels secretly open, as a dike on the point of collapse lets the torrent burst through—this is called the water demon. And as water and fire seethe against each other, body and soul clash and chafe, spreading like a wheel turning without rest, a ring without a rim—this is called the wind demon. These three demons are the three passes, and to slay the demons and cross the passes there is no other means than the one sword of wisdom; that is to say, endure and endure again! Be resolute and resolute again! Be stern and stern again! Therefore however hungry, one may not eat the tiger's food; however thirsty, one may not drink the poisoned cup—such is the saying of endurance. When two men grapple, each straining to wrest the other's blade, even though his hand runs blood he will not let go of the knife; and a routed army, cutting its way to escape, though an arrow strike its back, must endure the pain and not turn back—such is the saying of resolute endurance. When a viper stings the hand, a brave man instantly severs the wrist with his blade; when a poisoned arrow strikes the body, the hero instantly endures the pain to scrape the bone clean—such is the saying of stern endurance. At this moment when a thousand pounds hang on a single hair, whoever can hold firm and endure through will move heaven and earth and ghosts, and his own practice will be fulfilled. If a single thought of doubt wavers, one will surely be unable to hold the line. The other is but a wild flower by the roadside, gone to nothing in the blink of an eye; while you, for the sin of lust, will henceforth have your years diminished and your fortune and rank cut short, and may even incur the calamity of death. One destined for wealth and honor is changed to poverty and baseness; one destined for peace is changed to disaster; one destined for a son becomes childless; one who hoped for noble sons and worthy grandsons begets instead children of low degree. And there remain the retribution of hell, the retribution of the next life, the retribution of a beast's birth, the retribution of debauched wives and daughters, the retribution of impoverished descendants, and the retribution of courtesans and actors. All these boundless calamities and evil retributions are drawn upon oneself by the single deviation of a moment's thought. How heartbreaking! How dare we not endure? How dare we not endure!

The most effective means of stemming lewd conduct is for fathers, elder brothers, teachers, and friends to instruct and guide their juniors at all times, seeing to it that they firmly believe in cause and effect. When a shameful deed is done in a dark chamber, the eyes of the gods see it as clearly as a flash of lightning. If a person firmly trusts the rites, the law of cause and effect, and the retribution of fortune and misfortune, without a doubt, then when he meets the temptation of the world he will of a sudden wake and turn back the light upon himself, and will not lapse into any shameful act.

In the haunts of wind and flowers, of snow and moon — the places of pleasure and romance — how many men have stumbled! By them a man brings on the ruin of half a lifetime and a whole life of poverty and dejection; he cannot so much as see his own shadow without shame and dread — and how few there are who can hold fast to the right path and remain undefiled! All day long a man may forbid himself lust, and yet the lustful mind burns all the fiercer; when he meets another he speaks of curbing desire, and yet the seeds of desire only grow more rank! If he still gives loose rein to passion and does not repent, he is bringing on himself the day when the measure of his evil is full; but if he was deluded at the outset and can awaken in the end, then calamity will gradually depart and blessing follow after. Mr. Xie Shangcai of the Song dynasty said: “The way of Heaven surely sends down calamity upon the man who commits sexual misconduct, but never upon the man who has repented and reformed.” How true those words are!

Since the retribution for sexual misconduct is so grave, the merit of preventing it and the guilt of enticing others into it can hardly be light either. Therefore I pray that everyone may let the blue lotus bloom upon his tongue and wield the colored brush upon his desk, setting forth the principle of action and response and its recorded cases, to rescue and raise up the multitudes of deluded beings! Let such writings be passed from hand to hand and men exhort one another; now crying out aloud in the public square, now pleading earnestly behind closed doors. Do not fear men's mockery, and do not shrink from being called a pedant; if only the persuasion is tactful, it will surely awaken deep reflection in the hearer and profit him beyond measure. Would not one who does this be a gentleman who loves others through virtue and seeks abundant blessing for himself?

Among the sins of the mouth in our own day, none is graver than the love of talking about women and recounting lewd matters. Men probe and dwell on such things from every side and study them together, one singing and a hundred joining in; and because the speaker savors it so, the hearers are set itching to try it themselves. You should know that the sin of sexual misconduct, and the secret faults that others hide, touch a person's lifelong reputation and integrity; a single careless word may breed endless calamity, and nothing offends the wrath of Heaven more. Would it not be far better to speak often of the retribution of chastity and of lust, and so uphold the moral teaching and the bonds of human relations, thereby winning blessing from Heaven?
Words of Good Counsel (9)

The Record of Heavenly Warnings says: “Whoever writes or prints books that teach lewdness, defiling men's hearts and corrupting their minds, will surely fall after death into the Unintermitted Hell (commonly called the Avīci Hell), and will not leave it until the lewd books he wrote and printed have utterly vanished from the world, and the men who did evil after reading them have likewise exhausted their retribution.”
Words of Good Counsel (10)

Yuan Liaofan of the Ming dynasty said: “He who gathers up lewd and wicked books, and the writings that expose men's private faults and slander their families, and burns them all, will surely have sons and grandsons loyal, filial, true, and righteous. But he who loves to read lewd tales and novels, who praises and retells their stories, and who keeps lewd books and pictures in his house, will surely have sons and grandsons who become prostitutes and actors!”
Appendix

The chapter titled Turning Back from the Sea of Desire in The Collected Works of Anshi records various teachings on abstention from lust, clearly ordered and suited to each occasion as exhortation and prohibition. As space is limited, the more important portions are respectfully excerpted below for reference.

For a maiden, the years of waiting in the inner chambers for betrothal are the beginning of her lifelong reputation and chastity. If a man without conscience robs a maiden of her chastity, her parents and kinsmen alike are shamed and their faces lose their light. Even if someone afterwards takes her in marriage, the truth will usually come out that she is no longer a virgin, and she will be sent back to her parents' house; and so she will often die of shame and grief. Even if the matter is concealed through the marriage, she will live inwardly in constant shame and fear; for once the great principle of her honor has been broken, a thousand years cannot wash it clean. Therefore every man with a conscience should sternly guard himself beforehand!

When a widow keeps her chastity, even ghosts and spirits admire and revere her, and the court too commends and rewards her. If a man destroys the chastity she has guarded through such hardship, then she and her family will feel they dare not show their faces, and her dead husband in the underworld will hate him above all. Let a man but put himself in her place and weigh it with his own heart, and he will feel a chill at the bottom of his own! We ought rather to find ways to preserve her good name, to help her win renown and keep her chastity whole, and to cultivate an even richer virtue — far more than merely refraining from violating her!

Are not maidservants also maidens? A man wants his own daughter to be chaste — can he then destroy the chastity of another man's daughter? A maidservant is also another man's wife: a man wants his own wife to keep her honor — can another man's wife then be made to lose hers? Rich and poor, high and low, are indeed not equal; but every person's reputation and honor are equally precious. How can a man throw away his conscience and gravely commit so heavy a sin? Moreover, some wives, from jealousy, beat their maidservants or serving women, and even take their lives; and the churlish servant, in turn, will talk back and betray his master. Worse still, father and son, each unaware of the other, may come to share the same woman — that is, commit incest; or elder and younger brother may in their folly lie with the same woman; and perhaps a child of their own flesh is born, only to fall, for want of any proper status, into the lowly position of a concubine. Later generations, knowing nothing of these secrets, may in their ignorance offend against her again with misconduct. Between them, though in name there is the distance of master and maidservant, in fact there may be the blood bond of brother and sister! Such deeds as corrupt manners and morals are truly too painful to speak of. Why is it that men always suppose that maidservants and servants are easy to violate, and dare to commit lewdness against them, never knowing that they ought to keep themselves in check?

A wet nurse holds a respected place among the eight classes of mothers, and a Buddhist nun keeps her quiet watch in the hallowed purity of the Buddha's gate; to offend against such women is to heap sin upon sin. The lawsuits, punishments, and disasters that fall upon a man in this present life are only the lightest part of it!

There are many indeed who, when a woman runs to them in the blindness of her passion, seize the occasion to commit misconduct. Never think that because she throws herself into your arms, it would be heartless to refuse her. If at such a moment a man can see through it and endure it, then the deep virtue he accumulates and the rare integrity he achieves will be known to Heaven of itself, and he need not wish that others should know. This is the pass between good and evil, the boundary between calamity and blessing; here above all a man should spur himself on!

To take one's pleasure and sport with prostitutes seems to be no great sin; yet a man falls into the prostitute's snare and often ruins his family by it. His parents cast off this son who frequents brothels, his kinsmen grow distant, and his wife above all hates him; and so he cuts himself off from all human ties and loses the integrity that would have kept him pure as jade. Once he contracts a venereal disease, sores break out over his whole body; his eyebrows fall, his nose rots away, and in the worst cases not a patch of skin is left whole. There was a friend of mine whose genitals rotted away, and he said: “This is what came of one moment of wild impulse that I could not hold in check — a lifetime of emasculation, my line cut off, my body ruined; though I weep and repent today, it is too late!” There was also a man of Anhui who, having contracted such a disease, was covered from head to foot with foul sores; the son he begot was born wholly red without skin, and could not be kept alive, and died. Alas! Men say, “Whoring does no harm to one's hidden virtue.” That is sinful talk! Who knows but that such a man is no different from one already sentenced by the unseen powers! I beg you all to guard against it strictly — strictly!

When men commit sexual misconduct — that is, homosexuality — there are six reasons why it must not be done. Such conduct is utterly foul; it shames the face, injures the body, and ruins virtue. Since reverence is lost, the sense of shame is gone as well: that is the first reason. A man casts off the wife of his youth and instead serves and dotes upon some youth, in violation of the natural way of Heaven and Earth, of yin and yang, so that his likes and dislikes are turned awry: that is the second. Men of this kind are frivolous in conduct and careless of propriety; they may even go stealing jade and filching fragrance, defiling the women of their own households: that is the third. Three feet above a man's head the gods surely stand; the gods are angered by such foul and lewd conduct, and the punishment they send down cannot be light: that is the fourth. The king's law has its express statutes, sternly punishing sodomy; moreover lewdness borders close upon killing, and easily rouses the intent to kill, so that a man loses his precious life: that is the fifth. To discharge one's seed at random, not for the sake of continuing the family line, is folly of the utmost degree, and only hastens the ruin of one's own life: that is the sixth.

I exhort all people everywhere: those who have never committed sexual misconduct must earnestly hold themselves in check, shun misfortune and turn toward what is auspicious, and keep all their lives the precept against a second partner — that is, never have relations with anyone but their own wife. Those who have already committed such misconduct should all the more quickly and earnestly reform, and moreover do good deeds abundantly, printing and distributing books that warn against lust and exhorting people far and wide, to atone for the sins they committed before. Only thus can disaster be turned into blessing!

Formerly Yao Tingruo of Tongcheng in Anhui printed and gave away handbills on which men swore to abstain from sexual misconduct. On them he wrote: “Of all virtues, filial piety comes first; of all evils, lust stands at the head. What sets man apart from the birds and beasts is the mind he cherishes. The wild goose, though but a bird, will not yet break its ranks; how can man, endowed with the four virtues, fall below the birds and beasts? Taking this as our ground, we swear to rid ourselves of lust. If a lewd thought should arise, calamity will surely fall upon us; if we break this precept, calamity will surely reach our sons and grandsons. We pray only that the greatly compassionate and greatly merciful will take pity and witness this vow, guard and uphold us, and silently protect us, that we may be preserved life after life.” All who receive this handbill shall gather a few like-minded friends, copy these eighteen lines on another sheet, and write down their own addresses and native places, each signing his name and affixing his seal or fingerprint; then, before the Dipper Sovereign, or before Emperor Wenchang, or before Emperor Guan, or before the holy images of all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they shall swear the oath and burn the handbill, vowing to keep the precept forever and never forget it, and shall renew the vow each year. Once the several friends have sworn to keep the precept, they shall at once contribute funds to print ten thousand copies of this vow-and-precept handbill for free distribution, so that this excellent method may be handed down without end. On the back of the handbill a few maxims and examples of retribution must also be added, so as to warn the world.

There was a scholar of Guixi who failed in every examination. Not knowing why, he went to beseech the Daoist Celestial Master Zhang, burning incense and submitting a memorial to have the celestial register of examinations searched. The god then wrote in reply: “This scholar's destiny contained a degree and office; but because he transgressed against his aunt, his rank and name have been struck off.” When the Celestial Master had finished searching the register, he rose and told the scholar what the god had said was the reason for his failure. The scholar said, “But I have never wronged my aunt!” So he wrote out a petition appealing to the god and pleading his own case. The god wrote again: “It is true that you never wronged your aunt in deed; but you wronged her in your thoughts!” The scholar was then overcome with shame and his regret came too late — for in his youth he had seen how beautiful and alluring his aunt was, and in that moment a lewd thought had arisen.

In the Zhengde era of the Ming dynasty there was a scholar named Zhao Yongzhen. In his youth he met a man of extraordinary gifts who told him, “When you are twenty-three you will surely pass the examinations and win rank.” When he sat the provincial examination in his twenty-third year, his essays were so excellent that the chief examiner had already resolved for several days to select them; but to his surprise, in the later sessions he slipped again and again, and in the end he did not pass. Zhao Yongzhen was deeply grieved, and prayed to Emperor Wenchang for a dream to tell him the reason for his failure. Emperor Wenchang said: “You were meant to pass this year's provincial examination; but because you have lately dallied with the maidservant in your house and enticed the daughter of your neighbor — though no adultery was in fact committed — your thoughts were topsy-turvy and your lustful fancies clung on without cease, so that your mind grew daily darker; and therefore the rank and name appointed for you in your destiny have been erased.” When Yongzhen heard the god's explanation he wept bitterly, vowed and resolved to reform, and did good works on a great scale; he printed and distributed wholesome books warning against lust, to awaken the world. In the next provincial examination he indeed took first place, and rose in office to be a provincial administration commissioner.

At eighteen Li Deng took first place in the provincial examination, but from then until he was fifty he could never pass the metropolitan examination. Li Deng went to visit Dharma Master Ye Jing and asked him the reason. The master thereupon inquired of Emperor Wenchang, who ordered a divine clerk to show the master Li Deng's register of office. On it was written: “At Li Deng's birth the Heavenly Emperor granted him a jade seal: at eighteen to be first in the provincial examination, at nineteen to be top laureate, at fifty-two to be appointed Right Chancellor. But because after taking first place at eighteen he secretly spied on the neighbor's daughter while she bathed, his rank and name were delayed ten years and he was demoted two classes; again, because he seized the house and land of his elder brother Li Feng, his rank and name were put back another ten years and he was demoted three classes; again, because he committed adultery with a respectable woman of the Zheng family, his rank and name were put back yet another ten years (in all, he has been penalized with thirty years' delay); and now he has again committed adultery with his neighbor's daughter. Truly he piles up evil without ever repenting; Heaven has already struck off his rank and name, so that Li Deng will never pass the examinations so long as he lives!” Dharma Master Ye told Li Deng these words, and Li Deng died grieving and ashamed.

Alas! How many years must a grandfather accumulate virtue before a descendant can become a top laureate and a chancellor! Yet Li Deng wrought evil himself and stripped away every rank of top laureate and chancellor that was his, betraying the grace of Heaven and betraying his ancestors. He counted pleasure the one thing that mattered, and set rank, wealth, and honor aside as if they were nothing at all; and for the sake of a few secret and petty lusts he lost the abundant blessing and emolument that were originally his — how pitiable! Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: “Even if yours were the destiny of a top laureate and chancellor, it is not hard to wipe it out with a single stroke of the brush.” And if one's destiny is not that of a top laureate and chancellor, there is still less to be said.
Supplementary Notes

Shi Naian, author of The Water Margin, wrote into his book many episodes that encourage lewdness, theft, and the taking of life, teaching robbery and lewdness in the extreme; and in the end his son, his grandson, and his great-grandson were all born mute. Wang Shifu, author of The Romance of the Western Chamber, excelled at depicting clandestine love affairs between men and women, so that many who read the play conceived lewd thoughts and desires; and before the book was even finished, Wang Shifu himself could no longer master his passions and bit through his own tongue and died. And Yuan Zhen, a poet of the Tang dynasty, seeing that his younger cousin Cui Yingying was as beautiful as a heavenly immortal, wished to take her as his wife; when she refused him, Yuan Zhen in his anger wrote the book Record of a Meeting with an Immortal, inventing an illicit affair for his cousin, slandering Cui Yingying's good name and covering her with shame for a thousand years, and leading readers of later ages to imitate such clandestine meetings. In the end Yuan Zhen died in the utmost agony, and after death his corpse suffered the retribution of being struck and burned by lightning.

Again, Huang Shangu, a poet of the Song dynasty, loved to write lush and voluptuous verse. Once he went with Li Boshi, the famous painter of horses, to pay their respects to Chan Master Xiu of Yuantong. The master first admonished Li Boshi, saying, “You should not spend the strength of a whole life on painting horses; if every thought in your mind is of a horse's body, I fear you will fall in the next life and be reborn as a horse!” Huang Shangu laughed to hear this, and the master rebuked him: “Do not make sport of another.” Shangu said, “Am I too to fall into a horse's womb?” The master said: “Boshi thinks of horses and falls into a horse's body, but that is his own affair alone. What you write, however, are lewd and voluptuous verses that stir the lustful minds of countless men in the world and cause many to lose their chastity. Such a sin is far more than falling into a horse's womb; I fear the Niraya hell is waiting for you to come and be punished!” Master Xiu was a famous and enlightened monk of the day; when Huang Shangu heard his admonition he was both terrified and ashamed, and from that time he laid down his brush and never wrote voluptuous verse again.

In the Tang dynasty there was a censor named Li Yan. Once, on a mission to Guangdong by order of the court, he suddenly came upon a tiger, which leaped into the brush and then spoke to him in human speech: “Ai! I came very near to wounding my old friend!” Li Yan said, “How that voice resembles the voice of Li Wei, who passed the examination in the same year as I!” The tiger said, “It is long indeed since we parted and saw each other last.” They fell to talking of their former dealings, and everything felt wholly familiar. Li Yan asked the tiger, “Li Wei, how did you come to be a tiger?” The tiger said: “One day, as I sat in meditation, I suddenly heard a whirring sound outside the door, and in an instant I went mad and took the form of a tiger. To meet an old friend today — how could I not grieve!” Li Yan asked Li Wei, “Is there anything in your life that you regret?” Li Wei answered: “Once, in the countryside outside Nanyang, I violated a widow. Her family found out and secretly plotted to kill me; and so, when I was drunk, I slaughtered her whole household. That is the thing I regret most in all my life.” Having said this, the tiger gave a great roar and went off.

Wang Qinzheng of Diyang county carried on an illicit affair with his neighbor's wife, and the two agreed to elope. But Wang Qinzheng was afraid her husband would discover them and come after them — and to his horror the woman thereupon murdered her husband. Shocked beyond measure, Wang Qinzheng fled at once by himself, running without pause until he was seventy li away in Jiangshan county, and he thought to himself, “I have fled far enough now; I must be clear of the disaster.” Then, feeling hungry, he went into an inn to eat; but the innkeeper set out food for two. Wang Qinzheng asked him, “I am eating alone — why have you prepared food for two?” The innkeeper said, “Just now I saw a man with loosened hair standing beside you — are you not two?” At these words Wang Qinzheng knew that the vengeful ghost was following at his side, and he went to the magistrate and gave himself up. Wang Qinzheng and the neighbor's wife were put to death at the same hour.

While Zhang Bao was serving as prefect of Chengdu in Sichuan, he saw the wife of Li Wei of Huayang county, a woman of such beauty and charm that she was called the loveliest in all Sichuan. Zhang Bao determined to have her for himself, and so he entrusted many people to let her secretly know of his infatuation; in time Li Wei's wife was moved as well. Just then it happened that Li Wei's acceptance of bribes was exposed, and Zhang Bao at once impeached him before the court and had him exiled beyond the mountain passes; and Li Wei died on the road into exile. Zhang Bao then bribed Li Wei's mother with a great sum of money and forcibly took Li Wei's wife into his house, thus fulfilling his wish to possess another man's wife. After the marriage he gave himself up to joy with her without a thought of parting; yet before long the woman fell ill, her mind grew clouded, and she saw Li Wei's ghost following at her side; and soon she died of her illness. Before she died she said to Zhang Bao: “I am grateful for the great kindness you have shown me, and so I dare not fail to tell you: my former husband Li Wei has appealed his grievance to the Heavenly Emperor and will soon come to take your life. If you only keep deep inside your residence and never go out, he may not be able to seize you; but the moment you step outside, he will surely have you.” Having spoken, the woman died. Not long afterwards Zhang Bao too fell ill, and because he kept firmly in mind her warning on her deathbed, he guarded himself with the utmost care and did not dare go out. One evening at dusk, as Zhang Bao sat in the hall, he saw far off beyond the gate a red sleeve beckoning to him; in his confusion he took it for Li Wei's wife, and hurried down from the hall and out past the gate — where he ran straight into Li Wei's vengeful ghost. The ghost seized him and beat him soundly, crying out as he struck: “Zhang Bao, you thief! If I had not waved a red sleeve at you, would you ever have come out?” A little while later Zhang Bao's nose began to bleed, and after he had told his family what had just happened, he died.

Yan Wu, a military commissioner of the Tang dynasty, as a young man lived next door to an army officer. He saw how very beautiful the officer's daughter was and tried every means to entice her, and in the end the two eloped together. The officer went to the capital and laid a formal complaint against Yan Wu before the court, and the court issued an edict for his arrest. Fearing that he would be condemned, Yan Wu killed the officer's daughter and destroyed her body to erase every trace. Later Yan Wu fled to Sichuan, where he suddenly fell ill and saw the officer's daughter standing before him, accusing him: “It was indeed my own moral failing that I eloped with you; but I never wronged you! Even if you feared condemnation, why did you not leave me and go? Instead you murdered me — you were truly cruel! I have already appealed my grievance to the courts of the underworld, and tomorrow I shall take my revenge.” Yan Wu, both ashamed and afraid, begged her to spare his life. But on the following morning, sure enough, Yan Wu died.

Alas! At such a moment the whole authority of a military commissioner was of no use to Yan Wu at all! People today are forever seeking death at the least provocation, never knowing that once dead, affection turns to hatred, and grievance answers grievance without end!
Story Eight:

Xu Zhaoxin of Jinjiang in the Ming dynasty passed the provincial examination in the wu-wu year. Once, on his way to Funing prefecture to pay his respects to his teacher, he happened to pass a nunnery and took a fancy to a young nun; relying on his power and position, he violated her by force. The very next day Xu Zhaoxin suddenly bit through his own tongue and died. There was also a man of Jinjiang named Wang Wu, a fine writer of considerable reputation. One day Wang Wu brought wine to Chengtian Temple to drink, and going into the sutra hall he saw a young novice monk sitting upright there reading a sutra. Wang Wu ordered him to drink, and when the novice refused, Wang Wu embraced and molested him. On the third day after Wang Wu returned home, he suddenly began striking his own face, reviling himself, and bit through his tongue, dying in a pool of blood.
The deaths of Xu Zhaoxin and Wang Wu were only their retribution in this present life; their true retribution lies in hell!
Story Nine:

Once there was a man who had done evil all his life. One night a kinsman of his was lodging in his house, and heard two voices speaking. One said, “The master of this house has filled the measure of his evil; he ought now to receive his retribution!” The other said, “Is the master of this house to suffer the retribution of having no sons or grandsons?” The first answered, “That retribution is too heavy!” The other said, “Then is he to suffer the retribution of fire?” The first answered, “That retribution is too light!” The other said, “Oh — then it is Wang Xiaoxiao!” The first answered, “Yes, it is Wang Xiaoxiao!” The kinsman who was lodging there heard these words and was much astonished, though he did not know what they meant. Several years later, the master of the house became infatuated with a prostitute named Wang Xiaoxiao and brought her home as his wife, yielding to her in everything and following her every word. And sure enough, Wang Xiaoxiao estranged him from his own flesh and blood, drained away his family fortune, and he died.
Story Ten:

There was a monk named Xingyun. Once, when he saw a lotus flower, a lustful thought suddenly stirred in him; and that very night a woman knocked at his door. Xingyun opened it and saw a woman standing outside with a maid beside her, who announced, “I am Lady Lotus.” The woman's beauty was radiant and surpassing, and Xingyun, overjoyed, fell into tender and lingering talk with her. Presently the candle went out; and the attendant in the next room heard Xingyun crying out in torment, and the woman saying to him in a stern voice, “Why did you let a lustful mind arise in vain? If I were truly a woman, I would never consent to lie with you!” At this the attendant ran at once to gather the other monks of the temple, and together they broke down the door and rushed in; and they saw only two yakṣas — and Xingyun's head was already parted from his body!

The cases of calamity brought on by lust related above begin with the case of the scholar of Guixi, and it is precisely there that the profound meaning of the Most High's words — “to let a thought arise is already to make her your own” — is set forth, urging men to hold a heart of reverence from the very outset, and, when the eye sees and the heart stirs, to take an even firmer and more urgent grip upon themselves. Yet the case of Xingyun told here is not a matter of the mind arising at the sight of beauty, but of a man building images out of his own fancy for no reason at all, like mirage towers raised without any clam, or a marketplace conjured where there is no sea. Such dark and phantom evil of the mind is simply a man seeking out his own suffering and hunting his own death! In the end the yakṣas came to his door and killed him — so monstrous and strange a disaster is truly cruel and grievous beyond words. Who can read the case of Xingyun without his heart turning cold and his courage failing? That he is made the conclusion has a deep meaning in it. I beg you all to ponder it carefully!

All the stories told above are the bitter, cruel retributions that come of sexual misconduct; what follows are the blessings and good rewards that come of abstaining from lust and repenting of such sins.

In his youth Tang Gao applied himself with vigor to his studies. One night, as he sat reading under the lamp in his study, a beautiful young woman, unable to restrain herself, tried to tease and entice him and tore a hole in the paper window of his study. Tang Gao at once mended the paper and wrote a verse upon it: “A papered window torn is easy to mend; a hidden virtue injured is hard to amend.” Some time after this, one evening at dusk, a monk passing by Tang Gao's gate saw a plaque of the top laureate hanging above the door, with two lanterns hung to either side bearing two lines of verse — the very verse Tang Gao had written on the paper window. The monk found it very strange and asked Tang Gao what it meant. Later Tang Gao indeed came first in the whole empire and was made top laureate.

Wang Tianyu once met a man of extraordinary gifts who read his physiognomy and said, “Your features are like an arhat's, yet you will have no son and will not live long.” Hearing this, Wang Tianyu ceased to set store by wealth and took pleasure in giving alms and doing good. One day, while he was a guest at Qingjiangpu, his host's wife — young and beautiful, and struck by his elegant bearing — came secretly to the room where he was staying; but Wang Tianyu shut the door fast and would not let her in, saying through the door, “How could I destroy your good name?” At these words the woman felt deeply ashamed and went away. Later Wang Tianyu again met the same man who had read his features, who said to him: “What hidden virtue have you accumulated! Your features have suddenly changed: I see that you will have a noble son, and that you will live to be more than eighty.” And in time it was exactly as the physiognomist had said: Wang Tianyu had a son who rose to high honor, and he himself lived past eighty.

When we look at the worthy men of old, we find that they were able to refuse women who came running to them and threw themselves into their arms. Some were strong through the single word “forbearance” — that is, not doing to others what one would not have done to oneself; others feared to injure their own hidden virtue, dreading that the sin would cut short their blessing and their years. Their learning may have differed in some respects, yet all alike accorded with the rectitude of heavenly principle and the peace of the human heart; and for both parties concerned it was a way that left both whole. At such a moment, when blessing comes, the mind grows clear, and the joy of it is like already soaring up among the blue clouds — one need not wait for the reward to arrive before feeling glad. Yet the ways of refusing a woman who runs to one are not all the same, and a man must understand them thoroughly in advance, so that when he truly meets the case he will not be bewitched. There are many instances, to be sure, where a woman, sternly rebuked to her face, knows the difficulty and withdraws at once; but there are also cases where she is refused and still will not go. Lu Rong, for example, refused by pleading that his illness was not yet healed and so putting the matter off to another day; and if at such a time one may simply open the door and leave, then Cao Fen's leaving at once to lodge elsewhere may also be counted as handling it well. There are women, again, who threaten death: when Mao Lumen refused the maidservant who came running to him, she said, “If you will not consent, I have only death before me” — and still Mao Lumen was unmoved. And there are women who throw themselves at a man and, refused all night long, still will not go away: Doctor Chen, for instance, said again and again, “It must not be, it must not be,” and then pushed open the window and stood outside in the courtyard the whole night, vowing never to do anything improper. There are also cases where a man firmly refused the temptation of a gift of a hundred taels of gold, and would on no account lie with the giver. Such lofty moral purity and such clear-sighted resolve are worthy of our imitation. If the door of the room is already shut and the woman still keeps watch and waits outside, then on no account may the door be opened. The next morning a man should make some excuse, take his leave, and go home; and if the other party still invites him to come back, he must on no account return. Yet he must never speak of the matter so long as he lives — not even to his own wife may he reveal it — and only then is he a gentleman of abundant virtue. From this he will pass the examinations and win rank, hold high office, bring glory to his ancestors, and shed blessing on his descendants; and compared with gaining the same by other means of piling up merit, the difference in difficulty is very great indeed!

Formerly in Zhejiang there was a commandant who engaged a tutor to come to his house and teach his sons. The tutor once caught a chill and had to sweat the illness out before he could recover, so the commandant told his son to bring a quilt to cover him. It happened that a shoe of the commandant's wife had been rolled up inside the quilt by mistake. When the tutor recovered, he returned the quilt, and the shoe that had been tucked inside it fell out beside the mat; neither the tutor nor the commandant's son noticed it, but the commandant did. The commandant then suspected that his wife and his sons' tutor were carrying on an illicit affair, and his wife, denying it, was deeply aggrieved. The commandant sent a maidservant, pretending to convey his wife's bidding, to invite the tutor to a meeting; the tutor was very angry when he heard it and berated the maid. The commandant then forced his wife to go in person, while he himself hid by the door with a sharp blade in his hand, waiting for the tutor to open it. But the tutor refused to open the door, saying to the lady, “Your husband has honored me by engaging me to teach your children; how could I do such an immoral thing?” To the end the tutor would not open the door. At dawn the next day he made an excuse to take his leave of the commandant, saying that he could no longer teach the children. The commandant said to him, “Sir, you are truly a gentleman of integrity!” and then told him the whole truth, apologized, and earnestly urged him to stay. That same year the tutor passed the examinations and won rank.

In Yugan there was a physician named Chen, whose medical skill was of a high order. A poor man fell ill and was at the point of death, and Doctor Chen cured him, never seeking any reward. Some time afterwards, one evening, he passed by the man's house, and the man invited him to stay the night. The man's mother said to her daughter-in-law, “It was he who saved your husband's life! Why do you not spend a night with him, and so repay his kindness?” Hearing her mother-in-law's words, the wife could only murmur her assent; and when night came she went to Doctor Chen's room. Doctor Chen refused her, saying, “Your mother-in-law would not approve of your doing this!” The wife said, “But this is my mother-in-law's own wish!” Doctor Chen said again, “But your husband would not approve of your doing this!” The wife said, “My husband's life was saved by you, so I have no need of his consent!” Doctor Chen said, “This must not be done.” The wife then tried to force him, and Doctor Chen said again and again, “It must not be! It must not be!” So he sat until dawn, and taking up his brush he wrote the two words ‘Must not’ over and over upon the table. At last, when he was all but unable to master himself, he cried aloud once more, “These two words, ‘Must not’, are truly the hardest of all!” Then he pushed open the window and went out to stand in the courtyard, and did not leave until the sky was light. Afterwards Doctor Chen's son went to seek official rank, and the chief examiner was about to strike out and reject that son's essay, when suddenly he heard a cry of “Must not!” come through the air, and so he read the paper over once more. Just as he was again about to strike it out, he heard “Must not! Must not!” cried out in succession from the air; at last the examiner read the paper through once more, and still decided to reject it; when suddenly he again heard a great cry from the air saying, “These two words, ‘Must not’, are truly the hardest of all!” and the cry went on without cease, and for that reason the chief examiner admitted Doctor Chen's son. In after years Doctor Chen's son in due course passed the imperial examination and became a presented scholar.

All the cases related above are instances of a mind established in unselfishness; yet since cases in which heavenly principle and human desire did battle were lacking, this account of steadfastness on the very brink of disorder has been set down, to serve as a model for later ages.

In Jinhua there was a man named Qi Wang. He had reached the age of fifty and still had no son. A physiognomist said to him, “There is an evil air upon your face; you must have done something against your conscience.” Qi Wang said, “In my youth I committed sexual misconduct, and in hidden places where no one could see I violated the wives and daughters of others.” The physiognomist said in alarm, “For sins of this kind a man ought to be cut off from descendants altogether! You must know that of all sins sexual misconduct is the hardest to repent of; nothing but the accumulation of great goodness can turn back the will of Heaven.” Qi Wang accordingly reformed and repented. In the first year, whenever others wished to do a good deed, he gladly gave, and never stinted; the physiognomist said, “What you have done is not yet enough.” Another year passed; whenever he met with a good deed that was hard to do, Qi Wang was always the first to contribute, and what he gave was more than half of the whole; the physiognomist said, “What you have done is still not enough.” In the third year Qi Wang performed good deeds single-handed, unwilling to let others have a share. The physiognomist said, “The lines of hidden virtue have appeared upon your face; you need no longer worry about being without a son.” In the end Qi Wang did indeed beget a son, and when he reached the age of seventy he could still dandle his grandson in his arms.

In the Ming dynasty there was a man named Lu Qing, who by habit loved to talk of lewd matters and to peep at women. By the time he was thirty his family was utterly poor, and his two sons died one after the other. One day Lu Qing suddenly dropped dead, and he saw his grandfather, who said to him in great anger, “Our family has accumulated goodness for two generations, and by your destiny you should have enjoyed wealth of tens of thousands; but you set your heart on beauty, and your mouth and your eyes alike created evil, until your store of blessings was all but exhausted. I feared that you would truly commit the evil of sexual misconduct, and that then there would be no hope for the descendants of our Lu family; therefore I begged and implored the King of the Underworld to have you seized and brought to the courts of the dead to see for yourself, so that you might know what is at stake.” Lu Qing said, “I have heard that to violate the wives and daughters of others brings the retribution of ending one's line; in truth I was much afraid of that retribution, and so I never committed it!” A judge of the underworld beside him said, “As if it were only the ending of one's line! If a woman comes of her own accord to entice a man, and he simply follows the current and does not refuse her, the sin is no more than the ending of his line. But if a man himself lures and forces others, and does so again and again; if he destroys the moral order of other families and causes them to abort, to kill their children, to kill their husbands, what monstrous crimes are these, and how should they be only the ending of one's line? As for the sin of sexual misconduct, the laws of the world of the living punish it far too lightly, but the laws of the world of shadows are the strictest of all. The moment a man stirs a lustful thought, the Three Corpse Spirits report it, and the Kitchen God and the City God make truthful memorials of it; and if they conceal or omit anything, that is a grave fault. Look at today's judgment, and you will know.” After a while the ghost attendants brought many criminals who had committed the sin of sexual misconduct before the hall; all of them were in chains and kneeling on the ground, and the King of the Underworld gave his orders in a stern voice: “So-and-so is to become a beggar, mad and mute; so-and-so is to become a prostitute and blind; so-and-so is to be an ox for two lifetimes; so-and-so is to be a pig for ten lifetimes.” When the King of the Underworld had finished giving his orders, the ghost attendants dragged them out to be reborn. Lu Qing was so frightened that his hair stood on end. The underworld judge said, “There are worse things than this! You must never covet a moment's pleasure and so lose your human body; you should shun license as you would shun an arrow, and you should print and distribute essays to warn the world.” Before long the King of the Underworld sent Lu Qing back to the world of the living. Lu Qing then printed ten thousand copies of A Record of a Journey through the Underworld to warn people, and did his utmost to do good; by the time he was forty he had two sons in succession, and his household was worth tens of thousands, exceedingly wealthy. Lu Qing then resolved to cut himself off from worldly ties, and went to the Southern Sea to cultivate the Way. This record was made for him by Cai Jing, a fellow townsman of Lu Qing.

The two cases related above are both good rewards won by repentance of sexual misconduct; for men who have already stumbled they steady the resolve to repent, and this too is a way of turning calamity into blessing. Alas! The sin of lust cannot be fully written nor fully told with brush and speech. All we can do is hope each day that whether a man be clever or dull, whether he has never committed the fault or has already committed it, each will deeply reflect and search himself, and discover his own heavenly conscience betimes; that is all.
To owe another goods or money and have no wish to repay them; instead, to wish him dead, so that the debt need not be paid.

To owe means that in a time of want one borrows for an urgent need; but as the days lengthen one no longer wishes to repay, and by so doing one betrays the kindness of the one who lent to meet that need. The Scripture of Central Admonition says, “If one owes another money or goods and is not yet able to repay, one should keep it firmly in mind and constantly consider how it may be returned. But if, in order to avoid repaying, one wishes the other dead, so as to wipe out the fact of one's debt, such a mind is that of a jackal and a wolf even now, and in the life to come it can by no means escape the retribution of repaying as a dog or a horse. Is this not stupidity of the utmost degree?”

Bai Yuantong owed Yang Yun four thousand five hundred cash, and Yang Yun pressed him for payment again and again; but Bai Yuantong never repaid it. Later a donkey was born in Yang Yun's household, and this donkey suddenly spoke in human speech, saying, “I am Bai Yuantong. Because I owed your family four thousand five hundred cash, I have taken the form of this donkey. Now the shop in the West Market that sells donkeys also owes me money, and the sum happens to be exactly four thousand five hundred cash; sell me to him at once, and so the debt I owe your family will be cleared!” When Yang Yun's son heard this he did as the donkey said, and after the donkey had been sold to the donkey shop it died two days later.

In the Han dynasty there was a man named Yan Chang, who served in the commandery office as a subordinate official. The governor of the commandery at that time was named Diwu Chang. Having been summoned by the court on business, he left a million three hundred thousand in accumulated salary in Yan Chang's keeping, entrusting him with its safekeeping, and Yan Chang buried the money in the ground. Later, when Diwu Chang was near death, he called to his side his only grandson, then just nine years old, and told him, “I have three hundred thousand in cash left in the keeping of the official Yan Chang.” When the grandson grew up he went to call on Yan Chang and asked him to return the money his grandfather had left with him. Yan Chang, seeing Diwu Chang's grandson, was both grieved and glad, and at once brought out the money to return to him; and the seals and markings on it were exactly as before, never having been opened. After counting it the grandson said, “My grandfather said there were only three hundred thousand, yet here are a million three hundred thousand; this extra million I dare not take.” Yan Chang said, “Your grandfather must have spoken mistakenly when he was gravely ill; you need have no doubt of it.” With that he returned the whole sum to Diwu Chang's grandson. Afterwards Yan Chang was promoted, and rose to be a provincial governor.
Whenever one begs or entrusts something to another, if it cannot be granted as one wishes, cursing and resentment arise.

The gentleman understands principle, and rejoices in Heaven and accepts his lot; therefore he does not lightly beg or entrust matters to others. If he lightly begs and entrusts things to others, he is already no true gentleman. And if, having asked a favor, he cannot have it as he wishes, he should only turn and examine himself well; but if for that reason he curses and hates the other, then he has truly become a petty man through and through.

In the Song dynasty a certain Mr. Lu came by night with a hundred taels of gold and offered them to the then prime minister Wang Dan, asking Wang Dan to help him obtain the post of transportation commissioner for Jianghuai. Wang Dan said to him, “Your ability is not yet sufficient to bear this office. Though we are friends, I dare not set aside public duty for private feeling!” Hearing Wang Dan's words, Mr. Lu felt ashamed, and took his gold and left the prime minister's residence. From then on, at dusk each day, he burned incantations, hoping that Wang Dan would soon die. One night he dreamed that a spirit rebuked him, saying, “Wang Dan is loyal to his country, yet you curse him to die soon; on this account the High God has sent down a judgment, and you will be punished before long.” Sure enough, within a few days Mr. Lu was dead.

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, “When I ask a favor of another, my own situation may be most urgent; yet the person I ask may lack the power to help, or may be hindered by circumstances. Then of ten requests nine will fail and only one succeed, and this is but the ordinary way of things. If for that reason I recklessly curse and resent the other, will he change his whole manner and turn about to sympathize with me and help me because of my cursing and resentment? This only adds to one's own afflictions in vain. Such a person not only does not know the will of Heaven, but does not understand the ways of the world either.”

Xie Liangzuo of the Song dynasty said, “All things in this world have, in truth, their appointed measure; human strength cannot reckon against it. In all my life I have never asked a favor of anyone, nor written a single letter to a great officer of the government. Someone urged me to do so, saying that only thus might I be promoted, and I said to him, ‘How could he promote me? If I am promoted, it is because I have the destiny to be an official.’”

Fan Zhongxuan of the Song dynasty said, “Though a man be utterly foolish, he appears altogether clever when he is blaming others; though a man be utterly clever, he appears altogether muddled when he is forgiving himself. Know then that if a man could blame himself with the mind with which he blames others, and forgive others with the mind with which he forgives himself, then he need not fear that he cannot become a sage or a worthy.” All those who, when their requests to others fail, give rise to cursing and hatred, ought to ponder again and again the words of these two gentlemen.
To see another meet with a setback or a disappointment, and to say that this is the evil retribution called down by his past faults.

A setback means meeting with what cannot be done, being placed in a position where one's aims are thwarted. The affairs and circumstances of this world are by nature such that failure is easy and success hard, that adverse conditions are many and favorable ones few. Sometimes one's time and fortune are out of joint, so that all one does goes amiss; sometimes one has by chance committed a fault, and it is too late to mend it even with regret. Alas! The hardships of the world and the difficulty of success have drawn this lament from every age. Yet there is a kind of person who has no human feeling: in ordinary days he loves to associate with others for the sake of appearances, but when a friend meets with difficulty or suffers a failure, he time and again keeps himself out of the affair, and moreover stands by mocking and thwarting him, saying, “This was all brought about by his own fault!” Alas! Let such a person reflect carefully: can it be that in all his life he has never once done a single thing amiss?

In the Ming dynasty there was a man of Hanzhou named Wang Sheng, who loved to point out the faults of others. A neighbor of his lost a son, and Wang Sheng reproached the neighbor, saying, “It is just because you have done evil that you have this retribution!” Before long Wang Sheng had two sons, but both fell ill and died young.
