The neighbor in turn mocked him, saying, “I should say your evil is graver than mine, since both your sons have died!” Again, Wang Sheng's elder cousin of the same clan was ranked in the fourth class in the annual examination, and Wang Sheng reproached him too, saying, “Your essay is too absurd; how could you hope to be ranked in the upper class?” In less than a year Wang Sheng also sat the examination, and his rank came out as fifth class; his elder cousin in turn mocked him, saying, “No doubt my younger clansman's essay is even more absurd than mine, since he has been ranked in the fifth class!”

Guan Zhong said, “I once took counsel together with Bao Shu, yet I only grew poorer, and Bao Shu did not think me stupid; for he knew that times may be favorable or unfavorable. Three times I took office, and three times the ruler drove me out; yet Bao Shu did not think me unworthy, for he knew that I had met with an unpropitious time and could not put my ambitions into practice.” From this we see that even the heroes of antiquity often met with setbacks. What is precious is to have a friend who truly knows one, to encourage and console one in time of poverty and difficulty. How can one take advantage of another's slight failure to strike him when he is down? Such a person has not only lost the moral duty by which friends should pity one another, but has also turned his back on the humane heart by which they should support and encourage each other. Such a person rejoices in the misfortunes of others, is neither humane nor righteous, and so will surely draw disaster upon himself.
To see another with a maimed body or an ugly appearance, and instead of pitying, commiserating with and protecting him, to mock him.

When a man's limbs are maimed or his appearance is ugly, either he committed evil in a former life, or it is a calamity inherited from his parents. Meeting such a person, one ought to pity, commiserate with and protect him; how could one have the heart to mock him? Moreover, whether a man can establish himself and achieve anything depends on his capacity and understanding, not on his body and looks. Zhou Bo, though he stammered, rose to be prime minister; Yan Zi, though small of stature, was able to make his ruler illustrious. Examples of this kind are recorded in the histories and may be called too numerous to count. Furthermore, those whose bodies are imperfect are apt to feel bitterness toward themselves; if one laughs at them for that, one has trodden upon their sore spot. The mother of Duke Qing of Qi laughed at Que Ke, and Qi was thereby invaded; the favorite beauty of Lord Pingyuan of Zhao was put to death for laughing at a man with crippled feet; and in Zhao County a man was killed for laughing at Mengchang Jun as a petty fellow of small stature. These are all overturned carts before us, which we may take as mirrors.

The Buddhist scriptures speak of retribution in kind, meaning this: if a person in this life has a crooked mind, then life after life his body will be incomplete, his mouth twisted and his eyes askew, his four limbs maimed. That is to say, evil done in a former life has produced an imperfect body in this life. How then, when a thought arises in the mind, can one fail to be on guard and in fear, lest one's thoughts drift into depraved and perverse imaginings?

The Essentials of the Daoist Canon says, “In the marital relations of husband and wife there are many prohibitions, and they are especially strict when the weather and the solar terms change. For example, in the three days before the spring equinox, when thunder is about to sound and the solar term is changing, if one does not observe abstinence from marital relations at such a time, then any child born will be hard to bring to bodily completeness, and will surely meet with misfortune; for husband and wife at such a time profane the majesty of Heaven.” This is to say that parents, by want of care in their marital relations, bring about incompleteness of body in their children.

Lu Qi, a minister of the Tang dynasty, had a face both green and blue. Guo Ziyi once fell ill, and the officials of the court came one after another to his house to inquire after him, so that all of Guo Ziyi's concubines and maids came out to meet the visiting officials, and Guo Ziyi did not forbid it. But when Lu Qi arrived, Guo Ziyi dismissed all his concubines and maids and warned them not to come out. Someone asked him why. Guo Ziyi said, “Lu Qi is ugly of face and sinister of heart; if the women saw him they would certainly laugh at him. If one day he comes to power, then my household will surely suffer, and be wiped out by him!” Later Lu Qi did indeed become prime minister, and at that time he repaid every grudge against anyone who had ever offended him; only Guo Ziyi's family came through unscathed, suffering no revenge from Lu Qi.

Hou Yuangong was very ugly. When he had just passed the provincial examination, others, because he was rather old and ugly too, did not know to respect him; and some frivolous fellows painted his likeness upon a kite, and took the kite outside to fly it. When Hou Yuangong saw it he was not angry at all; instead he laughed, and wrote these lines upon the kite: “Who would believe my worth while I lie hidden and unknown? Only now are my name and traces made known. A craftsman, for no cause, has painted my likeness; riding the wind, it lightly borrows strength, and with one lift mounts into the high sky. Scarce blown and puffed, its body steadies by degrees, and one might think it bound for the moon palace. When the rain is done, the evening sun glows red: how many, standing on the flat ground, look up and watch me in the purple heights?” In that very year Hou Yuangong passed the examinations and won his degree, and in time rose to be prime minister. The people of his native place were much ashamed, and did not dare to meet him face to face.

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, “The body and looks a man is born with are in themselves nothing to be relied upon. To be bent and humpbacked, crippled and sick, none of these can be known in advance. Once the beautiful eye is pierced it goes blind; once the nimble foot is broken one becomes lame. Zengzi, when he was about to die, called his disciples to his bedside and said, ‘Open the blanket and look at my feet and hands. The Book of Songs says, “Be careful and cautious, as though standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as though treading upon thin ice.” Only from this day do I know that I may escape injury to my body.’ Zengzi's words remind us that the body, hair and skin are received from our parents, and that not daring to injure them is the beginning of filial piety. We have not even time enough to cherish our own bodies; how dare we go and mock others?”
To see another's ability, which may be praised and made known, and not only to withhold praise and not make it known, but to block and suppress him.

To see another's ability and suppress it differs from concealing his good deeds and thwarting his strong points. Concealment carries the sense of shutting a thing away in darkness, while thwarting carries the bitter pain of breaking and snapping, and this goes a step further still. For to withhold praise that might be given is suppression. Compared with concealing another's good deeds and thwarting his strong points, the guilt may seem a little lighter, yet the principle to be inferred from it grows finer and deeper the more it is examined.

In the Warring States period, Li Si and Han Fei were both students of Xun Qing. Li Si knew that his own ability was no match for Han Fei's. When the King of Qin read Han Fei's writings, such as The Difficulties of Persuasion, he wished he could meet Han Fei at once. Later the King of Han sent Han Fei on a mission to Qin, and the King of Qin talked with Han Fei with great delight and was exceedingly pleased. At this point Li Si, afraid that Han Fei would win the King of Qin's favor, spoke slander of Han Fei before the king, so that Han Fei was thrown into prison; and then he had Han Fei take poison and kill himself. Han Fei wished to plead his own case in person before the King of Qin, but Li Si gave him no chance to have audience with the king, and so Han Fei died in prison. Later Li Si was framed by the eunuch Zhao Gao and imprisoned, and Li Si too wished to plead his own case before the king; Zhao Gao likewise gave Li Si no chance to have audience with the king; and in the end Li Si's whole household was exterminated. Those who understand principle hold that this is the Way of Heaven returning good and ill, karmic retribution not erring in the slightest.

Sun Bian of the Song dynasty was a man of Meishan. He did not know Tang Jie or Wu Zhongfu, but because he admired their uprightness of character he recommended them strongly to the court, and on that account the two were promoted by the court to be censors. Zhang Xungong had never met Wen Lugong, that is Wen Yanbo, but having heard that Wen Yanbo was a man of open and honorable character, he recommended him with all his strength to the emperor the moment he met him; and later Wen Yanbo indeed became a general in the field and a minister at court, and his merit served the state. Yang Jingzhi cherished talent greatly, and learning that Xiang Si, a scholar of Jiangbiao, was outstanding in ability, he presented him with a poem: “Everywhere I see your poems, and all are good; but when I look upon your character, it surpasses the poems. All my life I could not bear to hide another's goodness; wherever I go I tell everyone of Xiang Si.” All these gentlemen were able to recommend, without the least selfishness, men of true ability who could serve their country and their people. Those who cannot win worthy men for the state not only block and beat down the worthy who come after them, but also cut off the seed by which blessings are sown for the common people. Hence we know that to recommend and win one man of talent for the state is a work of great goodness and utmost benevolence; and by the same token, to envy the worthy and able is a great evil.
To carve a wooden image of a man, write spells and charms upon it, and bury it in the ground, in order to work bewitchment and harm against others.

According to the Xuandu Code, “If a man accumulates two thousand seven hundred faults, a great harm will be born: in his household there will arise wizards and witches. Yet to be born a wizard or a witch is already to have committed sin in a former life; and now to use sorcery and evil arts to bury spells and work bewitchment against others deepens one's own sin all the more, and in the life to come one will fall into hell. And if a man with an evil mind, wishing to harm another, employs wizards and witches to bury spells and work bewitchment against him, then his sin is even graver than that of the wizards and witches themselves. Evil cults that use such sorcery of buried spells to harm others commit, by the laws of this world, a capital crime; and by the laws of the underworld it is graver still.”

In the Tang dynasty, Gongsun Chuo, the registrar of the Wangwu county office, had only just taken up his post when he suddenly dropped dead. One day he appeared in a dream to the county magistrate and said, “I have a grievance, and I beg Your Honor to redress it for me and clear my name. My life had not yet come to its appointed end; but I was done to death by the slaves of my household, who used the sorcery of buried spells, so that they might plunder my property. My old home is at Heyin. If Your Honor will secretly choose a few sharp and capable men and send them with a warrant to Heyin to make arrests, not one of them will slip the net. Beneath the eaves of my main hall, under the seventh row of tiles counting from the east, my image lies buried, carved of wutong wood and pinned with cloth; and after this length of time it has already begun to change.” The next day the magistrate did choose several sharp and capable subordinates and sent them with a warrant to Heyin county to make arrests; and he also wrote an official dispatch to inform the magistrate of Heyin county. All the slaves in Gongsun Chuo's household were arrested, and beneath the eaves of the hall a wooden figure more than a foot long was found, covered with nails, while the wood had gradually changed into flesh, and when struck it gave out a dull, hoarse sound; and all the millet and wheat in Gongsun Chuo's household had been stolen and sold by the slaves. The magistrate then reported the facts to the prefect, and had all the slaves put to death by the extreme penalty.

From ancient times the sorcery of bewitchment has mostly had its origin among women, slaves and concubines; for they wish by such means to shore up their own power, and hope to win favor and trust forever, and this desire is even more eager than the desire for profit. Therefore we should cultivate ourselves and regulate our households, guard the gates of our own homes, and not let sorcerers and members of evil cults come and go in the house, nor have dealings with them; this is the way to cut off the source. As for those who hold office, they too should intensify the search and strictly prohibit such sorcery and evil arts, so that they vanish utterly and no longer do harm in the world; the merit of this is very great.
It means to use poison to kill trees.

Every plant and tree in the world is a living vitality bestowed by Heaven and Earth. Gao Chai, a disciple of Confucius, could not bear to break off growing trees, and so Confucius praised Gao Chai for his compassion. The Buddha said, “When trees are old, spirits and gods perch upon them, and so they must not be cut down lightly; and to cut them down often brings disaster.” If cutting them down is not permissible, how much less is it to use poison to kill trees?

Ru Yunqu of Taoyuan was by nature sinister and cruel. Being at odds with a neighbor, he secretly poisoned to death all the fruit trees and other trees the neighbor had planted. One day, returning from a trip, Ru Yunqu in a daze saw lamplight flickering and heard the clangor of weapons, and he was bound by many soldiers and pushed along among the trees. A spirit rebuked him, saying, “Grass and trees too are lives bestowed by Heaven! How could you vent your anger upon them and kill them? Conduct such as yours comes mostly from the disharmony of your five viscera!” Thereupon he ordered the soldiers to cut open his belly and tear out his lungs and liver. At this Ru Yunqu woke in terror, and thereafter he contracted a strange disease of agonizing pain in the heart and belly, and died.

Chen Shi engaged a geomancer to examine his family's ancestral graves, and the geomancer saw a great tree in front of the graves, planted at someone else's grave site. The geomancer thought, “This blocks the heavenly heart; that tree must certainly be removed if there is to be any hope of passing the examinations.” So he urged Chen Shi to buy some fish bones and secretly poison the tree to death. Chen Shi, however, refused to do so, saying, “Both of us are only seeking good fortune, and besides, this tree grows so luxuriantly; how could I have the heart to kill it?” In less than a year the tree was by chance blown up by a great wind, roots and all, and so the heavenly heart that the tree had blocked was suddenly opened wide. Chen Shi's son Chen Kui thereafter passed his examinations in quick succession, and rose to be a censor.
To feel resentment and anger toward one's teacher because of his reproof and instruction.

Anger toward a teacher is not the same as to slight one's teacher: slighting means to treat him with disrespect for no reason and without cause, whereas here it is to conceive resentment and anger toward him because of his reproof and instruction. In ancient times the rule by which a disciple served his teacher was that he might not offend his elder, nor conceal his own faults from him; whenever the teacher gave reproof or guidance, he ought to receive it with an open mind and a gentle spirit. How could he feel resentment and anger toward the teacher? If a man resents and rages at his teacher for reproof, he must be a person of slight virtue and no blessing.

Wang Huidao of the Ming dynasty was by nature exceptionally clever: he could read a book once and never forget it, and could recite it at once; by the age of eight he could write essays. Yet his manner in serving his teacher was extraordinarily arrogant; at the slightest displeasure he would curse his teacher furiously behind his back. One day, sitting alone in his study, he suddenly yawned, and out of his mouth jumped a ghost, which pointed at him and said, “Wang Huidao, you might have taken first place in the empire and passed as the chief graduate; but because you resent and rage at your teacher and show no respect to your elders, the High God has already struck your name from the register of emolument, and I too shall leave you from this day on!” Having spoken, the ghost vanished. When Wang Huidao then read over the books he had studied before, he did not know a single character.

Wei Zhao, a great scholar of the Eastern Han, when young met Guo Linzong and thought, “A teacher of texts is easy to meet, but a teacher of men is hard to come by.” So he asked to attend upon Guo Linzong and do the work of sweeping and cleaning. Guo Linzong once fell ill and ordered Wei Zhao to cook porridge; when the gruel was ready, Wei Zhao brought it to Guo Linzong to eat. Guo Linzong then shouted at Wei Zhao, saying, “In cooking gruel for one's elder, if one does not serve it with attentive respect, it makes the elder unable to eat!” Wei Zhao cooked the porridge again and served it with respect; and Guo Linzong scolded him in the same way three times over, yet Wei Zhao's countenance did not change in the slightest. Then Guo Linzong said to him, “At first I saw only your face; from this day on I know your heart.”

Deng Zhi of the Song dynasty was a private school teacher who was good at using methods of guidance and encouragement to teach his students; the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty never left his lips, and whenever he met anyone he would earnestly and wholeheartedly explain and guide them. In the reign of Emperor Shenzong, his eldest son Deng Wan became a Hanlin academician, and his second son Deng Ji together with two grandsons all passed the metropolitan examination in the same list. Everyone said, “This is the good reward won by Deng Zhi's wholehearted and utterly sincere teaching.” Broadly speaking, the temper of ordinary children can mostly be changed by teaching within a short time; yet there are also children spoiled and unruly by nature, prone to go astray and to be lazy, and these depend upon their teacher to guide them with skillful means, so that they understand principle and awaken and turn back early.
To clash with and offend one's father and elder brothers.

The clash spoken of here differs from the secretly insulting mentioned above: the sin of secretly insulting one's ruler or parents is hidden and deep, while the sin of clashing with father and elder brother is quite plain. Any slight sign of insubordination in word or deed is a clash. You must know that father and elder brother stand first among the five human relationships, and that filial piety and fraternal duty come first among the ways of man. Therefore toward one's father and elder brother one should be respectful and compliant, with a gentle voice and a cheerful countenance. Even if a father is somewhat partial, or an elder brother bullies and tramples upon one, one can only explain matters with patience and forbearance, and examine and cultivate oneself. Should the father or elder brother still cling to delusion and refuse to change, one must keep a peaceful and even heart; and in time one will naturally feel that such conduct is thorough and fitting. But if one harbors even a little anger, one will surely commit the sin of clashing with father and elder brother, and so violate the moral order and rebel against the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty, and be intolerable to Heaven and Earth.

In the Ming dynasty there was a man of Ehu named Fei Hong. Once, while playing chess with a friend who had ranked with him in the same year’s examination, the two contended against each other and Fei Hong jokingly slapped his friend, who was displeased. Fei Hong deeply regretted it and went to his friend’s house every day to beg forgiveness, yet his friend would never come out to meet him. When Fei Hong’s father learned of this he was angry, sealed up a bamboo board, and sent a man to deliver it to the capital, instructing Fei Hong to strike himself with it. Fei Hong then took his father’s letter and the bamboo board to his friend’s house and flogged himself three times; only then did the friend come out to meet him, and the two threw their arms about each other and wept. Fei Hong said: ‘This is the wrong I committed—why are you weeping too?’ The friend said: ‘You still have a father to urge and reprove you, while I can no longer find even one to urge and reprove me!’ From that time on the two were as affectionate as before.

From this we may see that even after his father had passed away he was still moved to grief over such a matter—so we know that while his father was living he could never have had the heart to offend him. Yet today, although many fathers are still alive, the time we share with them is not necessarily long! The brevity of life and the certainty of parting, when we reflect on them, wrench the heart. How can we fail to be filial, respectful, and reverent?

Cui Xiaowei, a man of the Later Wei, served his elder brother Xiaofen with great reverence and gentleness; in sitting, standing, advancing, and withdrawing, he followed his elder brother’s commands in everything. Not a single coin or a foot of cloth did he ever take into his own private stores, and the women of the household too loved one another—a situation rarely to be seen in the world today!

The Ming scholar Yan Maoyou said: ‘People today are unfilial to their parents simply because they are unwilling to search their hearts and reflect. Consider only this: where does your body come from? Where will your parents go in the end? Since the new branches and leaves have already grown forth, the old root is about to wither! We use only the most ordinary food and drink to support our parents and make them glad—how can that repay so much as one ten-thousandth of their kindness? If we think in this way often, the filial heart will naturally arise.’ He also said: ‘People today do not honor their elder brothers simply because they are unwilling to turn the mind back and ask themselves. Just think of the vast and boundless universe—how short a time since I came into being! And in the boundless sea of humanity, how many are truly one’s own blood brothers? Grown up together in childhood, playing together, in old age we ought to support one another; so the affection between brothers naturally becomes sincere. If people would but take these two stories of Fei Hong and Cui Xiaowei, together with the words of Mr. Yan, and read and ponder them deeply, they would naturally be moved to tears streaming down both cheeks, and their true nature of filial piety and fraternal love would be set fully before them. So why need the retributions for offending one’s father and elder brother be listed again?’
